title: Lib Dems use conference to set out £2bn plan to cut fuel duty
author: Peter Walker; Alexandra Topping
content:
The Liberal Democrats have used their conference to unveil a £2bn plan to cut fuel duty, part of a series of policy proposals intended to tackle worries that not enough voters know what Ed Davey’s party stands for.
The proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period came as polling showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which only launched as a political party in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – to their 71.
Davey will set out the fuel duty idea, along with a reduction in the £3 cap on bus fares to £1 and a 10% reduction in rail fares, in his main speech to the event in Brighton on Tuesday.
Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader and Treasury spokesperson, outlined in her speech on Sunday proposals to create economic growth through closer ties with Europe, part of an existing plan to try to rejoin the EU single market.
In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.
His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.
“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”
While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about anyone challenging Davey, some say they are frustrated that the party’s message is too vague and is not being heard by voters, a phenomenon highlighted in polling by More in Common, which was presented at the conference.
One key finding was widespread uncertainty among many voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea of this, lower than that for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed just over a year ago by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.
Other parts of the research showed that just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, versus 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.
One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event at which the findings were presented that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its messaging.
The More in Common research found that the strongest predictor of support for the Lib Dems was a local branch of the upmarket bakery chain Gail’s, with the party doing five times as well in the 2024 general election in the least deprived parts of the country than the most deprived.
after newsletter promotion
“If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south.
Most of Davey’s MPs nonetheless note that he has delivered the party’s best election result for a century, and many expect this total to grow further at the next election even though they have flatlined in national polls, in part due to heavy tactical voting.
But some at the conference do privately say they would like a bit more. “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election,” one longtime party activist said.
“It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”
summary: At their party conference, the Liberal Democrats announced a £2bn plan to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for three months, alongside reductions in bus and rail fares. The policy launch follows polling revealing that many voters remain uncertain about what the party stands for and that its messaging lags behind other political groups. Despite these concerns and static national polls, leader Ed Davey defended the party's impact, pointing to consistent local election successes.
key_points: The Lib Dems unveiled a £2bn plan to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for three months.
Additional transport proposals include reducing the bus fare cap to £1 and cutting rail fares by 10%.
Polling presented at the conference showed only 39% of voters have an idea what the Lib Dems stand for.
Research indicated the party performs significantly better in less deprived areas than in the most deprived parts of the country.
Ed Davey defended the party's relevance, citing eight consecutive years of council election victories.

title: Minister dismisses Burnham’s past Trump criticism as ‘politics’ ahead of meeting
author: Athena Stavrou
content:
A government minister has dismissed Andy Burnham’s previous comments about Donald Trump as “politics” ahead of the prime minister’s expected meeting with the US president.
The prime minister is set to travel to New York for the UN general assembly, in one of his most important trips abroad since taking over from Sir Keir Starmer.
Mr Burnham will reportedly meet the US president on the sidelines of the event, in what will be their first in-person conversation and a major diplomatic moment.
They will likely discuss a number of difficult topics, including the UK’s sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements, Ukraine and the war in the Middle East.
Speaking to broadcasters on Sunday, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson was asked whether the encounter could prove awkward in light of past remarks, including Mr Burnham’s 2021 assertion that “any politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now”.
“Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics, and the president knows that,” Ms Phillipson, who is also equalities minister, told Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme.
Mr Trump has been largely positive about Mr Burnham’s first weeks as prime minister, after relations with his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, dramatically deteriorated in the final months of his tenure.
![Donald Trump was amongst the first world leaders Mr Burnham spoke to after taking office](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/afcdcc0632f721455b4acf466d3c8b16Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTM2Nzkw-2.85361099.jpg)
The leaders have spoken twice on the phone since Mr Burnham became prime minister, but have recently been at odds over major issues including the Falkland Islands and Northern Ireland.
During his tenure as the mayor of Manchester, Mr Burnham heavily criticised Mr Trump, insisting he would not be welcome in the city and claiming that he had a “poisonous” politics.
He later climbed down on the comments, telling reporters in August he “tries to find common ground” with other politicians.
“Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style,” he said.
I don’t know, I think I see that he was, I guess, the mayor of a town. I hear he’s extremely liberal, extremely, so that means he probably won’t open up the North Sea
He added that he was “looking forward to meeting in person” and said he had a “good phone call” with the US president on his first day in office.
Shortly before Mr Burnham was confirmed as Britain’s new prime minister, Mr Trump described him as an “extremely liberal” politician who was “mayor of a town”, and “probably won’t open up” the North Sea for further oil and gas drilling.
Mr Trump was among the first world leaders Mr Burnham spoke to after taking office, with the prime minister having extended an invitation to Manchester to the president, as the pair discussed football, defence and the war in the Middle East.
![Burham said he would ‘find a connection’ with Trump](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/12/362fd848847ad5aa7c62a3da051490d2Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NjQyNTEx-2.85793891.jpg)
Mr Trump later claimed the prime minister had pledged to “open up the North Sea” in the phone call.
He said: “He said he’s going to open up North Sea oil. If he does that, you’re going to be a wealthy country.”
Mr Burnham meanwhile said the first exchange was positive, describing the US president as “really warm”.
Last week, the pair held their second phone call, where they agreed on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire” in Ukraine, and Mr Burnham briefed Mr Trump on plans to implement a trade ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements.
He said he’s going to open up North Sea oil. If he does that, you’re going to be a wealthy country
Notably, the US president did not publicly respond to the sanctions.
But the prime minister has been forced to hit back at Mr Trump on several occasions, particularly on issues concerning the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Northern Ireland.
The US president has previously indicated he might not back the UK’s sovereignty over the Falklands if Argentina launched an attack, after Argentina’s president Javier Milei, an ally of Mr Trump, reiterated his country’s claim to the islands in a national televised address.
In response, Mr Burnham said the UK would be “relentless” in defending the Falkland islanders’ right to be British.
The president then waded into the dispute again during a visit to Dublin, when he suggested the UK would not “be willing to travel that far” if Argentina invaded the Falklands as it did in 1982.
![The US president claimed unification was inevitable as he spoke to reporters in Ireland](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/12/01M2DY8JDD52M86QE008MQGQKM.jpg)
He also called Mr Burnham “a very nice guy” but on “on the liberal side” on his visit, but opened up a fresh political row over Northern Ireland.
The US president claimed Irish unification was inevitable as he spoke to reporters alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin, adding it “may as well happen now”.
He said: “I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.”
In response, Downing Street pointed to comments from Mr Burnham rejecting the prospect of an immediate border poll.
summary: Government minister Bridget Phillipson has dismissed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s past criticism of Donald Trump as standard politics ahead of their anticipated first in-person meeting at the UN general assembly. The leaders are expected to discuss complex international topics, including Ukraine, Middle East conflicts, and trade bans on illegal Israeli settlements. While their initial phone calls were positive, the pair have recently disagreed on issues such as Northern Ireland and the Falkland Islands.
key_points: Cabinet minister Bridget Phillipson dismissed Andy Burnham's previous remarks about Donald Trump as politics ahead of their meeting at the UN general assembly.
Mr Burnham and Donald Trump are expected to discuss difficult topics including Ukraine, the Middle East, and UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements.
The two leaders have previously clashed over major geopolitical issues, including the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and the future of Northern Ireland.
Despite past criticism—such as Mr Burnham's 2021 remarks—both leaders have described recent phone calls positively, with Mr Trump praising the prime minister as a nice guy.

title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
author: AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul
content:
![The BBC's Laura Kuenssberg sits opposite Earl Spencer in a room at the Althorp estate.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/f04c/live/5fddaaf0-b506-11f1-91cc-c5691e33b858.png)
- Published
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".
In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".
Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.
In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".
Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.
Earl initially told Diana's crash was 'not too serious'
Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.
He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious".
But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister.
"And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."
Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's death
Earl Spencer describes 'giddy tone' in Charles' voice during call after Diana's death
Describing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle.
"I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC.
"I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."
In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla.
When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility."
![A graphic featuring Princess Diana and her brother, Earl Spencer, with the text "Princess Diana My Sister's Story".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d128/live/483b6a00-b451-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday
Comments 'will not be a surprise' to William and Harry
Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end.
Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it.
"I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."
He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'."
"I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate.
![Prince William and Prince Harry bow their heads as their mother's coffin leaves her funeral service](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/9423/live/36d10f10-b4ef-11f1-947c-4906c0564be0.jpg)
Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffin
Responding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.
"I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life.
"I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said.
"I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."
The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment.
When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"
On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.
He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments.
'I know lots of things about the King' not in the book
Talking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties.
"I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained.
"This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."
When put to him that the statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."
Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book.
"It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied.
"It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister. And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."
![Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex arrive to meet volunteer first responders from Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, during a visit to Bondi Beach](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/3fe7/live/df9ce1a0-b4ef-11f1-947c-4906c0564be0.jpg)
Earl Spencer said he was concerned about security for Duke and Duchess of Sussex
Harry and Meghan's media treatment 'echoes' Diana
When asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family, Earl Spencer told the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security.
"I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said.
"As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."
It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.
When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant".
"It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said.
"[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."
![Prince Harry and Prince William, left, follow the hearse with the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II moving towards St. George's Chapel](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/77c3/live/38e071a0-b4f0-11f1-947c-4906c0564be0.jpg)
The earl said he hopes his nephews resolve their differences
'I hope William and Harry resolve row'
Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry.
"I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said.
"And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."
He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage".
"I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all â I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said.
Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interview
Reflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997.
Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.
A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.
Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana.
"People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there. And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."
The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.
The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."
Earl supports 'a modern monarchy'
Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy".
Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."
When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."
He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."
An emotional tribute to a sister he misses every day
Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister Diana
As the interview came to an end, Earl Spencer was asked whether he would ever be able to get over his sister's death.
Visibly emotional, he said he misses Diana "every day", adding "that's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it."
But his upcoming book, he said, is a way for him to have a final say on Diana's life before stepping off "into the sunset".
"One of the reasons I called this Swan Song actually is because it's my sign off," he said.
"I have been Diana's brother, this is my final take on the situationâ¦ I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, a celebration of her."
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
  - Published2 days ago
 ![Earl Spencer](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/906/cpsprodpb/9ab3/live/011a4280-b380-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
  - Published3 days ago
 ![A young Prince William stands next to Earl Spencer, a young Prince Harry and Charles at Diana's funeral. They are all wearing dark suits with ties and are facing ahead solemnly.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/c3f8/live/92718a00-b1fe-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
- ![Prince Charles](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/1636/live/3b051820-ae7d-11f0-ba75-093eca1ac29b.jpg)
- ![King Charles wears a sandy-coloured overcoat and white shirt while attending a service at the Church of St Mary the Virgin, close to the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, England, on 26 January, 2025.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/b7ef/live/d4c7ce40-a8fa-11f0-92db-77261a15b9d2.jpg)
summary: Earl Spencer defended his new memoir about his late sister, Princess Diana, stating that writing it was his duty as an eyewitness to history. In a BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg, he reiterated claims that then-Prince Charles made a callous remark about Diana's death during a phone call after an argument over her funeral procession. Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on the assertion, stating that grief can cloud memory, but the earl insisted his account is accurate.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.
Buckingham Palace responded that the King believes fraternal grief can affect judgment and colour memory over time.
The earl stated that he knows additional information about the King that he chose to leave out of the book because it was irrelevant.
He expressed concern over Prince Harry lacking police protection in the UK and noted parallels between press treatment of Harry and Meghan and the late Princess Diana.
Earl Spencer linked Diana's vulnerability before her death to the deceitful 1995 BBC Panorama interview conducted by Martin Bashir.

title: ‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton
author: Alexandra Topping; Peter Walker
content:
Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight.
“There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.”
Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend.
But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building.
Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. However, Babarinde, the Eastbourne MP, is taking aim at targets from big tech to crypto billionaires. “People are looking for a force to help break some of those giants and give power and cash back to people who this country is meant to be working for,” he says.
That people are seeking alternatives to the status quo is undeniable, but whether they are looking at the Liberal Democrats is a matter of debate.
The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months.
The Lib Dems gained 153 councillors in England in May and six seats in the Scottish parliament, although the party’s advances were more modest than those of the Greens and Reform UK. The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, also struggles to command attention. Lib Dem MPs grumble that Nigel Farage only has to sneeze to attract media covverage, while Davey has to resort to bungee jumping.
“You’ve got a very crowded multiparty system. You’ve got Reform saying any old shit in the media and getting coverage for it with no plan for delivering,” says Babarinde. “As Liberal Democrats, we’re not going to fall into that trap. But what we have got to be clear about is the diagnosis of the problem, who it is standing in the way and what needs to be done.”
He dismisses the idea that the party is yet to produce eye-catching retail policies – “There’s oodles and oodles of it!” – but says it needs to reach beyond its middle England strongholds with digital campaigning that is as strong as its much-envied ground game.
Babarinde, who has spoken about his mother being subjected to domestic abuse and how it shaped his politics, has experience engaging with hard-to-reach communities. He set up a social enterprise smartphone repair service staffed by former offenders and at-risk youth more than a decade ago, which earned him an OBE.
After a stroll through the East End, he points to the stand in Spitalfields market where they had pinned up sheets of A4 paper with “Cracked It” written across them in felt-tip, and laughs. “I would never have got my phone repaired there,” he says. “But when people were giving their money over … I was seeing these guys think: ‘Oh my God, wow! Someone wants my skills. They want what I can offer.’”
after newsletter promotion
![Josh Babarinde walks past rows of clothing racks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f1a573374bc9eab06029361996c8fabd987e794a/866_0_5800_4640/master/5800.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Do the Lib Dems want what the ambitious Babarinde has to offer? Despite being elected in 2024, he was elevated to the role of president in November, giving him a vital say in strategy and organisation. He bats away the inevitable question about whether he would like the top job – but when asked if he is a natural leader, he smiles.
“I roll up my sleeves and get stuck in,” he says. “When I saw those young people in the East End prolifically involved in crime amid a lack of opportunities. I wasn’t waiting for someone to swoop in to come to address that issue. I decided to come up with a solution.”
So if the problem is that the Liberal Democrats – despite a seemingly advantageous political backdrop – are stuck on 11% in the polls, what does he see as the answer? “The solution is exactly what is in the strategy we’re talking about this week,” Babarinde says.
“I stood to be party president because I thought I had something to offer: to help develop a new strategy for the party so we can reach new heights.”
summary: Liberal Democrat president Josh Babarinde adopted a combative stance ahead of the party's annual conference in Brighton, urging members to challenge modern giants like big tech and crypto billionaires. Despite securing 71 MPs in the 2024 election, the party has remained at roughly 11% in the polls amid a crowded multiparty system. Babarinde believes the party must pair its strong ground game with improved digital campaigning to expand its reach beyond traditional middle England strongholds.
key_points: Josh Babarinde called on Liberal Democrats to take on modern power giants and challenge the status quo.
The party won 71 MPs in the 2024 election but has remained stuck at about 11% in opinion polls.
Babarinde emphasizes the need for strong digital campaigning to complement the party's ground game and reach new communities.
Babarinde previously founded a social enterprise smartphone repair service for at-risk youth, earning him an OBE.

title: Manchester teenager missing for eight days found ‘safe and well’ by police
author: Nicole Wootton-Cane
content:
A Manchester teenager missing for eight days has been found “safe and well” by police.
Lillia, 13, disappeared after leaving her family home in Bolton on Friday 11 September, sparking a major search for the teenager.
Earlier on Saturday (19 September) Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers trawling CCTV in the hunt for Lillia have identified a further sighting of her at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on Monday 14 September.
![13-year-old Lillia missing since 11 September](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/17/18/01M2R4CVATST4V4ENN2BD3GDSK.jpg)
This followed a previous sighting earlier that morning, when the missing girl was seen boarding the number 36 bus from Salford before getting off in Manchester city centre.
In a statement released on Saturday evening, GMP thanked people for sharing its appeal and said: “We can confirm that she has been found safe and well in the city centre.
“She is currently with our officers, and her next-of-kin have been informed of this update. We will release more information in due course.”
The 13-year-old’s mother made a tearful appeal for her daughter to come home on Friday.
She said: "Lill, I love you so so much.
"My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe. We all you need back home safe and well."
![Lillia at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on 14 September](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/19/11/01M2WM53S3ZAC93836MWX9PRKC.jpg)
Police previously identified a sighting of Lillia at the Trafford Centre last Saturday (12 September), saying she caught a bus from there towards Altrincham.
She was seen at a McDonald's in Piccadilly Gardens the following day, before being pictured boarding a bus from Salford to Manchester last Monday morning.
summary: A 13-year-old girl from Manchester who went missing for eight days has been found safe and well by police. Greater Manchester Police located her in the city centre following a major search that included public appeals and reviewing multiple CCTV sightings. Her next-of-kin have been informed of the update.
key_points: Lillia, 13, went missing after leaving her Bolton home on Friday 11 September.
Police and her mother launched public appeals and tracked her movements through CCTV.
Sightings during her disappearance included the Trafford Centre, Piccadilly Gardens, and Manchester Piccadilly bus station.
Greater Manchester Police confirmed on Saturday evening that she was found safe and well in the city centre and is with officers.

title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’
author: Yassin El-Moudden
content:
Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of “fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning”, as she repeated her call for the prime minister to cut the welfare budget to fund increase spending on defence.
Speaking to the Telegraph, the Tory leader said that “Burnham may be a people pleaser but difficult choices cannot be avoided through dither and delay”.
She said the government had to “fund our defence properly” at a time when former military chiefs have raised questions about Britain’s preparedness for war.
Badenoch said: “Our government is fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning. In France and Poland, leaders are taking action now against the growing Russian threat. What is our government doing? Has anyone heard from Wes Streeting, the former head of the National Union of Students, who has rocked up as defence secretary?”
Discourse on the “welfare v warfare” debate has grown louder in recent days since Burnham’s comments during prime minister’s questions on 9 September that national security could not “come at the expense of social security”.
The Tory leader said Burnham was sending a “dangerous” message that he would not cut welfare to fund the military, which was “heard loud and clear in Moscow as well as Manchester”.
She added: “We have to stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history when Russia is testing our resolve week after week. It’s time to get serious.”
The UK has promised to commit 3.5% of national income to defence by 2035, in line with a pledge by Nato members, but there is growing pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, to outline how further increases will be achieved before next month’s budget.
Adm Lord West, a former security minister under Gordon Brown, said Britain’s military was in “quite a parlous state”.
“In many ways, one could argue we are already at war. We are certainly in the grey zone – whether it’s cyber-attacks, drones getting near the edge of somewhere or threats to underwater cables,” he added.
Lord Dannatt, a former chief of the general staff, said: “My bottom line is that Andy Burnham, and regretfully I would now add John Healey, are playing fast and loose with the nation’s security.”
The Conservatives have proposed capping housing benefit to raise £4bn to spend on defence. The party has rejected suggestions that the policy would make people homeless but suggested some would have to “move somewhere cheaper.”
The Tories will hold their annual conference in Birmingham in two weeks.
summary: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has criticized Andy Burnham, accusing him of avoiding difficult choices regarding national security and welfare spending. Badenoch argues that the government must cut the welfare budget to increase defence spending in response to growing Russian threats. Former military figures have also expressed concern over Britain's current military preparedness and the government's approach to national security.
key_points: Kemi Badenoch urged the government to cut the welfare budget to increase defence spending in response to the Russian threat.
Badenoch criticized Andy Burnham's stance that national security should not come at the expense of social security.
Former military chiefs, including Adm Lord West and Lord Dannatt, raised concerns about the parlous state of Britain's military.
The UK has pledged to commit 3.5% of national income to defence by 2035, aligning with Nato members.
The Conservative Party has proposed capping housing benefit to raise £4bn for defence funding.

title: Girl, 13, missing from home for a week is found ‘safe and well’
author: Liz Perkins
content:
![Thirteen-year-old Lillia had been missing for more than a week](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503577456_17898539748580_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqYXjog94lRMOHxImHynYRZVy8LebjoLJcDzvopcuM9LQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Thirteen-year-old Lillia had been missing for more than a week](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503577456_17898539748580_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqYXjog94lRMOHxImHynYRZVy8LebjoLJcDzvopcuM9LQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A 13-year-old girl who went missing over a week ago has been found “safe and well”.
Lillia, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, was reported missing by her family on Sept 11.
A spokesman for Greater Manchester Police said: “Thank you to everyone who shared our missing appeal for 13-year-old Lillia, who has been missing since Friday, September 11, 2026.
“We can confirm that she has been found safe and well in the city centre.
“She is currently with our officers, and her next-of-kin have been informed of this update. We will issue more information in due course.”
![Lillia's mother Jessica had issued an emotional appeal for her daughter's return](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503571451_17898540662540_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaivqAvBJWkUV8VzepAMjBRkCIv3505E63jNjQF1Hma4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Police said they had been working through hours of CCTV footage before a further sighting of her emerged at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on Monday.
She is believed to have boarded the number 36 bus in Salford and alighted at the station.
Her mother, Jessica, in an emotional appeal on Thursday, called for her daughter’s return.
She said: “Lill, I love you so so much. My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe.
“We all need you back home safe and well.”
Lillia’s aunt Nina posted on social media as part of the family’s appeal. “As a family we have no idea what has made Lillia become untraceable,” she wrote.
Police originally said Lillia was also seen at 1.50pm last Saturday at the Trafford Centre shopping complex in Stretford, where she boarded the 247 bus towards Altrincham.
It was unclear how long she stayed on the bus or where she got off. Officers reviewing CCTV footage identified a further sighting of Lillia last Sunday at around 8.20pm at McDonald’s on Market Street in the city centre.
summary: A 13-year-old girl from Bolton who had been missing for over a week has been found safe and well by police in Manchester city centre. Greater Manchester Police confirmed she is with officers and her next-of-kin have been informed. Prior to her being found, her family had issued emotional public appeals for her safe return.
key_points: Thirteen-year-old Lillia was reported missing by her family on September 11.
Police confirmed she was found safe and well in the city centre and is currently with officers.
Investigators reviewed hours of CCTV footage and tracked sightings at the Trafford Centre, a McDonald's on Market Street, and Manchester Piccadilly bus station.
Lillia's mother and aunt had previously issued emotional public and social media appeals for her return.

title: Inside the 30-year family feud driving Diana's bitter brother
author: Charlotte Lytton
content:
“I want to speak on Diana, Princess of Wales’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.” That was how Earl Spencer described his motivation for writing Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, published next week.
With the 30th anniversary of the former Princess of Wales’ death approaching in 2027, Earl Spencer had been “inundated” with interview requests, he said, which convinced him to “write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths.”
Those thoughts and memories have proven explosive, which Earl Spencer, 62, must have anticipated. He claims that when the then-Prince Charles called him in the aftermath of Diana’s death, “he sounded giddily elated – like a lottery winner.” In an extract published in the Daily Mail, he said that, after clashing over whether the princes should walk behind their mother’s coffin (the idea was “ghastly,” he told the now-King) “[Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana… ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!'”
Shorts
The allegations are so striking that Buckingham Palace made the unusual move of issuing a withering statement in response – something they refrained from even following the publication of Prince Harry’s memoir, Spare. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, a spokesperson said.
Earl Spencer says he decided to write Swan Song, three decades after Diana’s death, simply to set the record straight about his sister. But are there other factors at play? Motivations that might convince him it was worth going to war with Buckingham Palace?
**
![File photo dated 06/09/97 of (Left to right) Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and King Charles III, the then Prince of Wales, waiting as the hearse carrying the coffin of Diana, Princess of Wales prepares to leave Westminster Abbey following her funeral service. The 29th anniversary of Diana, Princess of Wales???s death falls on Monday, just days after her youngest son the Duke of Sussex returned home with his family to live in the UK. Issue date: Sunday August 30, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Fiona Hanson/PA Wire](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_310004099_c9c47b.jpg?w=644)
Since her death in 1997, Earl Spencer, who succeeded his father as Viscount Althorp in 1992, aged 27, has in many ways become a custodian of Diana’s legacy; she is buried on an island on the Althorp estate where Earl Spencer lives.
The two youngest Spencer siblings were particularly close in childhood during their parents’ bitter divorce, while their elder sisters, Lady Jane Fellowes and Lady Sarah McCorquodale, were away at boarding school. Diana saw herself as part-sibling, part-mother figure to her brother after their mother left the family home when she was six and Earl Spencer, three.
The pair shared similarities their elder sisters didn’t, Diana believed, telling her biographer Andrew Morton that “[Charles] will always suffer because he’s like me.” In Swan Song, Earl Spencer writes they both suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria – “intense emotional pain in the face of rejection or criticism”; they, too, shared the same sense of humour, he has said. He called his sister “Duch” (short for ‘Duchess’, because of how she carried herself); her moniker for him was Carlos (a Spanish riff on his name, Charles).
Along with their closeness, there were periods of “coolness,” according to Morton, including when Diana asked to stay at the Garden House at Althorp in the aftermath of her marriage breakdown in 1992, and was turned down by her brother because of “the inevitable police and press interference” that would ensue. (He offered her another house on the estate instead.)
Terse words were also exchanged via letter about the “mental problems” she suffered while battling bulimia. Before she died, Earl Spencer was living in South Africa and seeing his youngest sister six or seven times a year. Her passing, he said, felt like “an amputation”.
![Lady Diana Frances Spencer (1961 - 1997), playing with her brother Charles Edward Maurice, the Viscount Althorp, in the grounds of Park House, Sandringham when she was six years old. (Photo by Hulton Archive/Getty Images)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_309011694_1884ef.jpg?w=644)
As self-appointed custodian of her legacy, he promised to protect her sons. In his 1997 eulogy at Westminster Abbey, he famously pledged that Diana’s “blood family” would do all they could to help guide the boys. Earl Spencer said Diana left him as their guardian, although he acknowledges this carried no legal standing while their father was alive.
In the intervening decades, more of a distance opened up between Earl Spencer and his nephews. Even by 2002, when asked about his relationship with the princes, he said that “they may not be encouraged to stay in touch with their mother’s side of the family.” He added that he had spoken with their father just once during that time.
As adults, it’s clear that Harry has spent more time with his uncle. Harry’s decision to step back from royal duties, and his well-documented struggles with King Charles, have encouraged a closer relationship. In July, before the Sussexes moved back to Britain, Harry, Meghan and their two young children visited Althorp, posting pictures of the estate online.
Both Harry and Charles have felt compelled to go public with their own recollections of events within the Royal Family; indeed, Harry’s breaking of the royal omerta is likely to have been another factor in Charles’ decision to write about his sister. And, given Prince Harry was reportedly paid $20m (£15m) for Spare, there is no doubt that royal memoirs can be a lucrative business (Earl Spencer has written nine nonfiction books since 1998, four of them Sunday Times bestsellers).
Swan Song also follows the huge success of Earl Spencer’s 2024 book, A Very Private School – a highly personal account of his time at boarding school, where, he recounts, he was beaten with a cricket boot and thumped round the head, blood drying in his hair. The acclaim he received on publication may well have encouraged him to dig deeper this time, baring parts of his sister’s past that might otherwise have remained buried.
As to money being a motivator, although Earl Spencer’s personal fortune stands at an estimated £150 million, his outgoings are sizeable. In 2020, the energy bills alone at Althorp were over £130,000, which, adjusted for inflation and energy costs, would now be closer to £150,000. Then there are the three divorces to pay for, the first of which resulted in a £1.8m settlement to be paid by him, while he was ordered to pay legal costs, estimated at over £2m, in another court case related to his third divorce. He married his fourth wife, Cat Jarman, in 2026.
Swan Song is likely to be a bestseller; it is to be translated into 12 languages, and an audiobook read by its author will also be released. “When I finished the recording, I thought: ‘That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say — and [Diana] would, I reckon, have approved of every word,” he said of his work.
While he has taken comfort in what his sister would have made of his words, others appear less impressed. Royal correspondent Jennie Bond said that “I do not know what purpose it serves. It can only go to hurt, I think, William and Harry, who love their father and probably undoubtedly love their uncle as well. To see the family torn apart by this serves no purpose.”
In 2002, Earl Spencer admitted it was “time for me to put a line under being the man who made the speech at his sister’s funeral and to have my say about some of the misrepresentations that were the fallout from it”. Twenty-four years later, he has finally decided to do so.
Given the fracas it has already caused pre-publication, the only remaining hope is that it does make good on what he promised was his original aim: showing the world that his sister was “a one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young”.
summary: Earl Spencer has written a new book titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, in which he shares explosive memories of Diana, Princess of Wales, and alleges that King Charles made callous remarks after her death. Buckingham Palace issued a rare statement responding to the claims, suggesting that grief can cloud judgment. The book's publication also highlights Earl Spencer's role as custodian of his sister's legacy, his close childhood bond with her, and potential financial and personal motivations behind the project.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims that then-Prince Charles sounded elated after Diana's death and made a harsh remark about forgetting her.
Buckingham Palace responded unusually to the allegations by stating that fraternal grief can cloud reason and judgment.
Earl and Diana Spencer were exceptionally close during their childhood due to their parents' bitter divorce.
Prince Harry and his family recently visited Althorp, reflecting a closer relationship with his uncle compared to Prince William.
Earl Spencer's book follows his previous bestselling memoir and comes amid notable personal expenses and energy costs for the Althorp estate.

title: Scottish Labour’s new leader backs Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields
author: Patrick Greenfield
content:
Scottish Labour’s new leader Michael Marra has backed the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields in the North Sea in one of his first acts after being elected, calling for a “more rational” approach to energy policy.
On Saturday, the MSP for North East Scotland won a near two-thirds majority to lead the party in Holyrood, becoming Scottish Labour’s 11th leader. He replaces Anas Sarwar after his shock decision to resign in July to join Andy Burnham’s new government as a trade minister.
Dundee-born Marra said he would urge the British prime minister to back both fossil fuel projects despite warnings over their environmental impact. Neither is covered by the ban on new licences for drilling in the North Sea because their applications were already in the system when the Labour government took power, and there is growing expectation that ministers will approve the Jackdaw gasfield in the coming weeks.
“I want Rosebank and Jackdaw to be approved,” Marra told reporters shortly after his election. “It’s the biggest issue in my region in terms of people’s voting intention. We need to have a more rational policy position that delivers for the Scottish economy and Scottish jobs.”
In his acceptance speech at the Dynamic Earth science museum in Edinburgh, Marra said he would spend time reconnecting with Scottish voters after a bruising defeat in this year’s elections.
“May hurt so much because we know the SNP didn’t deserve a fifth term in power. But the truth is Scotland didn’t think we would be much better,” he said.
“Scots know what we are against. They can’t tell you what we are for. And that vacuum was filled by the poison, racism and bigotry of Reform. We must be clear in our values. We must lead with our values,” he said.
“For a decade now, Scotland has gotten weaker. We must reconnect with the country if we are ever to form a government in Holyrood to face these historic challenges.”
Marra faces an uphill battle to reverse the party’s fortunes in Scotland. While 37 Labour MPs from Scotland sit in Westminster, the party has lost seats at every Holyrood election since devolution in 1999.
In May, the party suffered its worst ever results – winning just 17 seats as the SNP retained power. Labour has as many seats as Reform in Holyrood, just two more than the Scottish Green party and five more than the Conservatives.
In a subdued campaign with few policy differences between candidates, both Marra and his main rival, Joe Fagan, were criticised for struggling to outline the circumstances in which Scotland should be allowed a second independence referendum.
Marra said that he thought the party had become overly focused on middle-class voters in Scotland, and vowed to build a broader electoral coalition that was centred on the needs of the country.
When asked again about the level of public support that would mean Scotland should have a second independence reference, Marra said the SNP’s failure to get an outright majority in Holyrood in May signalled that it was not a priority for voters.
“The people of Scotland do not want a referendum right now. We will continue to make the case for a stronger Scotland in a changing UK. It’s imperative to me that we are not in this for the status quo. I’m in this to make sure that we can see a stronger Scotland,” he said.
In total, 6,751 votes were cast in the leadership election, representing 49.43% of the Scottish Labour party membership. Fagan won 2,485 votes, while Marra won 4,266.
Dr Eric Shaw, a research fellow at the University of Stirling who co-authored The Strange Death of Labour in Scotland, said the party had to reconnect with working-class voters to win back support.
“The party is facing three main issues: the continued salience of independence, the association between Scottish Labour and Labour in Westminster, and the erosion of Labour’s historic base in Scotland. The plight of the party is reflected in the fact that Labour did better among the professional middle class than it did in the working class in the most recent election.”
Dr Ewan Gibbs, a lecturer in economic and social history at the University of Glasgow, said the new leader had to ask difficult questions about who the party was meant to represent in Scotland.
“We are approaching 20 years of failure with the government in Holyrood if we look at the performance of public services, educational attainment, ongoing income and wealth inequality in Scotland. But Scottish Labour isn’t a party that seems equipped to mobilise that opposition and disappointment at the moment.”
summary: Michael Marra was elected as the new leader of Scottish Labour, securing a near two-thirds majority in his leadership bid. In one of his first acts, he backed the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw North Sea oil and gasfields to support the Scottish economy and jobs. Marra acknowledged the party's historic struggles in Holyrood and emphasized the need to reconnect with voters, build a broader coalition, and oppose a second independence referendum.
key_points: Michael Marra won the Scottish Labour leadership election with a near two-thirds majority, replacing Anas Sarwar.
Marra called for the approval of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields to protect Scottish jobs and the economy.
He stated that the people of Scotland do not want a second independence referendum at this time.
Marra aims to rebuild the party by reconnecting with voters and broadening Scottish Labour's electoral coalition beyond the middle class.

title: New Scottish Labour leader elected
author: Sabrina Miller
content:
![Michael Marra describes himself as being 'rooted in Labour'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503678381_17898141360520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhaQcnQgX1lblZ3yiN-_RsGJoXaIvubr1VJ_EGf3sIxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Michael Marra describes himself as being 'rooted in Labour'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503678381_17898141360520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhaQcnQgX1lblZ3yiN-_RsGJoXaIvubr1VJ_EGf3sIxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Michael Marra has been named the new Scottish Labour leader.
Mr Marra replaces Anas Sarwar, who resigned from the post in July after the party’s worst Scottish parliamentary electoral results in the history of Scottish devolution.
Mr Marra, the North East Scotland MSP, defeated Joe Fagan by 4,266 votes to 2,485.
Reacting to the results, Mr Marra said: “To be entrusted with the leadership of our Scottish Labour party is a singular honour and a great responsibility.”
He added: “I’m very grateful for your trust and I take on the duty of advancing our cause of a fairer, more equal Scotland with all that I can possibly give.”
Mr Marra inherits a party with 17 MSPs, making them the joint second-largest party in Holyrood, tied with Reform UK.
![Michael Marra (L) is congratulated by Joe Fagan (R) as he is announced as winner of the Scottish Labour leadership contest](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503677833_17898142299620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwekapBZ1c_8650LP5YH00zA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Speaking after the votes were read out, Mr Marra added: “Scots know what we are against. They can’t tell you what we are for.
“Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services.
“The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity.”
Despite overseeing the disappointing Scottish parliamentary electoral results, in which Labour lost five seats, Andy Burnham handed Mr Sarwar a peerage in the summer so that he could become the Minister of State for Trade in his Government.
Mr Sarwar has stood by his previous calls for the House of Lords to be abolished and replaced with a democratically-elected chamber, despite being made a peer.
‘Rooted in Labour’
Born in Dundee in 1979, Mr Marra studied history at the University of Glasgow before securing a master’s degree in economics and international development from the London School of Economics.
Before launching his own political career as a councillor in 2017, Mr Marra worked as the head of policy and public affairs for Oxfam Scotland before becoming a senior adviser to Iain Gray, the former Scottish Labour leader.
He won his Holyrood seat in 2021 and was given a front bench role as education spokesman. He was allowed to miss the final vote on reforms that would have made it easier for people to change their legally-recognised sex. It was alleged at the time he would have voted against the proposals.
He describes himself as being “rooted in Labour”, telling party members during the campaign how he went on trade union marches as a child with his sister and his parents.
Mr Marra is the younger brother of Jenny Marra, a Labour MSP. He is married with three children.
summary: Michael Marra has been elected as the new Scottish Labour leader, defeating Joe Fagan in the leadership contest. He succeeds Anas Sarwar, who resigned following the party's poor performance in the Scottish parliamentary elections. Mr Marra inherits a party with 17 MSPs and has pledged to focus on social justice and the eradication of poverty.
key_points: Michael Marra defeated Joe Fagan by 4,266 votes to 2,485 to become the new Scottish Labour leader.
He replaces Anas Sarwar, who resigned in July following the party's worst Scottish parliamentary electoral results.
Mr Marra takes over a party with 17 MSPs, tying them as the joint second-largest party in Holyrood with Reform UK.
Before his political career, Mr Marra worked as head of policy and public affairs for Oxfam Scotland and as a senior adviser to Iain Gray.

title: Jim Ratcliffe: UK is ‘on the slide’ from days when it had world’s ‘greatest empire’
author: Daniel Lavelle
content:
The co-owner of Manchester United Sir Jim Ratcliffe has described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.
Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giant Ineos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain is in decline because of high taxes and immigration.
Ratcliffe’s latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country was being “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.
The billionaire told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline from the days when, he said, “we were a great people”.
He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk. But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”
Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.
He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.
“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident. And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.
While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.
Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such as the 1958.
The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.
The billionaire also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.
after newsletter promotion
He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”
In response to the billionaire’s criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.
A spokesperson told the BBC that they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”
Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.
“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.
“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”
summary: Manchester United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe stated in a recent interview that the UK is in decline due to high taxes, immigration, and policies that drive away wealth creators. He also criticized the government's energy and North Sea resource decisions, warning of potential gas shortages this winter. The government responded by defending its economic growth efforts and expressing confidence in the nation's energy security.
key_points: Sir Jim Ratcliffe claimed the UK is on the slide due to high taxes and immigration.
Ratcliffe criticized the UK for encouraging wealthy individuals to relocate instead of celebrating wealth creation.
He warned that the UK could run out of gas during a cold winter due to a lack of further investment in North Sea resources.
The UK government stated it is confident in the country's energy security and is working to deliver economic growth.

title: Man stabbed to death on 'millionaire's row' in London as manhunt launched for killer
author: Megan Howe; Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![How London's youth courts are trying to blunt knife crime I Tristan Kirk Special Report](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/18/19/11/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-20-21-05.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Police were called to affluent Lloyd Baker Street at around 11.20pm on Wednesday following reports of a stabbing.
The victim was taken to hospital where he died on Thursday.
His family have been informed and are being supported by specially trained officers.
Detectives have launched a manhunt to find the killer. No arrests have been made.
Floral tributes have been laid at the scene by the victim’s family and friends.
Lloyd Baker Street is known for its expensive properties, with homes selling for as much as £2.25million in the past year.
![A man has died following a stabbing in Lloyd Baker Street](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/18/19/11/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-20-21-05.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
A Section 60 order was authorised in the wake of the fatal stabbing, granting officers enhanced powers to stop and search people and vehicles.
The order ran from 4pm on Friday to 6am on Saturday.
Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart, who leads policing in the local area, said: "This is a tragic incident, and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young man who has lost his life.
“You can expect to see additional officers in the area providing visible reassurance and working with partners to keep the public safe.
“The victim was found in a residential street, and members of the public may have information of vital importance to our investigation. If you can help, please come forward.”
Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101, quoting reference CAD 8475/16SEP.
summary: A man was stabbed to death on Lloyd Baker Street in London late Wednesday night, prompting a police manhunt for the killer. The victim was transported to a hospital where he died on Thursday. Authorities have authorized a temporary Section 60 stop-and-search order and increased police presence in the area as the investigation continues.
key_points: A man was fatally stabbed on Lloyd Baker Street in London following an incident reported at around 11.20pm on Wednesday.
The victim died in the hospital on Thursday, and his family is currently being supported by specially trained officers.
Police have launched a manhunt for the suspect, and no arrests have been made so far.
A Section 60 stop-and-search order was authorized in the area from Friday afternoon to Saturday morning.

title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
author: Sean Coughlan
content:
![Diana, The Princess Of Wales Visits Washington, USA for a Gala Dinner held by The American Red Cross, to raise funds for landmine victims around the world.  1997](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/dc52/live/508ec510-b377-11f1-9023-9990160baacc.jpg)
- Published
The legacy of the shocking death of Diana, Princess of Wales, is still the rawest of wounds for the royals, as demonstrated by the no-holds-barred memoir from her brother Earl Spencer.
It might be almost 30 years ago, but Buckingham Palace's unusually angry rebuttal to the book's allegations of a callous response to his ex-wife's death from the then Prince Charles shows how much this still matters.
That late summer in 1997 was a moment when the Royal Family looked out of touch, lacking in empathy for Diana's loss, and at peril of losing public support, as people laid siege to the palaces with flowers.
While the royals dealt with their own private grief, they were also facing a reputational disaster, at risk of becoming the focus of public dismay at the sudden death of the "People's Princess" in a car crash in Paris.
![A multi-coloured sea of floral tributes to Diana, Princess of Wales, lie outside the gates of her London home.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1df2/live/24a35f50-b378-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
An outpouring of public grief saw flowers laid outside palaces and Diana's homes
"It was a very febrile mood. Everyone was taken by surprise by the strength of feeling, and the strength to which the Royal Family was unpopular. The palaces were deemed to have treated Diana badly," recalls royal author Valentine Low.
Low was inside Westminster Abbey for Diana's funeral and vividly remembers the public response to the electrifying speech made by Earl Spencer.
"I heard this noise. I couldn't quite make out what it was, and then I worked out it was the crowd outside the abbey, who'd been listening on the speakers," he says.
"That noise appeared to come through the stone walls of the abbey and it was the most extraordinary thing - as people then started to applaud inside the abbey. It was so astounding, in front of Charles and all of the Royal Family."
A volatile public mood followed Diana's death, with the late Queen Elizabeth eventually having to respond with a live televised address paying tribute to the princess and acknowledging how difficult it can be to articulate grief.
"We have all been trying in our different ways to cope. It is not easy to express a sense of loss, since the initial shock is often succeeded by a mixture of other feelings: disbelief, incomprehension, anger - and concern for those who remain," said the late Queen.
A fresh-faced new prime minister, Tony Blair, was said to have been a modernising influence on sending such a direct message - an intervention later depicted in the movie, The Queen, starring Helen Mirren.
![Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry, Prince Charles and the Duke of Edinburgh follow the coffin to the funeral cortege of Diana, Princess of Wales as it arrives at Westminster Abbey on September 6, 1997 in London, England.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3606/live/ece31060-b377-11f1-9023-9990160baacc.jpg)
There was disagreement about whether it was right for the princes to walk behind Diana's coffin
So many of the current tensions in the royal world can be traced back to the trauma of those events. The death of a mother at such a young age was inevitably a huge shaping influence on her sons - and it can feel as though those unresolved tensions are still playing out.
In the Duke of Sussex's memoir Spare, Diana's absence is a huge presence, his sense of loss unabated. There is still a graphic sense of his distress at walking behind her coffin, with Prince Harry mentioning Earl Spencer's opposition.
"Mummy's brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell. 'You can't make these boys walk behind their mother's coffin! It's barbaric'," wrote Harry.
Harry's accusation that the interests of the institution of the monarchy had been put above the happiness of individuals has been part of the narrative that saw him stepping down as a working royal and remaining at loggerheads with his brother, Prince William.
![The Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, speaking at her funeral at Westminster Abbey 06 September.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/704/cpsprodpb/a1de/live/8757ea20-b374-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
There was a wave of applause from outside Westminster Abbey when Earl Spencer finished his eulogy
The disputes that followed Diana's death, within the family and between in-laws, are still being aired loudly in Earl Spencer's book - Swan Song: Diana, My Sister - and in the global news coverage it has triggered. It opens up old questions about King Charles's character, his treatment of the young princess and his relationship with the now Queen Camilla.
On social media, Diana's fans are believing Earl Spencer's version of events, says Prof Pauline Maclaran of Royal Holloway, University of London. She says the royals remain "highly vulnerable" to anything that evokes the story of a "beautiful princess whose life was cut short in such tragic and ambiguous circumstances".
Royal commentator Jenny Bond described it as a "fantastically hostile, absolutely rude book... it's a very unpleasant portrayal of a man - but it's his memory of it, and who knows who's right?"
![Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales (1961-1997), and her sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, attending the Princess's funeral service at Westminster Abbey, London, England, 6th September 1997.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/df22/live/fcf8d460-b374-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Prince William was 15 and Prince Harry just 12 at their mother's funeral
At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."
He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.
Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.
The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".
Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.
Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.
Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.
The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.
Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".
There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.
That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".
Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997.
"This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.
![King Charles III (then Prince Charles, the Prince of Wales), Lady Jane Fellows (left) and Lady Sarah McCorquodale with officials at RAF Northolt to meet the coffin of Diana Princess of Wales, as it arrives from Paris where she was killed in a car crash, 31st August 1997.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1217/live/bf29a8c0-b375-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
King Charles walks with Diana's sisters Lady Jane Fellows (left) and Lady Sarah McCorquodale to meet her coffin as it arrives in England
Earl Spencer, in a statement ahead of the book's launch, said he had been "inundated" with requests for interviews about his sister, with the upcoming 30th anniversary prompting him to write down his own memories "rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time".
He is fiercely defending the accuracy of his claims, in interviews over the weekend, including with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.
In it Earl Spencer doubles down on his allegations about King Charles, saying: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.
"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."
Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died
In person, Earl Spencer is a very affable and charming figure, a writer who has had a first-hand view of some big royal moments and has the stories, sometimes scandalous, to show for it.
What makes his claims more potentially damaging is that he isn't writing as a pundit or commentator, but as someone who was sitting around the table with his in-laws and his own sister. It's a close up, emotional, insider's view, not a long lens and a headline.
If this book shows that the royals haven't escaped the legacy of Diana's death, then it also shows that neither has he.
You can watch Earl Spencer's interview with Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday from 16:00 BST on BBC iPlayer and on BBC One at 18:30.
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: Earl Spencer's memoir regarding the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, has reopened deep historical wounds and provoked an angry rebuttal from Buckingham Palace. The book alleges that the then Prince Charles made callous remarks following Diana's 1997 car crash, claims that the King's camp denies. Commentators note that the publication threatens decades of work by the Royal Household to rehabilitate the images of Charles and Camilla as the 30th anniversary of Diana's death approaches.
key_points: Earl Spencer's memoir contains allegations that the then Prince Charles responded callously to Diana's death during a phone call.
