Buckingham Palace issued an unusual rebuttal, suggesting that grief and trauma can cloud memory and that the conversation did not happen as claimed.
A YouGov poll shows public opinion is split on whether to believe the allegations in the book.
Experts suggest the book threatens to undermine three decades of work by the Royal Household to rehabilitate the public images of King Charles and Queen Camilla.

title: Woman gives police officer a lift in Nissan Micra while chasing man
author: Miriam Barker
content:
Police officer given lift by driver in Nissan Micra mid-chase
- Published
A driver came to the aid of a police officer who was chasing a suspect on foot - telling him to "get in" after stopping her Nissan Micra and offering him a lift.
The officer had been pursuing Jacob Roberts, 25, who had reverse-rammed a police car twice and crashed into parked cars and a building while trying to escape.
Roberts sped away from officers who had smelled cannabis coming from his van, with the chase seeing him drive in an erratic manner, failing to stop at multiple junctions, mounting pavements and putting pedestrians at risk.
The driver helped PC Kerswell catch up to Roberts, who was arrested and later jailed for one year and two months for a number of driving offences.
While fleeing from police in his white van, Roberts had driven into a dead-end street in Abercwmboi, Rhondda Cynon Taf, where he ditched the car and tried to escape officers on foot.
Police bodycam footage captured the moment the officer then runs to a red Nissan Micra driven by an un-named female driver and tells her: "I need a lift."
"Get in," the woman replies.
As she gave chase the woman is heard asking the officer to direct her, saying: "Where to?"
The officer is seen jumping out of the car after spotting the suspect and takes out his taser and arrests him.
During a search officers found two cannabis cigarettes on him.
Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years.
He was sentenced at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on 16 September, where he pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs.
Kerswell said: "Roberts was already banned from driving when he committed these offences - he showed complete disregard for all other road users, including pedestrians.
"I hope it acts as a deterrent for others who think of driving dangerously.
"It's lucky that no one was seriously injured during this pursuit. We hope this sentence will give Roberts time to reflect on his actions."
More top stories

 ![Megan sits in her car. she is smiling at the camera and has reddish to brown hair cut at her shoulders. She is wearing a blue jumper with a dragonfly on.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/2913/live/92b92920-ac52-11f1-9e64-05835b0b18f8.jpg)
- ![A close-up photograph shows a man wearing a dark patterned flat cap, black jacket, white shirt and dark tie, looking towards the camera in a near smile.
He is outside a modern brick and glass building. Behind the person is a large red sign featuring a Welsh dragon](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/0d29/live/76eff0e0-b29a-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.png)
- ![Queen Elizabeth II in blue meeting people in dark suits](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/958/cpsprodpb/c4ee/live/27a68920-b1f7-11f1-bd8b-ed45be4f6895.jpg)
summary: A female motorist in a Nissan Micra assisted a police officer by giving him a lift during a foot chase after a suspect. The suspect, Jacob Roberts, had fled in a van, crashing into parked cars and a building before abandoning the vehicle in Abercwmboi. With the help of the driver, PC Kerswell caught up to Roberts, who was subsequently arrested and sentenced to one year and two months in prison for multiple driving offences.
key_points: A driver offered a police officer a lift in her Nissan Micra to help him pursue a fleeing suspect.
The suspect, Jacob Roberts, had reverse-rammed a police car and driven erratically before fleeing on foot.
Roberts was arrested after the officer exited the car, deployed a taser, and apprehended him.
Roberts was sentenced to one year and two months in prison and disqualified from driving for three years at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court.

title: Footballer donates to fundraiser for Noah Woods' family as £88k raised
author: Emily Goodwin
content:
Noah Woods went missing in Brantham on Tuesday afternoon and Suffolk Constabulary confirmed on Wednesday that his body had been found in Decoy Pond, just yards from where he was last seen.
A JustGiving page has been set up to support his family during the "heartbreaking time".
Originally set up with a £20,000 target, the fundraiser has now been raised to £100,000.
Organised by the Good Dad's Club, 5,000 donors have already raised more than £88,145.
Among the contributors is Ipswich Town footballer Leif Davis, who donated £2,000.
It is understood the footballer joined the search for Noah on Tuesday night after leaving training, staying out until 3am.
The Just Giving page reads: "In light of the news regarding three-year-old Noah Woods, Good Dads Club is calling on our community to give whatever they can to ease the overwhelming burden on his family during this heartbreaking time.
"While no amount of money can undo these life-altering events, every single financial contribution will go directly toward helping Noah's family with expenses, navigating daily bills and taking the necessary time off work to grieve without the added strain of financial worry.
"Please consider donating today; no contribution is too small, and share this campaign so we can surround Noah's loved ones with the solidarity they desperately need."
Noah disappeared after running down an alleyway near Merriam Close.
On Wednesday afternoon, Suffolk Police confirmed that a child's body had been discovered in the Decoy Pond, a fishing lake close to where he was last seen.
Superintendent Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police thanked the community for their support during the search.
He said: "We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support, people putting on their boots and helping us search.
"As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community."
summary: Following the tragic discovery of three-year-old Noah Woods' body in Decoy Pond in Brantham, a fundraiser has been established to support his family. Organized by the Good Dads Club, the JustGiving campaign has raised over £88,000 from 5,000 donors. Ipswich Town footballer Leif Davis contributed £2,000 to the fund after reportedly joining the overnight search.
key_points: Three-year-old Noah Woods went missing in Brantham, and his body was found in Decoy Pond on Wednesday.
A JustGiving fundraiser organized by the Good Dads Club has raised over £88,145 toward a £100,000 goal.
Ipswich Town footballer Leif Davis donated £2,000 to the family's fundraiser.
Davis reportedly helped search for Noah Woods until 3 am on Tuesday night.

title: Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s death
author: Sammy Gecsoyler
content:
Earl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said of Diana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.
The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.
In an interview with the BBC, Spencer stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”
Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they? They’ve said that recollections may vary.”
![Diana in a black dress](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/58eb8b6f02366b460566624db559654e59e9935e/24_0_1263_1010/master/1263.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Spencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and said he told his friends and family members at the time about the comment “because it was so monstrous”.
The alleged comment was revealed on Wednesday in an extract from the memoir published in the Daily Mail. The comment by the then prince was allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says it reflected Charles’s “pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.
Among other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.
On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.
“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.
![Philip, William, Spencer, Harry and Charles walking in Diana’s funeral procession](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/98d10d9ba6c084602d253de85e618dacc1a206a5/114_0_1728_1382/master/1728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer says he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in her funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.
Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen.”
after newsletter promotion
But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”
Spencer wrote that he was stunned and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”
Spencer also claimed that Diana “never would have wanted” her sons to walk behind her coffin, to which Charles allegedly replied: “That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty.”
Swan Song is due to be published globally next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.
Four copies of the Dutch-language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.
Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.
Buckingham Palace did not issue a statement responding to the BBC interview, but on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
summary: Earl Spencer is standing by claims made in his upcoming memoir that King Charles made a callous remark about Princess Diana shortly after her death. Buckingham Palace suggested in a statement that Spencer's grief has clouded his memory, but Spencer maintains he is telling the truth and recalled the conversation to friends and family at the time. The book also details disputes over the funeral arrangements, including the decision for Princes William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims King Charles told him "rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough" during a phone call following Diana's death.
Buckingham Palace responded by stating that fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment, and colour memory.
Spencer insisted in a BBC interview that his recollection of the call is completely accurate.
The memoir alleges the disputed comment occurred during a heated argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

title: Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about King Charles
author: Laura Kuenssberg
content:
Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died
- Published
Princess Diana's brother has told the BBC exclusively that he is "telling the truth" about a phone call with King Charles in the days after his sister's death.
Earl Spencer claims in a new book the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.
In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".
But in his first interview since, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."
![Laura Kuenssberg interviews Earl Spencer](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/e617/live/244be3f0-b38d-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Earl Spencer spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"
Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.
"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."
Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".
In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."
When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."
Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.
The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.
![Earl Spencer with Princes William and Harry, and Prince Charles at the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, standing alongside members of the clergy to the side of the funeral procession, with floral tributes faintly visible in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/8c68/live/300ca980-b339-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, walked behind their mother's coffin alongside Earl Spencer and their father
In excerpts of his book published by the Daily Mail, Earl Spencer claims the phone call took place after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young princes to walk in the procession.
In his BBC interview, he says the King "went ballistic" and "ranted for a while", accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty.
"And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate," Earl Spencer said. "And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."
He said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was "just so stunned", adding: "I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him."
![Earl Spencer talking with Laura Kuenssberg at Diana's burial site on the  Althorp estate](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/7736/live/f7554fc0-b38d-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Diana is buried at the Spencer family's Althorp estate
Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.
In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".
Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.
A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."
The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood.
Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36.
Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".
In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.
The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST.
summary: Earl Spencer has defended claims made in his upcoming book regarding a phone call with King Charles following the death of Princess Diana. In an exclusive BBC interview, Earl Spencer maintained that the then-Prince of Wales told him "we'll forget her soon enough" during a disagreement over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in their mother's funeral procession. Buckingham Palace previously responded by stating that grief can cloud memory and judgment, though Earl Spencer insists he is telling the truth.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims in a new book that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over Princes William and Harry walking in Diana's funeral procession.
Buckingham Palace responded by stating that the pain of grief can cloud reason, affect judgment, and color memory.
Earl Spencer defended his account in a BBC interview, insisting he was "hyper alert" and that those were the exact words spoken.
Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is scheduled to be published next week.
Earl Spencer also alleges in his book that King Charles sounded "giddily elated" like a "lottery winner" during a phone call following Diana's death.

title: Flight chaos caused by millisecond software defect, says air traffic control body
author: Katy Austin; Tom Espiner; Simon Browning
content:
![Passengers wait for flights and connections at the South terminal of Gatwick Airport on September 09, 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/797/cpsprodpb/f648/live/18fc40e0-b34b-11f1-91a3-393282eb9f17.jpg)
Thousands of passengers were delayed by the NATS outage
- Published
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.
The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.
The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.
The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of its chief executive Martin Rolfe.
There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.
In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.
The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.
The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.
Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.
The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.
Martin Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption.
"It's our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong," he said.
"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."
Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.
"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.
This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.
In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.
There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.
Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."
He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".
Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."
![Addie Kitson sits in her airplane seat with a fluffy panda bear which she brought back from China after seeing many of them in China. She is a young woman with brown hair and blue eyes and a nose ring.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/91fd/live/a3694c90-b1da-11f1-a44b-aba96a7d56aa.jpg)
Addie Kitson was hit with almost Â£100 in unexpected costs when her flight back from China was diverted to Stockholm
Addie Kitson, 26, had been on holiday in China when her flight home was diverted to Sweden.
"I thought I landed fine" she told the BBC, "but then they went: 'Welcome to Stockholm' and I went: 'Ooh, that's not London'".
After being told about the issues affecting UK airspace, passengers were kept on the plane for a few hours, and then spent 19 hours inside Stockholm airport.
Addie ended up with nearly Â£100 in unexpected costs after having to buy refreshments, adaptors and to pay for Wi-Fi to work.
"I got one Â£11 food voucher that didn't even cover the cost of a sandwich in Stockholm airport", Addie said.
Addie questioned the rules around compensation, saying there had been multiple air traffic outages.
"It doesn't seem that extraordinary," she said.
summary: A recent air traffic control failure in the UK caused widespread travel chaos, leading to more than 2,000 flight cancellations and affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. National air traffic service Nats stated that the disruption stemmed from a millisecond software defect that produced corrupted data and reduced information for controllers. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the incident unacceptable and announced a Civil Aviation Review, while airlines demanded immediate compensation and improved system resilience.
key_points: The travel chaos was caused by a millisecond software defect affecting UK air space management on 8 September.
The failure resulted in over 2,000 flight cancellations and affected hundreds of thousands of passengers.
Nats stated that safety was never in question, but restrictions were placed on air traffic to maintain safety.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption completely unacceptable and noted a Civil Aviation Authority review is underway.
Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for incurred costs and a credible plan to improve system resilience.

title: Our brother did not match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
author: Aurelia Foster
content:
Watch: 'There was no urgency to clear his name' - sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect
- Published
The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".
Nicholas Brandram's sisters gave BBC Radio 4's Today programme a list of reasons why they believed their brother could not have been the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge, west London, in May 2017.
Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the Met investigation.
The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, and that a mandatory referral had been made to the police watchdog.
Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health had been deteriorating in recent months and that "every day was becoming difficult" while he was under police scrutiny.
They said it was "ridiculous" their brother - a banker and former army officer - was the suspect because:
- His identity did not match the profile of the pusher, saying their brother had a withered leg from an old army injury and a prominent military tattoo on his forearm
- The victim reported the attacker had brown eyes but their brother had blue
- Their brother lived in Notting Hill, had no connection with Putney and they had evidence to suggest he was in his Bond Street office at the time of the attack
- He willingly provided a DNA sample to the Met to speed up the inquiry but never received results, despite pleading with police to speed them up
"It's out there on the internet what the so-called Putney pusher looked like. We provided evidence very quickly to show that this did not look like our brother," the sisters said.
"Nine and a half years ago when the incident occurred, there'd been absolutely nothing connecting our brother to the attack.
"So this came completely out of the blue, off effectively an allegation which must have been either malicious or mistaken."
![Close-up headshot of a smiling Nicholas Brandram with short dark hair, blue eyes. He is clean-shaven. He is wearing a blue open-collared shirt outdoors, with a blurred background showing an outdoor seating area and buildings under a clear sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/e210/live/de7d3440-b293-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Nicholas Brandram was under police investigation over the 2017 incident
Describing Brandram's "hostile" arrest in June, Hicks said: "My brother woke up to a large handful of police officers wearing armed vests and with a film crew on the doorstep from the media."
The sisters said his mental health had been "deteriorating" following the arrest.
"His name was leaked on social media channels within a couple of days. And that's when the vitriol started online. Thanks to the leak," they said.
"He was reading everything that was online. Because he was still guilty online."
Brandram's sisters said: "The Met, they were negligent, they were reckless and they have, you know, failed our brother.
"They failed in their duty of care to our brother, to the wider family and arguably actually society because the Putney pusher is still out there."
A jogger 'pushed' woman in front of bus
The sisters said it seemed as though the Met had an "urgency" to arrest him and tell the press.
"He couldn't understand why there wasn't an urgency to help clear his name," they said.
Describing Brandram as a "very, very, very loved brother and uncle, father, son", the sisters said he was a "real family man" and "didn't deserve any of this happening to him".
The force said the investigation into the 2017 incident remained ongoing.
It added that it had no further comment to make in relation to the sisters' comments.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: The sisters of Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the "Putney pusher," have defended his innocence and criticized the Metropolitan Police following his death by suicide. They stated that his mental health deteriorated after months of intense police scrutiny and online vitriol stemming from a June arrest. The family argued that physical descriptions, alibis, and other evidence proved he could not have been the attacker in the 2017 incident.
key_points: Nicholas Brandram died by suicide following months of pressure from a Metropolitan Police investigation into a 2017 incident.
His sisters accused the Met of being negligent and reckless, failing in their duty of care.
The family stated Brandram did not match the suspect's description, noting he had a withered leg, a prominent military tattoo, and blue eyes compared to the victim's account.
Brandram provided evidence and a DNA sample to police, but never received results to clear his name while his name was leaked on social media.
The Metropolitan Police stated they recognize the strain of investigations and made a mandatory referral to the police watchdog.

title: Badenoch brings in lawyers after 94% Wandsworth Council tax hike
author: Ewan Somerville; Matt Chorley
content:
Watch: Badenoch says she will challenge government over Wandsworth tax hike
- Published
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.
She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous" but that "they're not doing it because they want to".
Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to see if an Â£84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.
The government has insisted it needs to reform the "outdated" council funding system to move money to where it is most needed.
Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over Â£1,000, compared to above Â£2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.
But this would nearly double with the planned Â£958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London.
There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.
Changes to the funding formula for councils announced last year will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. Wandsworth Council said it stood to lose Â£84m annually in funding by the end of the next three years.
Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".
"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.
"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.
"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."
Pressed by presenter Matt Chorley on how the rise will still mean Wandsworth's council tax is lower than many councils across the country, Badenoch said it would still worry some families.
"I think if you suddenly have a nearly 100% increase in your council tax, you would be extremely worried. Families have budgets," she said.
"Just because on average it's lower than somewhere else doesn't mean that people are going to be able to afford it."
She refused to say what alternative rate of increase she would propose, but questioned why a 40% cut was being imposed on the council when "Andy Burnham has not found 40% of anything to cut" himself.
She also defended her record as local government minister when the Tories were in Downing Street, despite Conservative governments having slashed some council grants.
Wandsworth Council's Tory deputy leader said on Tuesday: "Higher council tax will not be easy or welcome. We do not regard it as fair and will continue to challenge the government by every possible means."
Other London councils including Westminster, Richmond and Kensington and Chelsea are considering joining Wandsworth in using the Sustainable Communities Act to challenge government funding cuts.
As a result of the central government cuts, the usual cap of 5% annual council tax rises was lifted for all these councils as well as Windsor and Maidenhead in Berkshire.
Leader of the opposition in Wandsworth, Labour councillor Simon Hogg, said: "It's outrageous, it is stunning. People who don't know how to run the council panicking and making you pay the price.
"This increase is unfair, it's unnecessary and we oppose it."
However, the PoliticsHome website reported, external that three Labour MPs in Wandsworth - Rosena Allin-Khan, Fleur Anderson and Marsha de Cordova - have refused to back the council's appeal to the government to stop the funding cuts.
The three Labour MPs claimed the council "was in a strong financial position" before the Tories took over at the May elections earlier this year.
In a statement when the council tax rise was announced, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first.
"We're fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge."
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has instructed lawyers to potentially challenge the government over an £84m-a-year funding cut affecting Wandsworth Council. The cut has prompted a proposed 94% council tax increase in the south-west London borough, which the council blames entirely on the government decision. While the government defends the funding formula reform to redirect money where it is most needed, the planned hike has drawn heavy criticism and opposition.
key_points: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch announced that the party has instructed lawyers to look into challenging government funding cuts.
Wandsworth Council faces a proposed 94% council tax increase, translating to a planned £958 rise.
Wandsworth Council attributed the massive tax hike to an £84m-a-year funding cut resulting from government funding formula changes.
The government defended the changes as a necessary reform to move money to areas where need is greatest.
Other London councils are considering using the Sustainable Communities Act to challenge the government funding cuts.

title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into industry scheme
author: Harry Farley
content:
![John Healey smiles while wearing a suit and red tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/68b5/live/362ff930-b2e3-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
John Healey is meeting EU finance ministers on Friday
- Published
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.
But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.
Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.
That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.
The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.
There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.
Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.
Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.
"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses â wherever they are based across the UK â get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."
Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.
"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.
It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.
Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.
Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.
He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.
Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.
Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: UK Chancellor John Healey will warn EU finance ministers in Dublin against locking British firms out of the bloc's "Made in Europe" industrial protection scheme. He will advocate for closer UK-EU partnerships in manufacturing, tech, and defence while aiming to reduce the economic impact of Brexit. Healey is also considering the UK's participation in a new global defence investment bank to help manage growing military spending.
key_points: John Healey is meeting with EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to push for closer partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing.
He will urge the EU to design its "Made in Europe" Industrial Accelerator Act to deepen ties with the UK rather than erect new trade barriers.
Government officials are concerned that the EU's proposed industrial scheme could exclude British firms from European supply chains.
Healey is also considering joining the proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank to help lower borrowing costs for increased military spending.

title: Human remains identified as mum missing since 2019
author: Curtis Lancaster
content:
![A woman smiles into the camera making peace signs with both hands](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/20a1/live/d5866d50-b2a9-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019
- Published
Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.
Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.
Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.
A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.
Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.
Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".
![Two temporary tents and several people inside a taped-off area on a hillside with dark ground and sparse vegetation in the foreground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/8507/live/fdfd8b70-9d81-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The human remains were found after a wildfire in south-west London
Police said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels.
Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty.
"Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time.
"As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable."
He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance.
![Area of darkened ground and sparse vegetation cordoned off with blue-and-white tape and temporary fencing on a sloping embankment.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1560/live/42c879e0-9d82-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the public
London Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits.
The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45.
A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park.
Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a Â£20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation.
Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen.
Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unsolved.
Police previously said she did not have a permanent place of address, a vehicle or a bank account.
summary: Human remains discovered in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as Joanne Sheen, a mother-of-three who went missing in December 2019. Metropolitan Police found the bones in Feltham on August 12 after a member of the public reported them. A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder, and the investigation has now been handed over to Hampshire Police.
key_points: Joanne Sheen was last seen traveling from Fareham to Southampton on December 5, 2019.
Her remains were found in shrubland in Feltham on August 12 following a wildfire.
A 56-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.
Crimestoppers has reinstated a £20,000 reward for information regarding the case.

title: Charles sounded 'giddily elated' after Diana’s death, claims Earl Spencer
author: Caroline Davies
content:
The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death.
Earl Spencer also says he believed Buckingham Palace wanted William and Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin because the then Prince Charles was “adamant” he was going to walk and palace officials feared “members of the public might shout abuse at him”.
By getting Diana’s sons to walk, “that would surely guarantee against insults flying”, he wrote.
![Book cover with black and white portrait of Diana and the title ‘Swan Song: Diana, My Sister’](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8fd4f95773b213e1d08bc7f9026625e2e66d3e66/0_0_1838_2833/master/1838.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, has already made headlines, with Spencer alleging that during a heated phone call before Diana’s funeral, the king remarked: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”
Buckingham Palace issued a robust rebuttal on Wednesday evening, saying in a statement: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
In new extracts, published on Thursday on the website of the Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were “relieved – indeed pleased” at Diana’s death in a Paris car crash. It was his suspicion that Charles’s first reaction must have been to think how he could now marry Camilla Parker Bowles.
According to Spencer, Diana had confided in a friend that days before their wedding, Charles had told her “she needed to know he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her”, and she was certain he was “entering their marriage with his heart elsewhere”.
![Diana with short hair and black strapless dress with Charles in bow tie and black suit](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/87865076342e9b11267a8f56d019b254f5f18086/0_0_1680_1531/master/1680.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Diana tried to break off the engagement after finding a bracelet Charles had bought for Camilla, who is now the queen, he writes. But their father was “appalled”, telling her “it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point”.
Spencer says in the book that he also believes Charles may have contributed to the princess’s eating disorder, saying Diana’s waist shrank from 29in to 23.5in between the engagement and wedding after she was “devastated” at her fiance squeezing her waist and saying: ‘Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we.”
He was also convinced Diana had ADHD and, like himself, suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. He writes: “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further.”
The excerpt goes on to say that Diana told him she was going to get divorced and that “my husband is in love with his valet”.
Spencer, 62, has said he wrote the memoir to correct “untruths” told about his elder sister.
The row over the book overshadowed a busy day for the royal family, with the Duke of Sussex also entered the mix with an engagement of his own.
Harry, who it is understood was aware of his uncle’s book in advance but not its contents, arrived at the inaugural Invictus Spirit awards in London on Thursday evening in his first appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month.
![Laughing man with auburn hair and beard in bow tie and black blazer with medals](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/83fcae96cfe0196a330606a6262e39ba3315af69/0_249_2008_2530/master/2008.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Prince and Princess of Wales were on their first official trip to the Isle of Bute off the west coast of Scotland. The couple, who hold the titles of Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, visited the namesake town of Rothesay, dropped in at a shinty club and stopped at a pub while meeting community leaders and volunteers.
Charles, meanwhile, was appearing in public for the first time since Spencer’s allegations were aired, at an AI summit he had convened at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire. Addressing global tech leaders, he warned of the “existential dangers” of AI systems falling into the wrong hands.
As those who have created these technologies had warned, AI risked “developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life”, he said. The king spoke of the need for reassurance that “our humanity remains sacred” and “that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls”.
summary: Earl Spencer's upcoming memoir, 'Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,' alleges that King Charles sounded giddily elated following Diana's death and made callous remarks about her. The book also claims Buckingham Palace wanted William, Harry, and Spencer to walk behind Diana's coffin to protect Charles from public abuse. Buckingham Palace responded by stating that grief can cloud reason and color memory over time.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims King Charles sounded like a 'lottery winner' in a phone call immediately after Diana's death.
The memoir alleges Buckingham Palace arranged for Diana's sons and brother to walk behind her coffin to prevent the public from shouting abuse at Charles.
Buckingham Palace issued a rebuttal stating that grief can cloud reason and judgment years after a loss.
Spencer alleges that Charles told Diana before their wedding that he was not in love with her and previously made critical comments about her weight.

title: Charles’s rebuttal of Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana offers rare glimpse into palace thinking
author: Caroline Davies
content:
As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.
Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.
Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.
Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”
The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.
![Charles in the back seat of a car](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d39159dfbb9cd8e9f85a076503bb4c25b715eccb/0_0_2416_1616/master/2416.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.
Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.
But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.
However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”
That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.
Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.
What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.
When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.
In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.
![Harry and Meghan being interviewed by Oprah](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5edd035b0acac397640f40589f799e9945762ffb/205_0_3283_2627/master/3283.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.
Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.
One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”
summary: Buckingham Palace swiftly issued a rare public rebuttal to claims in Earl Spencer's memoir that King Charles made insensitive remarks about Diana shortly after her death. The palace stated that grief can cloud reason and colour memory, diverging from the traditional royal motto of never complaining or explaining. Former communications secretary Julian Payne noted that the personal nature of the allegations compelled the palace to set the record straight.
key_points: King Charles responded quickly to allegations in Earl Spencer's upcoming memoir regarding remarks made after Diana's death.
The palace statement suggested that grief can cloud reason and affect judgment over time.
Despite the usual "never complain, never explain" mantra, officials felt the personal nature of the claims necessitated a denial.
Former communications secretary Julian Payne indicated the strong feeling behind the palace's rare intervention.

title: Family of ‘Putney Pusher’ suspect blame police for his death
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Nicholas Brandram](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503407757_17896427083230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqz8PrEBUoq2NOeDT9dFlgS4yt3BU7yimAYJ8YD28sfCE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Nicholas Brandram](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503407757_17896427083230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqz8PrEBUoq2NOeDT9dFlgS4yt3BU7yimAYJ8YD28sfCE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The family of the “Putney Pusher” suspect have blamed the Metropolitan Police for his death.
In a statement on Thursday, the family claimed that Nicholas Brandram killed himself “after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation” into him.
They insisted that the 44-year-old was not the “Putney Pusher” and claimed the Met Police knew that he was innocent.
The family said: “The Met Police knew he was not [the “Putney Pusher”]. And yet, when Nick died, they had still failed formally to clear his name. That is a source of profound grief and anger for our family.
“There was no forensic evidence linking Nick to it, no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage. In fact, the evidence proved the opposite.
“Despite that, the police chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview.”
![CCTV footage of the man suspected of being the Putney pusher](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000136884222_17896425810130_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq4NbsJKmPLpdC_WK4vTS1GSMcSKwwHEFbGWrkuBs1wvg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Brandram, a descendant of Queen Victoria, was discovered at his home in Chiswick, west London, on Tuesday.
He had been detained by police in June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge, south-west London, on May 4, 2017.
CCTV footage from the time captured the moment a 33-year-old woman was pushed in front of the Number 430 bus.
Oliver Salbris, the bus driver, swerved and missed the woman’s head by inches while the jogger ran on.
In the statement, Mr Brandram’s family said that his lawyers “did the basic investigative work that should have been done by the Met Police”.
The statement said: “They pointed out that the published images of the man involved in the assault bore no resemblance to Nick: the victim had described the attacker as having brown eyes; Nick had distinctive blue eyes.
“Nick had a visibly wasted and disfigured calf dating back to his time serving with the Army, while the man shown in the footage did not. And Nick had a prominent forearm tattoo, which was not visible on the man in the images.”
The statement continued: “Nick made it clear he was keen to take part in an identification parade, but the police never organised one. He also provided email evidence sent from his office in the West End, demonstrating that he was not even on Putney Bridge when the assault happened.
“A previous suspect, also wrongly arrested, was cleared within days of providing an alibi. Nick was left on bail and remained under suspicion.
“The double standard is impossible to ignore. When the Met Police wanted to arrest Nick, there was urgency; when they wanted to search his home, there was urgency; when information about him reached the press, there was urgency. But when the evidence showed they had the wrong man, that urgency disappeared.”
![Nicholas Brandram](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000490844312_17896425731140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Brandram “was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence”, his family said.
Their statement added: “The Met Police were quick to expose Nick to suspicion and painfully slow to remove it. They failed him. And Nick’s family will now live with the consequences of that failure for the rest of our lives.
“Those who knew Nick will remember him for everything that made him the wonderful man he was. We will love him, and miss him, every day.
“But grief does not remove the need for accountability. We will continue to demand answers about how an innocent man was put through this, why he was not cleared when the evidence showed he should have been, and what the Met Police will do to ensure that no other family has to endure what ours now must.”
summary: The family of Nicholas Brandram, the 44-year-old suspect in the 2017 "Putney Pusher" investigation, has blamed the Metropolitan Police for his suicide. In a statement, they claimed he took his life after months of pressure from the police investigation, despite evidence proving his innocence. Mr Brandram was found dead at his home in Chiswick on Tuesday, months after being arrested in June in connection with the incident.
key_points: Nicholas Brandram's family blamed the Metropolitan Police for his death, stating he killed himself after months of immense pressure from a police investigation.
Brandram was arrested in June in connection with the May 2017 incident where a jogger pushed a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge.
His family stated that evidence, including eye color, a physical disability, and a forearm tattoo, proved he did not match the description of the attacker.
The family accused the police of failing to formally clear Brandram's name despite a lack of forensic evidence and the presence of an alibi.

title: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over book's claim on Charles and Diana
author: Sean Coughlan
content:
Watch: 'Searing' palace response to Earl Spencer's claim in Diana book
- Published
Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and death.
King Charles is accused of insensitively saying to Earl Spencer, in the wake of Diana's death in 1997, that "we'll forget her soon enough", according to excerpts published in the Daily Mail.
But the Palace has pushed back unusually strongly, angered by the claims and attempting to cast doubt on them.
"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.
The language is reminiscent of Queen Elizabeth's unexpectedly firm response to claims of racism by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2021, with the comment that "recollections may vary".
And the row threatens to overshadow a very crowded day for the royals - with the King, Prince William and Catherine attending events and Prince Harry making his first big appearance since returning to the UK.
Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, to be published next week, seems set to reopen a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family - written from the perspective of her own Spencer family.
The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.
Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's sudden death. And this book will give an insider's view on those events.
In the published excerpt, Earl Spencer claims the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.
Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."
It's a claim that's being rejected by the Palace, who see it as being entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.
Julian Payne, the monarch's former communications secretary, told the BBC that the King's apparent comments in the book were "just not language that I recognise".
He said the "highly unusual" statement from the Palace demonstrated the "strength of feeling that there must have been for them to feel that they needed to go out there and correct it".
![A composite image shows on the left Charles wearing a dark suit, blue shirt and red and blue tie, and Diana next  to him wearing a white and navy block dress colour and holding a single flower. On the right is Earl Spencer wearing a black suit jacket and chequered open-necked shirt and gesturing with his hands as he speaks to camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/be1e/live/3da6ac10-b25a-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Charles and Diana pictured during a visit to Hungary in 1990, two years before they separated, and Earl Spencer during a BBC interview in 2024
The dispute comes when multiple royal events will be jostling for attention.
King Charles is set to intervene in the debate about artificial intelligence, calling on AI industry leaders to prevent it becoming a destructive force.
"Those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny," the King is expected to say on Thursday, as he hosts a gathering of leading AI firms at an Dumfries House, in Ayrshire.
"The development of AI, its substance and its pace, are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure," the King will say.
The rapidly-advancing technology has raised fears about its safety, as well as a threat to jobs.
The King will be joined by AI minister Kanishka Narayan and representatives of tech firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia and Google DeepMind.
He will ask the question about how the benefits of AI can be harnessed while still ensuring that it remains safe, and raise the issue of whether there can be international co-operation in protecting it from being misused.
"The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations," he will say. "And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world."
Meanwhile, during the day, Prince William and Catherine will visit community and volunteering projects on the Isle of Bute.
The couple - who are called the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, rather than the Prince and Princess of Wales - will make their first official visit to the town of Rothesay.
They will see the traditional sport of shinty, visit a community-owned pub and hear about those working to protect the island's natural environment.
![The then Prince Charles and Earl Spencer meeting in South Africa in 1997](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/9234/live/8fdee250-b22c-11f1-8669-2bc48e768d35.jpg)
The then Prince Charles and Earl Spencer meeting in South Africa in November 1997, three months after Diana's death
Later, Prince Harry will hold his first big public event since returning to the UK, when he appears at the inaugural Invictus awards ceremony.
This will celebrate the "resilience, service and unconquered spirit" of those involved in the sports events for injured service personnel.
It's not yet known whether he will be accompanied by his wife, Meghan.
![Prince Harry, wearing a khaki shirt and navy trousers, holds Meghan's hand and as they cross a road, protected by a man in a blazer clearing the way for them to walk. In the background are a crowd of people taking photos.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/781/cpsprodpb/0a49/live/6fb7a340-b236-11f1-bad2-3b109fca7ebc.jpg)
Harry and Meghan pictured during a visit to Melbourne, Australia in April
It is unusual to have so many royal events at the same time, but it could be a sign of things to come, with Prince Harry and Meghan back in the UK and running their own programme of engagements.
A letter, sent on behalf of the King last week, made clear that the Sussexes are not carrying out royal engagements, but even as "private citizens" they are likely to get plenty of press attention for their visits.
The controversy over the letter suggested some tension in their return and raised questions about how they will fit into wider royal arrangements.
Harry and Meghan have already been in the headlines this week over switching schools for their children, after security fears over the school run.
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: Buckingham Palace has issued an unusually strong response to a forthcoming memoir by Earl Spencer, Diana's brother, which alleges that King Charles insensitively remarked "we'll forget her soon enough" after Princess Diana's death in 1997. The Palace pushed back against the claim, suggesting that grief can cloud memory and judgment. This row coincides with a busy day of engagements for multiple senior royals, including King Charles, Prince William, Catherine, and Prince Harry.
key_points: Earl Spencer's upcoming memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, claims King Charles made callous remarks and directed a stream of anger following Diana's death.
Buckingham Palace rejected the claim, stating that grief can cloud reason and color memory over time.

The controversy comes during a crowded day of royal events, including King Charles hosting an AI summit, Prince William and Catherine visiting the Isle of Bute, and Prince Harry appearing at an Invictus awards ceremony.

title: English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan
author: Ben Quinn
content:
Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum against plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby.
The result of the poll in Piddington, Oxfordshire, was announced on Wednesday morning after 312 people voted on Tuesday. A total of 285 people were in favour of independence from the UK while 26 voted against. One ballot was spoiled.
The poll was organised by campaigners for residents to demonstrate opposition to government plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a converted Ministry of Defence site in the town of Bicester.
Reacting to the news, a government minister said the burden of accommodating asylum seekers should not fall just on poorer communities and she would “gently” tell residents of the village that the government was working to bring down the asylum backlog.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, told Sky News: “We are getting that backlog down. We’re speeding up the processing of claims, and in the meantime, we don’t think it’s acceptable for all of the burden of shouldering not just asylum accommodation, but also many other forms of temporary accommodation, to fall on poorer communities.”
She added: “That’s what we saw under the previous government. Because accommodation is cheap in many, not just towns, but in particular postcode areas. People who live in more deprived communities have had to put up with almost … every other house in some instances … turned into HMOs [house in multiple occupation], and that is not OK.”
The dispute over the plans in Bicester come against a backdrop of tensions elsewhere over the location of accommodation for asylum seekers. After disturbances in Thetford, Norfolk, earlier this year, which far-right activists attempted to exploit, the local Labour MP there voiced his concerns that cheaper, working-class areas were being chosen as locations for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.
![A man holding a ‘Principality of Piddington’ sign at the village boundary in Piddington, Oxfordshire.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b6439f0364add07fc8223b90b49cb1ddf8f6dd92/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Tim Bearder, the leader of Oxfordshire county council, said on Wednesday that the result in Piddington showed that campaigners had done “an incredible job” to highlight their concerns.
“This referendum shows how strongly they feel about the proposal and that is partly about the proposal itself and partly about way the government has gone about it, without engaging with local people and looking at the feasibility of the site,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“It’s the wrong site for the local community and for the asylum seekers themselves,” said Bearder, who declined to say what alternative sites could be used.
The result was announced on Wednesday morning by a “returning officer” in front of an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall.
A parish councillor, Mike Nixon, said the proposed site had no pedestrian access areas, and that the nearest path was about a mile and a quarter away, down a busy unlit road.
The Home Office has previously said that the government is closing asylum hotels in what is expected to saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support and that it is working fairly to house asylum seekers across the country.
“As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area,” a spokesperson said.
summary: Residents of the English village of Piddington voted in a symbolic referendum to leave the UK in protest against government plans to house over 1,000 asylum seekers at a nearby site in Bicester. Out of 312 participants, 285 voted in favour of independence, while campaigners and local officials cited concerns over community engagement, site feasibility, and the placement of asylum housing in working-class areas. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy responded by stating the government is working to reduce the asylum backlog and acknowledged that poorer communities should not shoulder a disproportionate burden.
key_points: Piddington residents voted 285 to 26 in a symbolic referendum to leave the UK.
The protest was organized against government plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a converted Ministry of Defence site in Bicester.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy stated that the government is working to reduce the asylum backlog and agreed that poorer communities should not bear the brunt of temporary accommodation.
Local council leader Tim Bearder criticized the lack of government engagement and called the location the wrong site for both the local community and the asylum seekers.
Parish councillor Mike Nixon highlighted safety concerns regarding the proposed site, noting a lack of pedestrian access and unlit roads.

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case found dead at his west London home
author: Vikram Dodd
content:
A senior city banker suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a moving bus in the “Putney pusher” case has been found dead.
Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick, west London, on Tuesday.
He was arrested in June by the Metropolitan police in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridge pushed a woman towards an oncoming bus.
She only avoided serious injury after the driver swerved around her at the last moment.
Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain.
He was released on bail by detectives in June after being arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. In September, after answering bail, he was re-bailed with no conditions.
Video footage showed the woman being pushed by a male jogger. She fell into the road, with the jogger running on.
The Met wound down its investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. The case, which attracted considerable attention, was unsolved.
In a statement on Wednesday, the Met said: “At 19.12 on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London ambulance service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property.
“Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed.
“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.
“A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.”
after newsletter promotion
Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013 when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner, before driving off without leaving his details.
In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank.
He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.”
Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”
summary: Nicholas Brandram, a 44-year-old senior city banker and former military captain, was found dead at his home in west London on Tuesday. He had been arrested in June by police investigating the 2017 'Putney pusher' incident, where a woman was shoved into the path of a bus. Police stated his unexpected death is not believed to be suspicious, and a file will be prepared for the coroner.
key_points: Nicholas Brandram was found dead at his Chiswick home on Tuesday at the age of 44.
He was arrested in June in connection with the 2017 Putney Bridge incident where a woman was pushed toward an oncoming bus.
Police stated that his unexpected death is not being treated as suspicious.
Brandram worked as a director and senior relationship manager at HSBC and was a former military captain.

title: Body found in search for missing Suffolk boy Noah Woods, 3
author: Shivani Chaudhari; Lewis Adams
content:
![Noah, a three-year-old boy who has ginger hair. He is pictured sitting on a bed with a grey headboard and is looking directly at the camera and smiling.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/e4d0/live/8a926280-b1f1-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Noah Woods was described as looking "happy and healthy" by one of the last people to see him
- Published
A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed.
Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, after becoming separated from a relative.
Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond.
He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.
CCTV footage shows the last sighting of Noah at the playground
