Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed.
"Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said.
"We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."
Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.
People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.
Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.
Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.
Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.
![A police officer reading out a statement while holding an iPad or tablet with a black cover on it. He is wearing his police uniform and has black hair](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/115c/live/5ff5ce70-b1f3-11f1-bd8b-ed45be4f6895.jpg)
Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said: "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him"
Michael Crowley, who was working opposite the playground on Tuesday and was one of the last people to see Noah before he went missing, said: "He looked happy and healthy as anything."
Jessica Gammons, a mother-of-two from Kelvedon, in Essex, was among the many volunteers who went out to look for the toddler.
She said she felt compelled join the search, despite being heavily pregnant, because her son, like Noah, is three years old.
"I kept thinking to myself 'If this was my son, I'd want everyone possible to help,'" she said.
"It's such a sad situation. I can't stop thinking about him."
![A woman with long blonde hair and sunglasses on her head standing behind her two children. One is in a pushchair and the other one is standing up.
There are people sitting on a bench behind her and another man wearing a orange hi-vis jacket](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/200c/live/04e76880-b1fe-11f1-a4a7-291ff3d1006b.png)
Jessica Gammons, a mother of two, was among the volunteers who helped in the search
Searches had widened to include East Bergholt and Manningtree, over the Essex border, on Wednesday.
Divers from the Metropolitan Police were called in to search Decoy Pond, a nearby fishing lake.
The pond is about 350 yds (320m) away from the playground where Noah was last seen.
![Seven people - all dressed in blue overalls with blue helmets on - searching a field for Noah Woods.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/382d/live/b8518490-b1f5-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had joined emergency services in the search for the missing boy
![Annotated Google view shows Merriam Close playground, footpath, new-build housing estate and Decoy Pond.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/877d/live/888e74d0-b1f4-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Supt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family.
"We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service.
"As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place.
"I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this."
summary: Police in Suffolk have confirmed that a body of a child has been found in the search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods. Noah had disappeared from a playground in Brantham after becoming separated from a relative. Dive teams recovered the body from a nearby pond, and police are treating the death as unexplained but not suspicious.
key_points: Three-year-old Noah Woods went missing from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, on Tuesday afternoon.
Dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond during the search.
Police stated that the death is being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.
At least 1,300 members of the public joined emergency services and volunteers to help search for the boy.

title: Suffolk police release footage of Noah Woods as search for missing boy continues
author: Jamie Grierson
content:
A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old boy with autism, supported by hundreds of volunteers.
Suffolk police have said the hunt for Noah Woods remains a missing persons investigation with no indication anything sinister has happened.
Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and partially deaf, went missing after a visit to a play area in the village of Brantham on Tuesday afternoon when he became separated from a relative. Police have said Noah will not respond to his name if called.
In an update on Wednesday, Supt Tom Pearse from Suffolk police said: “This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.”
The force released new CCTV stills and footage of the little boy in the play area in Merriam Close just before he vanished.
It is thought that he ran down an alleyway beside the playground towards a nearby new-build housing estate.
The surrounding area includes woods and a pond and is near the River Stour and a railway.
Noah is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white T-shirt featuring the TV character Bluey, shorts, and black Vans trainers with a white stripe.
![Volunteers at Brantham leisurecCentre, as police officers continue their search for the three-year-old.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0b34149bc3457b298b71be01b53b5c0e135ebeac/0_0_6192_4128/master/6192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
On Wednesday, volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre.
They are part of a massive search operation led by police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs being used and a helicopter flying overhead.
As well as the ground search, officers are looking at CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches.
Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible.
He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.”
![Supt Tom Pearse speaking to volunteers at Brantham Leisure Centre](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/726a079242ab2e56176259d2c633befd76f065dc/424_0_5160_4128/master/5160.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the update from police on Wednesday, Pearse urged volunteers to report to the coordination centre and to avoid the railway and open water, which need specialist searching.
He said: “It has now been around 24 hours since Noah was reported as missing to us and we are doing everything we can to find him.
“We are extremely grateful for the support shown by the public. If you are helping please report into the coordination centre to ensure the search continues to be done in a systematic and coordinated fashion.
“This will ensure we can carefully plan and take account of people supporting the search.
“We politely ask people to avoid open waters and railways – these are areas that require specialist and professional expertise. We also ask that personal drones are not used as these can interfere with specialist search equipment.
“There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations.
“Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our inquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.”
Later on Wednesday, the far-right activist Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, appealed for his social media followers to join search efforts to find Noah.
The founder of Patriot Platform – the extremist group behind masked anti-migrant protests in Dover and Portsmouth this month – posted a video of himself in a car and said “we are on our way”.
Louise Madley, the manager of Brantham Leisure Centre, who has been helping to coordinate volunteers, said: “We welcome any extra volunteers, probably from tomorrow now.”
She said registration of volunteers would probably stop at about 5.30pm.
She said that on Tuesday night there were “a lot of people on the streets that hindered the police search and search and rescue, and it’s just safety as well of everyone involved – around this area it can be quite precarious”.
Advice from Brantham parish council to volunteers included: “You are looking for a frightened three-year-old. Think about slight movements in your peripheral [vision], high and low, tiny small spaces use all your senses whilst searching.”
They have been told not to grab or approach Noah if they find him, but instead to call police on 999 immediately and give their exact location using the What3Words app.
Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village, or who was driving through the area with a dashcam is asked to review the footage from 3pm on Tuesday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.
summary: A massive search operation involving hundreds of volunteers and emergency services is underway in Suffolk for a missing three-year-old boy named Noah Woods. Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal, and partially deaf, went missing after becoming separated from a relative at a play area in Brantham. Police are treating the disappearance as a missing persons investigation with no indication of anything sinister.
key_points: Noah Woods, three, went missing on Tuesday afternoon after becoming separated from a relative at a Brantham play area.
He is autistic, non-verbal, partially deaf, and will not respond to his name if called.
Suffolk police are treating the case as a missing persons investigation with no evidence of criminality.
Hundreds of volunteers are assisting police, fire, coastguard, and search and rescue teams.
Police have released CCTV footage of Noah and urged volunteers to report to the coordination centre and avoid specialist areas like railways and open water.

title: UK inflation pushed up by petrol and diesel price rises
author: Dearbail Jordan
content:
![A woman prepares to pay for fuel at the pump in a petrol station. She is wearing a pink cardigan over a pink and white patterned blouse](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d847/live/6dc55eb0-b1be-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
- Published
Rises in petrol, diesel and airfares pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in five months in the year to August.
Inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The cost of filling up a vehicle soared in August as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. Petrol prices jumped to their highest for nearly four years, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.
Meanwhile, the cost of flying jumped during the key month for summer getaways.
Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.
Oil hit more than $91 a barrel as the US-Israel war with Iran went on. That compares to around $73 just before hostilities began earlier this year.
As a result, average petrol prices have continued to climb and between July and August, they rose by 9.1p to 161.3p per litre.
"This is the highest price recorded since November 2022," said the ONS. At that point, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine had pushed up global energy costs.
Capital Economics said, at this point, the effect of higher oil prices has not spilled over into other areas such as food and drink, where the pace of inflation remained at 1.3% in the year to August.
But its chief UK economist, Paul Dales, said: "Everyone knows that bigger rises in inflation are on their way."
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said: "Rising crude oil and petrol prices increased both the annual cost of raw materials and the price of goods leaving factories respectively."
Dales estimates that a combination of higher oil and gas prices and "the eventual 'first-round' effect of businesses passing on some of their higher energy costs" will lead to inflation peaking at 4.2% in January.
'Things are down'
![Man looks at camera, wearing beige jumper over a shirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/788/cpsprodpb/ea10/live/529048e0-b19f-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Goran Raven says changes in oil prices have a "real-time impact" on small petrol retailers like his
As well as hitting drivers in the pocket, higher oil prices also affect forecourts.
Goran Raven, owner of Essex petrol station RJ Raven, told the BBC: "Things are down. We've got lots of pressure on us at the moment. I'd say we're about 20% down on this time last year."
Raven said changes in the oil price have a "real-time impact on us".
In recent days, Brent crude - the global benchmark for oil prices - has surpassed $100 a barrel.
"We only have small tanks here, so we need a tanker almost every day at the moment and we have to pay a daily spot price," said Raven. "When the price goes up, we have to go up with it. There's no way around it.
"The margins here are wafer-thin on fuel. People like to think we're earning a lot on it. Unfortunately, we really aren't. It's single digits of pence we earn per litre."
![Line chart of the UK's Consumer Price Index annual inflation rate, from January 2020 onwards. In the year to January 2020, inflation was 1.8%. It then fell close to 0% in late-2020 before rising sharply, hitting a high of 11.1% in October 2022. It then fell to a low of 1.7% in September 2024 before rising again. In the year to August 2026, prices rose by 3.1%](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/29d7/live/d13e38d0-b197-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.png)
The rise in inflation means it has moved further away from the Bank of England's 2% target.
The bank uses interest rates to control inflation.
The rate currently stands at 3.75% and the Bank of England is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to change it.
Chancellor John Healey, who is preparing to announce his first Budget next month, said: "The war in the Middle East is impacting on inflation worldwide, not just here at home. In our bills, our weekly shop and at the petrol pumps."
He said: "Despite this serious global uncertainty, our UK economy is proving resilient."
The most recent figures showed that the UK economy expanded by 0.4% in July, boosted by investment in artificial intelligence.
But, for the second quarter between April and June, Britain's economic growth slowed to 0.4% from 0.6% in January to March.
Commenting on inflation, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the government's "jobs tax and employment red tape are being passed on to consumers in the weekly shop and their mad energy policies are pushing up costs and leaving Brits exposed".
The government is cutting VAT on household electricity bills from 5% to zero on 1 October, saving a typical household about Â£45 a year.
At the same time, the price cap on both electricity and gas bills will rise by 4%.
It means a home using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay Â£60 a year more.
Yaelâ¯Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said the VAT cut will only partially offset the impact of higher gas prices, which have been rising because of the Iran war and disruption to global supplies, including liquefied natural gas.
"If gas prices remain around current levels, household energy bills could rise by a further double-digit amount from January, with an even larger increase possible if wholesale prices climb further," she said.
'Everything is extremely expensive'
![Selfie of Emma Ashfield, a young woman with long, dark hair, weaing a grey hooded sweatshirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/791/cpsprodpb/5e41/live/ef250980-b1a8-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.png)
Energy costs are a worry for Emma Ashfield
Emma Ashfield, a nursery worker from Northern Ireland who is raising her eight-year-old daughter, said everything is already "extremely expensive".
"You are trying to keep food on the table, [buy] clothes, trying to provide for them," she said. "You would basically need a second job."
With winter approaching, she says energy costs are another worry: "I find electric very priceyâ¦ and it is costly trying to heat my apartment too.
"My wee girl is always wanting the heating on, so that's another thing."
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "Trump's illegal war - egged on by the Conservatives and Reform UK - is once again hitting British families hard. This must be a wake up-call for the government."
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/5273/live/9464edd0-b1b7-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.png)
summary: UK inflation accelerated to 3.1% in the year to August, reaching its highest level in five months due to rising petrol, diesel, and airfare costs. Disruption to global oil supplies driven by conflict in the Middle East pushed oil past $91 a barrel, leading to higher raw material and factory gate prices. Economists project that inflation could peak at 4.2% in January as businesses continue to pass on increased energy costs.
key_points: UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the year to August, moving further from the Bank of England's 2% target.
Motor fuel prices jumped by 23% compared to the previous year, with petrol reaching its highest price since November 2022.
The conflict in the Middle East disrupted global oil supplies, pushing oil prices above $91 a barrel.
Economists expect inflation to climb further, potentially peaking at 4.2% in January.

title: Piddington in Oxfordshire votes to leave UK over asylum plans
author: Indy Almroth-Wright
content:
![Herbert is putting a piece of paper - his vote - into a ballot box attached to the entrance of a village hall. He is holding a walking stick and is wearing a black coat over a shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/679f/live/78d281f0-b139-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
Local resident Herbert Owen cast his vote and described the referendum as "the Battle of Britain"
- Published
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.
Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.
The 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall, the community hub of Piddington.
The referendum was organised by the local parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, there were 26 no votes, and one ballot paper was spoiled.
Delivering the result, Susannah Parden, vice chair of the parish council said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."
Following the result, council chair Tim McNally said: "This is an example of democracy in operation.
"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea.
"We have given a message to the world."
Responding to the village saying it had "roared", Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told BBC Breakfast: "I think they have â we have heard it, we are listening.
"I do really understand that when changes are made that affect your community it can be very distressing.
"We inherited an enormous asylum backlog, we are processing claims much more quickly, we are removing people who don't have the right to be here," she said.
"Small boat crossing fell this summer for the first time in many years because of the action we have taken.
"While we get a grip on the asylum chaos that we inherited we do need to make sure that we live up to our obligations and house people coming to this country seeking safety."
summary: Residents of Piddington, Oxfordshire, held a symbolic referendum to vote for independence from the UK in protest against Home Office plans to house over 1,000 male asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Organized by the local parish council, 312 votes were cast, with 285 voters choosing to leave the UK. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy acknowledged the village's protest, stating that the government is listening while defending its efforts to manage the asylum system.
key_points: Piddington residents voted in a symbolic referendum to leave the UK in protest of asylum plans.
The protest was triggered by Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at MoD Bicester.
Out of 312 ballots cast outside the village hall, 285 voted in favor of independence.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy stated that the government hears the village's concerns while addressing inherited asylum challenges.

title: Search under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playground
author: Yassin El-Moudden
content:
Police are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a three-year-old boy who went missing on Tuesday during a visit to a playground near the Suffolk-Essex border.
The boy, named Noah, was last seen at 3pm in Merriam Close in Brantham, near Manningtree, before being separated from a relative. Officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah was reported to have run down an alleyway near the playground towards a housing estate.
He is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey. Police also confirmed that Noah is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss.
The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined in the search efforts by Tuesday evening and that train services between Manningtree and Ipswich were running at reduced speed while searches continued.
Police have cordoned off the alleyway and there were reports of door-to-door inquiries in the area.
A spokesperson for Suffolk constabulary said late on Tuesday: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches. Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”
A coastguard helicopter was also seen circling the village, which is near the estuary of the River Stour, and there were reports of sightings of drones flying overhead.
Anyone who believes that they have seen Noah is being asked to contact Suffolk police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.
summary: Police and local volunteers are searching for Noah, a three-year-old boy who went missing from a Suffolk playground on Tuesday afternoon. The child, who is autistic, non-verbal, and has partial hearing loss, was last seen running down an alleyway toward a housing estate. Emergency services, a coastguard helicopter, and over 100 people have joined the search efforts, while residents have been urged to check their gardens and outbuildings.
key_points: Three-year-old Noah went missing from a playground in Brantham on Tuesday afternoon.
He is described as white with curly ginger hair, wearing a Bluey T-shirt, shorts, and white trainers.
Noah is autistic, non-verbal, and has partial hearing loss.
Over 100 people, emergency services, and a coastguard helicopter are involved in the search.
Police have asked local residents to check their gardens, sheds, and outbuildings.

title: Lucy Letby hospital consultant says inquiry makes for grim reading
author: Judith Moritz
content:
Watch: Former consultant hopes Letby inquiry recommendations will prevent deaths happening again
- Published
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading".
Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit.
He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.
"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC.
"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."
The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday.
In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital".
The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns.
Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned.
"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that."
Gibbs, who began working in Chester in 1994 and is now retired, agreed with the report's finding that hospital executives had multiple opportunities to act and potentially save babies' lives while the deaths were happening.
"But it was during that 11 months after Lucy Letby was moved off the unit, before the police got involved, that it was a very difficult atmosphere, very tense, very stressful dealing with the managers," he added.
Managers "were determined to ensure that we accepted Lucy Letby had been wrongly suspected of doing any harm," the senior doctor explained.
He also spoke of the failures of his and his wider team, specifically referencing a doctor who disregarded blood test results that suggested a baby had been poisoned with insulin in August 2015.
While one of his colleagues had missed the relevance of the results when they came back from the lab, it had been a collective team failure, Dr Gibbs concluded.
"Others of us were on call and covering the neonatal unit over the next week or two before the baby moved out of the unit. We all had the opportunity to review the notes."
![Custody image of Lucy Letby, who has long blonde hair and is wearing a red top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/7acf/live/e2ec92b0-b0da-11f1-b427-b9b4ddc559ae.jpg)
The inquiry looked into the actions of managers at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked
Letby is serving 15 whole-life terms for the murders and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), an independent body set up to examine potential miscarriages of justice, is currently reviewing her convictions.
In the weeks and months after Letby was convicted, questions about the case arose in the form of online conspiracy theories and discourse from serious academics, including medical experts and statisticians.
Gibbs said that the continuing support for Letby had taken a toll on him and other consultants, and that claims she had been wrongly convicted were "frustrating and difficult" to hear.
"I particularly find the misinformation that's on the internet is difficult to deal with," he said.
He added: "I haven't changed my mind that I think Lucy Letby is guilty."
However, he emphasised that, because of the "calibre of some of the people who've raised concerns", it is "important" that the evidence used to convict Letby is being examined by the CCRC.
  - Published3 hours ago
 ![A split composite of Lucy Letby's mugshot and the sign outside Countess of Chester Hospital](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/22a9/live/d6214980-b103-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
- ![Blond woman sitting at table with arms over books](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/34c7/live/76ff9680-b114-11f1-9754-4d2fea96a9ee.jpg)
summary: A former consultant paediatrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital has stated that the final Thirlwall Inquiry report on Lucy Letby makes for "grim reading" and accepted collective responsibility for failing to involve the police sooner. Dr John Gibbs apologized to the victims' families, acknowledging that hospital managers dismissed concerns while noting that consultants also missed critical clues, such as poisoned insulin test results. Despite ongoing online misinformation and an independent review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission, Dr Gibbs remains convinced of Letby's guilt.
key_points: Dr John Gibbs stated that the Thirlwall Inquiry report on the Lucy Letby case makes for "grim reading" and admitted consultants share collective responsibility for not contacting the police earlier.
The inquiry report concluded there was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit and found that hospital managers repeatedly dismissed doctors' concerns.
Dr Gibbs apologized to the victims' families, noting that he and his team failed to act on vital evidence, such as blood test results showing insulin poisoning.
Dr Gibbs described ongoing online misinformation and support for Letby as frustrating, though he acknowledged the importance of the Criminal Cases Review Commission examining the conviction evidence.

title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
author: Ian Aikman; Judith Moritz; Lauren Hirst
content:
![A split composite of Lucy Letby's mugshot and the sign outside Countess of Chester Hospital](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/22a9/live/d6214980-b103-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others
- Published
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders.
Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin.
Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier.
Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital.
Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt."
She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed.
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Letby with hospital managers, consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs, now retired, told the BBC the Thirlwall Inquiry report was "grim reading".
In a rare interview he said he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report, and said he wished they had been "brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier".
Chief executive and registrar at the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), Paul Rees, said he was "truly sorry for the NMC's failings" in the Letby case and that "we also did not act quickly enough to suspend Lucy Letby".
Watch: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby report
Sharing her findings at Liverpool Town Hall, Thirlwall described "dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding".
Letby was moved on to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team.
But the inquiry has found that alarm bells should have been sounded earlier.
There were several "missed opportunities" for hospital bosses to intervene, the report said, including when three babies died in one cluster in June 2015.
Parents of the babies were "kept in the dark for years" over the concerns that their babies might have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry also found.
Thirlwall described the lack of consideration shown to parents as "reprehensible".
The report is highly critical of managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
Hospital bosses carried out a number of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but did not invite Cheshire Police to investigate until May 2017.
Letby remained on site until her arrest more than a year later.
Cheshire Police said it would "carefully review" the contents of the report and "fully consider" relevant recommendations.
Thirlwall said the hospital's former chief executive Tony Chambers behaved in a "dictatorial manner" and had "intended" to obstruct a police investigation into deaths on the ward.
Chambers, along with director of nursing and head of safeguarding Alison Kelly and medical director Ian Harvey, "dismissed the idea that Letby was deliberately harming babies", Thirlwall added.
But whether these managers believed Letby was harming babies or not was "irrelevant", Thirlwall said, adding that action should have been taken as soon as concerns were raised.
In a joint statement, Chambers, Kelly and Harvey along with the hospital's former HR director Sue Hodkinson said: "We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations.
"Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time.
"Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital."
Letby "should have been removed from the ward," Thirlwall says
The inquiry also condemned wider NHS culture, finding evidence of "toxic negativity" that discouraged whistleblowers.
The chair of the British Medical Association said on Tuesday that whistleblowers in the NHS "deserve strong protections, and the inquiry makes it clear that these doctors did not get them".
Regulator the Care Quality Commission (CQC) was also criticised, with the report saying it did not show enough curiosity to look beyond what it was being told by the Countess of Chester Hospital.
Responding to the report, the CQC's chief inspector of hospitals said "crucial information" was not shared by the Countess of Chester, but that the commission as a regulator did not take a "sufficiently investigative and inquiring" approach.
Dr Tony Onon said the regulator had since changed its approach to assessments.
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she was "profoundly sorry" on behalf of the government for the failures set out in the report.
She said she had asked officials to "urgently develop plans" for cot-cams in neonatal units, and that the government would consider Thirlwall's other recommendations in full.
Cooper also said she expected NHS leaders across the country to uphold their safeguarding responsibilities.
She plans to meet Thirlwall, who made 17 recommendations including restricting access to insulin, later this week to discuss the inquiry in more detail.
![Image shows Lucy Letby, wearing a blue hooded top, being led in handcuffs from her house, in footage captured on a police body camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8230/live/82d26b60-b0ea-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Lucy Letby has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions
The consultant paediatrician who had tried to raise his concerns about Letby to hospital management said he accepted the police should have been contacted sooner.
Dr John Gibbs was working at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby carried out her crimes.
"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he said.
"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."
He also spoke about the failure of consultants to spot the significance of blood test results that suggested a baby had been poisoned with insulin in August 2015.
He described this as "a collective team failure".
He said: "Others of us were on call and covering the neonatal unit over the next week or two before the baby moved out of the unit. We all had the opportunity to review the notes.
"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that.
"In a careful way, Lady Justice Thirlwall points out how we could and should have escalated matters ultimately to the police earlier than we did."
Gibbs said he agreed with the report's finding that hospital executives had multiple opportunities to act and potentially save babies' lives.
'Unimaginable suffering'
Chief executive and registrar at the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), Paul Rees, said his thoughts were with the babies that died or came to harm and their families "who have endured unimaginable suffering and pain".
He said: "From the moment concerns about Letby were first brought to the NMC's attention 10 years ago we should have stepped up proactively, shown a sense of professional curiosity and triggered action at a senior level.
"We should have considered the possibility of deliberate harm much earlier than we did."
He said the NMC had since "strengthened our guidance on interim orders", which clarified to "our decision-makers that they can seek to restrict or suspend a professional's practice much earlier".
Thirlwall was clear that her inquiry was not an investigation into Letby's guilt, which some supporters of the jailed nurse still contest.
A number of Letby supporters gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall to voice their concerns over her conviction, calling for her release, before Thirlwall delivered her inquiry findings.
Now 36, Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.
She was convicted in 2023 and has been denied permission to appeal against her convictions twice.
summary: Following the Thirlwall Inquiry into nurse Lucy Letby's crimes, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper announced plans to urgently develop live-streaming cameras for baby wards. The inquiry report sharply criticized management at the Countess of Chester Hospital for a profound failure of safeguarding and governance, noting that some babies' lives could have been saved if action had been taken sooner. The report also highlighted missed opportunities by hospital bosses, regulatory shortcomings, and a wider NHS culture of toxic negativity.
key_points: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper stated that officials will urgently develop plans to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards.
The Thirlwall Inquiry concluded that some babies killed by Letby could have been saved if hospital managers had acted earlier.
The inquiry report heavily criticized the Countess of Chester Hospital's management for a profound failure of governance and safeguarding.
Recommendations from the inquiry include installing CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin.
The Nursing and Midwifery Council and the Care Quality Commission were also criticized for failing to act quickly enough or show sufficient investigative curiosity.

title: Leader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assault
author: Ben Quinn; Bethan McKernan
content:
The leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.
Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, had only been announced as Reform UK’s Welsh leader by Nigel Farage in February.
He was elected to the Senedd as leader of the opposition in May’s election to the Welsh parliament, when Reform UK emerged as the second largest party.
However, it emerged on Tuesday that Thomas would not be taking part in the first plenary session of the new Senedd term and questions for the first minister on Tuesday afternoon. Reform said he was absent for “personal reasons”.
In a statement later on Tuesday afternoon, Thomas said: “Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account.”
![Dan Thomas shaking hands with Nigel Farage on stage](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3dc55964b4b3471783adb8886d66fd8e51b87302/264_0_4484_3589/master/4484.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Gwent police said: “On Sunday 13 September, a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further inquiries.”
Thomas, a former Conservative leader of Barnet council in north London, is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly.
Eyebrows had been raised on Monday when Thomas was notably quiet when it came to commenting on the meeting of the nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, who had declared that: “Westminster’s time is coming to an end.”
His resignation comes as a heavy blow to Reform, which has poured significant resources into Wales, where it believes further inroads could be made in traditional Labour strongholds.
However, the perception of Thomas as a figure who was parachuted in by Reform headquarters has caused tensions.
It is believed Farage chose an outsider to the Welsh branch of the party in an effort to distance Reform from its former Welsh leader, Nathan Gill, who was jailed for accepting bribes to make pro-Russia statements in the European parliament.
Since the new Senedd opened in May, there have been frequent reports of infighting in the Reform group, and its performance in the Siambr so far has been notable for unparliamentary conduct.
Thomas previously led Barnet council between 2019 and 2022, when the north London council was seized by Labour, and defected to Farage’s Reform party last summer.
He stood down in December as a councillor for Finchley Church End – long synonymous with Margaret Thatcher – to move back to his south Wales valleys home town.
In May, Reform won 34 seats at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives in the newly expanded 96-seat chamber of the Welsh parliament, behind Plaid Cymru’s 43.
Reform had been aiming to become Wales’s biggest party, Thomas said, but it still performed better than any Welsh Conservative result on record and managed to increase its vote share from 1% in 2021 to 29% in 2026. With more than a third of the seats, the Senedd is the biggest political platform Reform has had to date.
At almost exactly the same time that Thomas announced his resignation, the Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd said she was defecting to Plaid Cymru – a party nearly on the opposite end of the political spectrum.
![Sarah Cooper-Lesadd](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9010d55f38dd24273de878c7257c3a2adf1022c7/0_3_1000_800/master/1000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
She said in a statement: “[Reform UK] … are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions.
“Their Senedd group is a staging post in the effort to get Nigel Farage into Downing Street and that was glaringly obvious at its conference this week.”
Ken Skates, the leader of the Labour Senedd group, said: “Nigel Farage chose to make Nathan Gill his leader in Wales and he turned out to be a Russian asset. He chose to take £5m from a crypto billionaire that triggered an investigation.
“He chose to meet two men in a pub in Clacton to discuss breaching electoral law. And he chose to make Dan Thomas his leader in Wales, who has now quit suddenly.
“That Farage and Reform are in such a dire mess is bad enough, but it’s also bad for Plaid, welcoming a Reform defector who just a few weeks ago characterised herself as being rightwing.”
summary: Dan Thomas has stepped down as the leader of Reform UK in Wales following his arrest and bail on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour. Appointed by Nigel Farage in February, Thomas stated he resigned to prevent his situation from distracting from the party's work in the Senedd. His departure is a significant blow to the party, which recently emerged as the second-largest party in the Welsh parliament.
key_points: Dan Thomas was arrested on September 13 on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour, and has been bailed pending inquiries.
Thomas stated he denies wrongdoing but stepped down to avoid negative headlines distracting from his Senedd team.
Reform UK became the second largest party in the Senedd following the May elections, where Thomas was elected as leader of the opposition.
Simultaneously with Thomas's resignation, Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd announced her defection to Plaid Cymru.

title: Three babies may have survived if hospital had acted over Lucy Letby concerns, inquiry finds
author: Josh Halliday
content:
Three babies may have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses and doctors had taken action over concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby, an official inquiry into the deaths has concluded.
A public inquiry led by Lady Justice Thirlwall found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.
In a series of devastating findings, the judge said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.
Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses may have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care.
Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016.
The former neonatal nurse protests her innocence and is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”.
The court of appeal has twice rejected Letby’s bid to challenge her convictions. The Criminal Cases Review Commission, which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal.
Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.
“There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.”
In her 822-page report, Thirlwall recommends sweeping changes to the NHS – including installing 24-hour cameras on every cot in a neonatal unit – and beefed-up oversight from the healthcare regulator, the Care Quality Commission.
However, the inquiry chair said she was not reassured that ministers would act on her recommendations after the abolition of NHS England and little clarity on which body would take responsibility.
She accused successive governments of an “inexcusable” failure to enact the reforms of similar public inquiries over the last 30 years.
Letby, who joined the Countess of Chester hospital from university in 2012, was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. In less than two weeks that month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year.
Senior doctors became increasingly concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives.
However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police.
Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016.
![Exterior of women's and children's building at the hospital](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/08bb40b68f37613e1fc910cc99d8e989944b5cad/0_345_5100_3060/master/5100.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The inquiry, which received evidence from nearly 400 witnesses, found that parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed. This was “reprehensible”, Thirlwall said.
Despite the concerns of senior doctors, the inquiry found that the hospital’s risk and patient safety department took no action until the end of June 2016, when two twin boys died unexpectedly. Thirlwall said the department “failed in its fundamental task to enhance patient safety”.
The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors.
Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found.
Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”.
She said the precise number of deaths that may have been prevented would never be known for sure.
However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm.
Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.
While Letby’s case has attracted international attention as potentially one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British history, there is no mention in the 822-page report of the questions surrounding her convictions.
Thirlwall last year rejected applications by Letby’s legal team and four hospital executives to pause her inquiry until the CCRC has decided whether it believes her convictions may be unsafe. She said at the time it was not Letby’s actions she was scrutinising, but those of her colleagues and senior managers.
The CCRC is assessing material from an international panel of experts convened by Letby’s legal team who believe there is no medical evidence she murdered or harmed any of the infants she was accused of attacking.
summary: An official public inquiry led by Lady Justice Thirlwall has concluded that three babies may have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses and doctors had acted sooner on concerns regarding nurse Lucy Letby. The inquiry found a complete failure to protect babies at the Countess of Chester hospital, citing dysfunctional management, a prolonged delay in calling the police, and a failure to understand safeguarding fundamentals. Letby is currently serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering and attempting to murder babies at the hospital, while her convictions face ongoing reviews by the Criminal Cases Review Commission.
key_points: Lady Justice Thirlwall's inquiry found a complete failure by hospital bosses and doctors to act on concerns regarding Lucy Letby.
The report concluded that two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.
Senior nurses and the hospital's risk and patient safety department effectively dismissed concerns and delayed calling the police for nearly two years.
The inquiry recommended sweeping NHS changes, including 24-hour cameras on every neonatal cot and enhanced regulatory oversight.
Letby maintains her innocence and her case is currently being reviewed by the Criminal Cases Review Commission.

title: Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK
author: Priya Bharadia
content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK.
The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection.
The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors.
It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.
Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision.
The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK.
The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision.
Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.
“The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”
The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals.
The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”.
The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic.
“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine.
“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.
“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are undergoing a publicly funded security review by the royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec) following their return to the UK as full-time residents. The committee has commissioned new risk assessments for both Harry and Meghan and requested details regarding their schedules and daily routines. This development comes after Harry previously lost a legal challenge regarding the withdrawal of his automatic tax-funded security when the couple stepped back as working royals in 2020.
key_points: Ravec is reconsidering the police protection level for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex after their return to the UK.
The committee has commissioned new risk assessments for both Harry and Meghan and asked for their schedules and daily routines.
Harry previously lost a legal challenge against the Home Office over the removal of his automatic tax-funded security in 2020.
A formal letter from King Charles recently reiterated that the couple are non-working royals akin to private citizens.
The couple recently switched their children to a new school due to security and practical concerns regarding the journey.

title: Experts quit Lucy Letby’s defence team over ‘scientific credibility’ concerns
author: Josh Halliday
content:
Two leading experts have withdrawn from Lucy Letby’s defence team over concerns about the “scientific credibility” of some of its evidence.
The former neonatal nurse is challenging her convictions for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the UK’s miscarriage of justice watchdog, is considering a dossier of evidence submitted last year by experts on her behalf.
Two experts withdrew from Letby’s defence team on Monday. They said that although they stood by their assessment that it was “very unlikely” two of the babies were poisoned, some of the arguments being put forward on her behalf were “inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology”.
Helen Shannon, a British chemical engineering expert, and Geoff Chase, a professor of bioengineering based in New Zealand, produced a 100-page report last year casting doubt on her convictions for poisoning two babies with insulin.
They told the Guardian last year there was a “very strong level of reasonable doubt” about those two convictions, which formed a central part of the prosecution case against Letby. The 36-year-old nurse was convicted in 2023 of trying to murder two newborn boys, known as Baby 6 and Baby 12, by spiking their feeding bags with insulin.
Letby is serving 15 whole-life orders after she was convicted across two trials at Manchester crown court of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, with two attempts on one of her victims, between June 2015 and June 2016.
Shannon and Chase said on Monday they stood by their assessment, but could not support other evidence used by Letby’s defence team relating to the insulin cases.
In a letter to the CCRC, the experts said: “Whilst it is entirely legitimate for the defence to advance multiple arguments, some of the other arguments now being put forward we cannot support as scientifically credible and which have, in our view, fundamental unresolvable problems.”
They said the strategy of Letby’s defence team, led by her barrister Mark McDonald, was “placing the long-term interests of Ms Letby at serious, unnecessary and unacceptable risk” and that those “consequences also extend to the families” of the babies who died and were injured.
![Mark McDonald](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/42f89c79a031b42909aa69343bea895b6bb70f96/466_0_4657_3726/master/4657.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
They added: “We cannot, with integrity, support arguments which are inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology … After disclosing these concerns, continued association with arguments we believe are demonstrably inaccurate creates a serious ethical issue under the professional engineering codes governing us in New Zealand and the UK, and exposes us to professional sanction.”
McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “We now have evidence from a number of leading international experts in insulin, endocrinology and laboratory medicine which fundamentally undermines the scientific evidence relied upon at trial. Importantly, the case does not stand or fall on any one expert.
“The strength of the new evidence lies in its breadth and convergence, with independent experts from different disciplines and jurisdictions identifying fundamental problems with the scientific basis upon which the jury were invited to conclude that babies [6] and [12] had been deliberately poisoned.”
The CCRC, which has been reviewing the convictions for 18 months, declined to comment.
A public inquiry into the murders will publish its findings on Tuesday. The review, led by Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall, is expected to highlight a number of missed opportunities for bosses to intervene after doctors raised the alarm about a spate of unexplained deaths on the neonatal unit in 2015 and 2016.
A criminal investigation is ongoing into potential corporate manslaughter and gross negligence manslaughter at the Countess of Chester hospital.
summary: Two leading scientific experts have withdrawn from the defence team of convicted former nurse Lucy Letby over concerns regarding the scientific credibility of certain arguments being used to challenge her convictions. While Helen Shannon and Geoff Chase stand by their previous report casting doubt on the insulin poisoning convictions, they stated that other arguments put forward by the defence are inconsistent with established science and physiology. Letby's barrister, Mark McDonald, maintains that the overall case relies on a broad range of independent expert evidence that undermines the original trial's scientific conclusions.
key_points: Two experts, Helen Shannon and Geoff Chase, withdrew from Lucy Letby’s defence team due to concerns over scientific credibility.
The withdrawing experts stated that some defence arguments are inconsistent with available evidence, science, and physiology.
Shannon and Chase previously co-authored a 100-page report casting doubt on Letby's convictions for poisoning two babies with insulin.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is currently considering the dossier of evidence regarding Letby's convictions.
Defence barrister Mark McDonald stated that the case does not rely on any single expert and is supported by international specialists from various disciplines.

title: Ministers seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegal
author: Pippa Crerar; Jessica Elgot; Kiran Stacey
content:
Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced.
In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt.
Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party.
Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons.
Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status.
The extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election.
However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill.
The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year.
Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028.
Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June.
“Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.”
![Taylor in Lords](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/02998141f3e43669ef9da5402c799df895ef94bf/258_2_652_521/master/652.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Sharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions.
“We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added.
However, MPs and peers who have been pushing for a full domestic donations cap are unlikely to be satisfied by the new amendments. Government sources have said they do not want to delay the bill’s progress further by considering such a cap, but are open-minded on further legislation. MPs have voiced anger in internal WhatsApp groups that the chance has been missed to cap domestic donations in this bill while it was in the Commons.
Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.
“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said.
“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”
Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations.
The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.
Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.
However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day.
In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.”
The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality.
Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps.
“The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.
“But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?”
MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament.
They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval.
Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said.
Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.
summary: The UK government plans to table retrospective amendments to legislation in the House of Lords to introduce stricter residency requirements for political donors, potentially thwarting Reform UK's unprecedented £72m donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Under the proposed rules, individual donors must prove ongoing physical presence in the UK aligned with tax residency standards, which could delay Reform's access to the funds until January 2028. While Nigel Farage defended the donations as fully compliant with current laws, cabinet ministers and trade union leaders criticized the large sums from wealthy individuals attempting to influence politics.
key_points: Reform UK announced two separate £36m donations from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
The government will table amendments to the representation of the people bill to enforce stricter physical residency requirements for political donors.
The proposed rules require donors to demonstrate an ongoing presence in the UK, potentially delaying Reform from accessing the funds until 2028.
Nigel Farage maintained that the donations comply with existing laws, while government ministers and union officials argued against wealthy individuals having undue influence on democracy.

title: Richard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’ | John Crace
author: John Crace
content:
Never in the field of British politics has so much been given to so many by so few. You’d have thought Nigel Farage would have wanted to explain Reform’s sudden windfall from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo himself. To bask in the glory of the donations from two down-to-earth, anti-establishment crypto billionaires. Men who know what it’s like to graft, who know the meaning of an honest day’s work for an honest day’s pay.
There again, Nige is keen not to appear as a one-man band these days and he could do with some downtime to enjoy his own £5m handout. And besides, he’s got a police investigation into Reform party funding to worry about. Even so, it wasn’t the best of looks to send Richard Tice out on to the morning media round. Dicky may have his talents, but he keeps them well concealed. His main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy. But he does always leave you guessing. Is he being wilfully stupid or is he naturally that half witted?
Dicky began with a howl of protest. No rules had been broken. He made that sound as if it came as a surprise to him. I guess that’s an easy mistake for anyone to make. Everything was in the rules as they exist. Labour was mounting a coup against Reform for having passed legislation through the Commons that would prevent donors living overseas from giving more than £100,000 until they had lived in the UK for more than a calendar year, backdated to March 2026. You’d have thought Nige might have clocked this. But he probably hadn’t been in Westminster that day. And you can’t trust Dicky to be over the details.
“Our money comes with no demands,” Dicky told Nick Robinson on the Today programme. Harborne and Delo were patriots. All they wanted was to save the country from being ruined by socialists and the rightwing Tories. Quite where he thought Reform fitted in on this particular continuum wasn’t clear. Presumably in the centre ground of British politics. Ordinary men and women who want to rescue their country from the do-goodery of the RNLI.
“Patriots” was doing some heavy lifting here. Harborne had decamped to Thailand in the 90s, had become a Thai citizen in 2011 and had taken a Thai name. Now we learned that Dicky believed in dialectics. The more someone looked as if they were trying to put as much distance between themselves and the UK, the greater their commitment to the UK really was. Chris had just been playing very hard to get. The reality was he had been begging HMRC to ask him back so he could pay his fair share to the exchequer.
Fine, said Robinson. When did he move back to the UK and does he now pay UK tax? Dicky was understandably clueless. He had no idea he was going to be asked whether Harborne complied with the law as it was going through parliament. I’m not his tax adviser, he protested, though if he was he would make sure he paid as little as possible. Dicky has always been upfront in his belief that only the little people pay tax. And as for Harborne’s whereabouts, he wasn’t his diary secretary. He just telepathically knew that Chris had complied with the law as it was and as it was proposed.
It was the same with Delo. No man had ever loved his country more. From Hong Kong. Who wouldn’t want to receive money from a billionaire who had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with money-laundering laws and had been pardoned by Donald Trump? Dicky had no idea when Ben had come back to the country. That sort of level of detail was well above his pay grade. He was just here for the front-of-house stuff. The meet and greet. No one should expect any more from him than that.
Then the killer line. “I hope you will trust the word of our compliance team,” said Dicky. They would assure listeners everything was above board. So touching. So sweet. Up till now, no one had any idea Reform even had a compliance team. They certainly hadn’t been much in evidence while James Orr and Dan Jukes had been negotiating a possible £500,000 gift from an overseas donor. And in the taped conversation, which Nige insisted he hadn’t been listening to, Farage had said, “it’s all above board”.
So, if it’s all the same, we won’t be taking the word of an imaginary compliance team. Nick pressed on. What did Dicky think had attracted two crypto billionaires to a party that had promised to cut taxes on crypto, to limit regulation of the industry and had threatened to remove the governor of the Bank of England if he didn’t play ball?
Dicky couldn’t quite put his finger on it. But he thought it was probably something to do with them really caring about a £500 tax break. And the pleasure of paying for Nige’s hideous suit. Champagne and oysters all round.
There was just time for Robinson to point out that, far from getting nothing for their donations, the two men had already got everything they wanted and more. “Not at all,” Dicky insisted. Because Reform had promised to deregulate and cut tax before the two men had handed over the £72m. Where can you go with someone as dim as Dicky? A tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity. Though Harborne and Delo just have.
It was left to Farage himself to clear up Tice’s mess later in the day in a BBC interview. Well, sort of. Yes, Delo and Harborne’s donations probably wouldn’t meet the necessary deadlines for the legislation going through parliament. But you couldn’t blame Reform for taking the cash. Rather it was the fault of the government for putting in place regulations that Reform might not now be able to get round. As so often with Nige, there was always someone else to blame.
Not that Labour was immune from a little hypocrisy. It had been Burnham who had tried to bury the plan to limit donations to all parties. Something the unions had pushed back against. But the £72m has rather concentrated everyone’s minds. Once the current legislation was through parliament there would still be a good year to pass another law to impose a cap. Down in Brighton, Angela Rayner wanted the TUC to know she was on their side. There was no equivalence between Labour funding from the unions and money from two crypto billionaires. Politics could be bought. Just by the right sort of people.
summary: Richard Tice defended Reform UK's acceptance of large donations from crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo during a media appearance, insisting all rules were followed. Tice described the donors as patriots despite their overseas residency, though he was unable to answer detailed questions regarding their tax status or whereabouts. The interview also highlighted questions over whether the donations were linked to Reform's policy promises to deregulate the crypto industry and cut taxes.
key_points: Richard Tice defended Reform UK's receipt of substantial donations from overseas-based crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo.
Tice maintained that no rules were broken by accepting the funds and claimed the donors acted out of patriotism.
During a media interview, Tice struggled to answer specific questions about the donors' locations and tax compliance.
Nigel Farage later addressed the donations, blaming government regulations rather than Reform for the timing of the funds.

title: Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nations
author: Bethan McKernan
content:
Westminster’s time is coming to an end, the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have said at a landmark summit aimed at putting the UK’s Celtic nations on the path to independence referendums.
The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth; the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney; Sinn Féin’s vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, and the president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, met in Cardiff on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding recognising that “the political landscape across these islands is changing”.
“Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the memorandum read. “No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.
“We call for the British government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction.”
![The party leaders sat at a table during a press conference](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3e5b30ccfbaf381659c4a23aebae3f98a506fe82/247_0_5384_4307/master/5384.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
