Since becoming prime minister in July, Andy Burnham has put regional devolution of power and resources in England at the heart of his agenda, but policy towards the devolved administrations has so far been muddled.
The summit was the first face-to-face meeting for the sister parties since Plaid Cymru won May’s Senedd elections, which put separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time. The leaders met in their capacity as party, rather than government, officials, discussing economic, energy and international cooperation as well as self-determination.
Scottish independence and Irish reunification resurfaced on the news agenda last week when Burnham wrote to Swinney to reiterate that a repeat of 2014’s Scottish independence referendum remained “off limits” after apparently misspeaking during prime minister’s questions.
The US president, Donald Trump, also weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK during a visit to Ireland, saying he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and the unionist power-sharing members of the Northern Ireland executive.
Plaid Cymru has ruled out an independence referendum in its first term, but Welsh ministers are seeking fuller devolution powers on a par with Scotland and Northern Ireland, which Burnham has said he is “open” to.
Monday’s summit involved “powerful optics” and an opportunity for the nationalist parties to show how they are prepared to work together, said Laura McAllister, a professor of public policy at Cardiff University.
McAllister added: “If you look under the bonnet, though, the aims and the timelines for independence as sought by each of these first ministers is fundamentally different, as of course is the constitutional framework in each country.
“If there is a serious discussion of reformulating UK relationships there has to be a presence for England at the table … the irony is that we have a UK prime minister that says he is a devolutionist, but the constitutional question is far more problematic for him.”
after newsletter promotion
Latest polling suggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum, while data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland.
On Monday, Sinn Féin’s McDonald said she expected an Irish reunification poll to take place by 2030, while the SNP wants a second referendum within the next five years.
Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers next month.
A UK government spokesperson said: “The prime minister’s approach to working with the first and deputy first ministers in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is based on partnership and collaboration.
“The UK government is focused on addressing the issues that matter most to families, including easing pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums.”
summary: The first ministers and leaders of Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland held a landmark summit in Cardiff, declaring that Westminster's time is ending and calling on the British government to facilitate constitutional change and self-determination referendums. While the nationalist leaders signed a memorandum acknowledging a changing political landscape, experts note their aims and timelines for independence differ significantly. Meanwhile, the UK government emphasized its focus on partnership, economic security, and addressing family priorities rather than engaging in constitutional debates.
key_points: Leaders from Plaid Cymru, the SNP, and Sinn Féin met in Cardiff to sign a memorandum recognizing momentum toward constitutional change and self-determination.
The summit marked the first time separatist parties have been in government in Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland simultaneously.
Latest polling indicates independence support stands at 47% in Scotland, 36% in Northern Ireland, and 32% in Wales.
Sinn Féin expects an Irish reunification poll by 2030, while the SNP aims for a second Scottish independence referendum within five years.
The UK government stated its focus remains on economic security and household finances rather than constitutional referendums.

title: Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's Â£72m windfall
author: Joe Pike; Chris Graham
content:
![Nigel farage, wearing a light blue suit and white shirt, gestures with his left hand](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/a3ff/live/37b95cf0-aff1-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Nigel Farage's party has accused Labour of trying to "rig the system"
- Published
The House of Lords will debate changes to the laws on political donations later on Monday after Reform UK received Â£72m from two billionaires in 24 hours.
Calls for restrictions are growing after huge donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.
The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a Â£100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.
The leader of one of Labour's biggest funders, Unite the Union, is among those backing limits on individual donations. In response, Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice said the proposed change shows Labour was "terrified" of the party.
"We believe that we've done everything in complete accordance with the laws," he told BBC Breakfast.
He accused Labour of trying to "retrospectively introduce legislation in order to significantly disadvantage another political party".
Tice said the party's donations would enable it to "get on a level playing field" with other parties, likened it to Labour receiving donations from trade unions, and that "competition is a good thing".
Earlier, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) Paul Nowak pushed back on suggestions that Reform's donations was the same as trade unions funding Labour and influencing policy, saying "trade union money is the cleanest, most transparent money in British politics".
Speaking to the BBC Radio 4 Today programme ahead of the first full day of the TUC conference, he said: "Every decision that unions take about political funding, members decide, it's all in the open.
"Any conversation I ever have with a minister or a politician, everybody knows what I'm talking about, nobody knows what goes on behind closed doors with Christopher Harborne, Ben Delo and Nigel Farage."
The sheer scale of Reform's record-breaking donation windfall has prompted an urgent debate across the parties.
On Monday, the bill that would introduce a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British voters living abroad returns to the House of Lords.
The rules were proposed in a review by former civil servant Philip Rycroft aimed at countering foreign influence in UK politics.
![Ben Delo sitting on a leather armchair with his legs crossed, wearing a blue jacked and black trousers, sitting in front of a blackboard with mathematical equations written in chalk.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1248/cpsprodpb/a35f/live/b4988c10-b004-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
The self-described entrepreneur and philanthropist, Ben Delo, made headlines over the weekend with a record-breaking Â£36m donation to Reform UK.
The Labour peer Lord Wills told Radio 4's Westminster Hour he intended to amend the bill so that donations from those living in the UK could also be capped.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, told the BBC a limit on individual donations was necessary.
Her union has donated large sums to Labour in recent years, but she argues that "billionaires splashing out millions" is different from "everyday workers giving 10p a week to a political fund".
Reform have said "Labour and their union pals know they can't win an election fairly so now they want to rig the system".
Questions remain over whether Reform will be able to keep all of the Â£72m.
Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, told the BBC on Sunday the donations were "entirely in line with the law as it is, and as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future".
The government has also proposed a minimum residency period in which the Â£100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.
This would be in place for the rest of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".
Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she did not "understand" their "circumstances".
The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.
BBC News has been told both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.
The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/5a02/live/374965a0-b008-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.png)
- ![Reform UK leader Nigel Farage is wear a turquoise-coloured suit jacket, white shirt and a red tie with white dots.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/7114/live/73ceb2f0-af95-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
  - Published1 day ago
 ![Christopher Harborne (left) and Ben Delo (right)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/afa5/live/b18ef1b0-aea8-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
- ![Ben Delo stands next to a woman at the launch of UnHerd's new club on 23 November 2022 in London. Both are holding champagne flutes and smiling](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/359/cpsprodpb/82f3/live/33fbc200-ae2b-11f1-aa6c-6bdc87a16780.jpg)
summary: The House of Lords is set to debate changes to political donation laws following Reform UK receiving £72m in donations from two British billionaires living overseas. The government's proposed legislation includes a £100,000 cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March, which would require non-complying parties to return the funds. While Reform UK accused Labour of trying to rig the system and disadvantage their party, supporters of the limit argue that reigning in mega-donors is necessary to counter foreign influence and excessive billionaire funding.
key_points: Reform UK received £72m from billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne in a 24-hour period.
The government proposed a backdated £100,000 cap on political donations from British expats to counter foreign influence.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner stated that rule changes would apply retrospectively, meaning non-compliant funds must be returned.
Reform UK accused Labour of trying to rig the system, while critics and union leaders defended the need to limit massive individual donations.

title: Essex security patrols to start in three places near asylum base
author: Alex Pope
content:
![Aerial shot of the housing blocks at an airbase. Four rectangular accommodation blocks can be seen, surrounded by grass, trees and roads. There are agricultural fields in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4c7d/live/3109cc10-72ec-11f1-b1db-af71d47507d6.jpg)
The former Wethersfield airbase has housed asylum seekers since July 2023
- Published
Patrols by private security guards are to begin from Monday at three Essex locations that asylum seekers frequently visit, a council has confirmed.
Six trained and uniformed "security operatives" would patrol Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford centres seven days a week, from 10:00 to 18:00, as part of a three-month trial, said Reform UK-led Essex County Council.
The initiative, named Operation Vanguard, was launched in direct response to concerns raised by residents and would "deter anti-social behaviour", it added.
It came after the government said it was looking to increase the number of people at MDP Wethersfield - which has been used to house single male migrants since 2023 - from about 800 to 1,220.
However, new Essex Police chief constable Rachel Nolan said crime linked to the large asylum accommodation in the county was "very low".
![Peter Harris looking at the camera while standing in a wood-panelled council chamber. He is wearing a suit and tie. The tie is maroon and the blazer is navy blue. There are portraits on the wall in the background. He has two metal pin badges on a lapel - one of the union flag and one of the Essex triple seaxes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b3be/live/8aa419a0-7162-11f1-909a-0f95894a566f.jpg)
Peter Harris, the leader of Essex County Council, said patrols would start on Monday
Speaking to BBC Look East presenter Susie Fowler-Watt, Nolan said: "Crimes and incidents associated with the Wethersfield site are very low.
"Certainly, as far as I've seen, there is absolutely no reason for anyone to be concerned about criminality associated with migrants from the Wethersfield camp in Essex."
County council leader Peter Harris said: "Six trained security guards, two each in Braintree, Chelmsford and Colchester, will provide a visible and reassuring presence on our streets, particularly for women and children.
"Our message is simple: the safety of Essex residents comes first."
David King, a senior Liberal Democrat county councillor, previously said the scheme "risks divisions and community tension".
"It could only work if the security officers integrated with already established arrangements," he said. "They won't know the place, they won't know the people, they won't be connected up."
Chelmsford City Council's Stephen Robinson, who leads the Lib Dem-run authority, said: "I think it's really important that we don't create division and that policing is carried out by the police."
Meanwhile, Conservative county councillor Lee Scott said: "We're not opposing it, but we are in the future looking at it to see if it's succeeding and making people feel safe."
The government does not record criminal offences by immigration status, but according to analysis by the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, external, foreign nationals in England and Wales are convicted at roughly the same rate as British nationals.
The council said the trial was "a direct response to concerns raised amongst local residents - particularly women and girls - over gatherings of male migrants in town centres who were regularly transported in by bus from the former military airfield to spend their free time".
"It intends to deter anti-social behaviour, provide reassurance to residents and businesses, and gather evidence about whether additional support may be required," a spokesperson said.
The local authority said it would be funded by drawing down Â£150,000 from the "community innovation and improvement fund"., external
There would be no additional cost to taxpayers and no increase in council tax as a result of the scheme, it added.
Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.
summary: Essex County Council is launching a three-month trial of private security patrols in Braintree, Colchester, and Chelmsford to address resident concerns regarding male migrants visiting from the former Wethersfield airbase. Six uniformed security operatives will patrol the three centres daily from 10:00 to 18:00 to deter anti-social behavior. While the council states the £150,000 initiative aims to reassure residents and women and girls, local Liberal Democrat councillors have criticized the plan for potentially creating community divisions.
key_points: Private security patrols are set to begin on Monday in Braintree, Colchester, and Chelmsford as part of a three-month trial.
Six trained and uniformed security operatives will work seven days a week from 10:00 to 18:00.
The initiative, named Operation Vanguard, is funded by a £150,000 drawdown from the community innovation and improvement fund with no extra cost to taxpayers.
The new Essex Police chief constable stated that crimes and incidents associated with the Wethersfield site are very low.
Some local Liberal Democrat councillors have raised concerns that the security scheme risks increasing community tensions and divisions.

title: Andy Burnham to host entrepreneurs and local mayors at No 10 on Monday
author: Julia Kollewe
content:
The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK.
Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential.
The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said.
“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”
Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors.
They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems.
Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey, the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October.
Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy.
Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July, boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September.
Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises.
Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.
In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.
He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.
summary: The prime minister will host business leaders, entrepreneurs, and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to promote his government as a partner for growth and investment. Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham emphasized the need for a culture shift in British business and pledged to reindustrialise the country. The meetings precede the upcoming October 28 budget by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey, who face economic challenges including rising borrowing costs and energy impacts.
key_points: Andy Burnham and local mayors will meet with entrepreneurs and chief executives at Downing Street on Monday.
The government aims to position itself as a stable partner for investment, job creation, and economic growth.
Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are preparing for their first budget on October 28 amid rising borrowing costs.
Healey has committed to boosting economic growth while controlling public spending and adhering to strict fiscal rules.

title: Will record donations to Reform be a moment of political change?
author: Jack Fenwick
content:
![Reform UK leader Nigel Farage is wear a turquoise-coloured suit jacket, white shirt and a red tie with white dots.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/7114/live/73ceb2f0-af95-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
- Published
When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking Â£36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback.
The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away.
In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper.
Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team.
But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest.
Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised Â£30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals.
This extra Â£72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country.
In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important.
Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election.
It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine.
Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely.
Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations.
Labour is already planning to introduce a cap on the amount of money a British citizen living overseas can donate.
There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes.
The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations.
Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules.
Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers.
The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger.
Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate.
But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
  - Published3 hours ago
 ![Robert Jenrick is wearing a blue suit jacket, white shirt and green tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/656d/live/74d3c480-af61-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
- ![Ben Delo stands next to a woman at the launch of UnHerd's new club on 23 November 2022 in London. Both are holding champagne flutes and smiling](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/359/cpsprodpb/82f3/live/33fbc200-ae2b-11f1-aa6c-6bdc87a16780.jpg)
- ![Rhun ap Iorwerth in the TV studio for Laura Kuenssberg's Sunday programme](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/c59e/live/c1d6d740-af6b-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
summary: Reform UK has secured two record-breaking donations totaling £36m, bringing its total funds raised since the start of the year to uncharted levels. The party plans to use the financial war chest to hire policy minds and up to 400 campaign managers across target seats. Meanwhile, the massive influx of funds has intensified political discussions regarding potential caps on party donations.
key_points: Reform UK received two record-breaking donations of £36m each, taking their total recent funding significantly higher.
The party intends to use the funds to build a strong ground campaign by hiring up to 400 campaign managers in target seats and recruiting policy minds.
Labour is planning to introduce a cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, though officials declined to confirm if it would affect Reform's major donors.
Other parties like the Liberal Democrats and Greens are calling for caps on domestic donations to prevent future mega donations.

title: Meghan Markle declares love for UK after 'disappearing overnight' from US
author: Barney Davis; Meghan Markle
content:
Meghan Markle has filmed herself splashing in a British puddle to celebrate moving back to the UK.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex shared a sweet Instagram Story of her children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet running and cycling together.
The couple have moved back to the UK in recent weeks and have been enjoying life with Meghan and Harry seen walking hand in hand in a forest.
The duchess turns around to whoever is holding the camera and says: ‘Come on, you, come on.’
The footage also shows one of the children sitting by a roaring fireplace, Lili wearing wellies while riding a bicycle with training wheels with a doll on the back and Archie running past his sister in his wellies.

Archie, seven, and five-year-old Lili have started the new school year in Britain after the family relocated from the US a little over two weeks ago, according to People magazine.

summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have relocated back to the UK from the US after living abroad for six years. key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle moved back to the UK from the US after a six-year absence.
An Instagram Story shared by the couple featured children Archie and Princess Lilibet enjoying activities in Britain.

title: Reform's Â£72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
author: Richard Wheeler; Jack Fenwick
content:
Watch: Donations 'entirely in line with the law', says Jenrick
- Published
Robert Jenrick has said Reform UK believed that Â£72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law".
The party's economic spokesman told the BBC that he did not expect that it will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.
The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a Â£100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.
"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.
Jenrick also told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "It might be that [Housing Secretary] Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.
"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."
BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.
Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".
As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed limiting how much those who move back to the UK can give to Â£100,000 in the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after they return.
The measures were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.
Rayner, who also appeared on the programme, said the changes proposed by the government were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March.
Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date.
"That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy."
There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.
The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.
It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions.
"It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this."
![A graphic showing the relative accumulated donations to major political parties between July 2024 and June 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0fa3/live/bc18b070-af5d-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Since the 2024 election, the Conservative Party has raised Â£37m, Reform has raised Â£35m before Delo and Harborne's large donations, Labour had raised Â£21m, the Liberal Democrats Â£17m and the Green Party Â£1.9m
Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box".
She would not be drawn on whether the proposed changes would apply to Delo and Harborne, saying: "I don't know the individual circumstances of those donors."
Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".
He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions".
Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending.
She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10."
A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals."
Jenrick said Delo and Harborne - who each gave Â£36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda".
Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.
The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.
Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". Delo had written in the newspaper the day prior that he wanted to enable Reform to put up a "fair fight at the next election.
The Â£72m from the two is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year.
Delo was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMex, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.
Reform's fundraising has come under scrutiny in recent months. This includes police announcing an investigation over allegations the party broke foreign funding laws in a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.
The party's leader Nigel Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m gift he received from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.
Both Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing in both instances.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Reform UK economic spokesman Robert Jenrick has stated that £72m in donations received from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are entirely compliant with current and future laws. The government is currently seeking to change donation laws regarding British expats and establish a new taskforce to tackle mega-donors. Meanwhile, other political figures and parties have raised concerns about large donations and called for stricter campaign funding caps.
key_points: Reform UK received £72m in donations from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
Robert Jenrick stated the donations comply with the law and does not expect the party to return the money.
The government is proposing legal changes to limit donations from British expats and individuals returning to the UK.
Other parties, including the Liberal Democrats and the Green Party, have called for tighter caps on political donations.

title: Peaky Blinders warehouse on fire again
author: Liz Perkins
content:
![A dramatic picture from the air shows the multi-storey building on fire at night. It is a very big fire, with a large fire engine in the foreground](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000502639970_17892524733880_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNJjoeBT78QIaYdkJdEY4CnGTJFJS74MYhNY6w3GNbO8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A dramatic picture from the air shows the multi-storey building on fire at night. It is a very big fire, with a large fire engine in the foreground](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000502639970_17892524733880_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNJjoeBT78QIaYdkJdEY4CnGTJFJS74MYhNY6w3GNbO8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A major fire has broken out for a fifth time in five years at a textile mill that has been used as a filming location for Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey.
Twelve fire engines were called to Dalton Mills in Keighley at 8pm on Saturday.
The fire led to cordons and road closures along the city’s Dalton Lane as firefighters tackled the blaze at the 150-year-old building.
Robbie Moore, the MP for Keighley, said “the situation cannot continue” after another major blaze at the mill.
The Grade II-listed building has featured in a number of television shows but was targeted in an arson attack in 2011.
The interior was destroyed by a 2022 fire and there was a further arson attack in 2025.
Two fires in the space of six days at the derelict site in February 2026 were “deliberate”, according to West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service (WYFRS).
Mr Moore, who represents Keighley and Ilkley for the Conservative Party, said in a video posted on X: “You already will have seen that we have had another major fire in the centre of Keighley, which is deeply infuriating.
“This situation just simply cannot continue.
“I’ve been calling on our local authority to secure this site as best as possible for years now, and this is our next major fire.”
WYFRS advised people to avoid the area, with a number of residents evacuated.
“Due to the severity of the incident and the potential risk to residents living in close proximity to the fire, a number of nearby residents are now being evacuated,” they said in a statement late on Saturday.
“Local Authority Emergency Planning officers are on scene and are providing support and guidance to those affected by the evacuation.”
West Yorkshire Police said on Facebook: “Please be aware that Dalton Mills are currently on fire.
“Dalton Lane in Keighley is currently closed to all traffic, as our colleagues from West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service are working to bring the situation under control.
“We advise people to stay away from the area, and residents in the vicinity to keep all doors and windows closed.”
summary: A major fire has broken out at the historic Dalton Mills in Keighley for the fifth time in five years, prompting road closures and the evacuation of nearby residents. Twelve fire engines responded to the blaze at the 150-year-old Grade II-listed building, which has previously been used as a filming location for Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey. Local MP Robbie Moore expressed deep frustration over the recurring incidents, stating that the situation cannot continue and criticizing the ongoing lack of site security.
key_points: A major fire broke out at Dalton Mills in Keighley at 8pm on Saturday.
Twelve fire engines were deployed to tackle the blaze at the 150-year-old building.
Roads were closed and nearby residents were evacuated due to the severity of the fire.
The site has a history of previous fires, including a 2022 interior destruction and incidents in 2025 and 2026.
Local MP Robbie Moore criticized the lack of site security, stating the situation cannot continue.

title: Major fire breaks out at Dalton Mills as huge emergency response rushes to scene
author: Sam Reed
content:
Emergency services are at the scene of a major fire at Dalton Mills in Keighley this evening.
Reports of a blaze at the historic mill complex first emerged at around 8pm on Saturday night.
In a statement, West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue confirmed 12 fire engines were in attendance.
A T&A reporter at the scene has confirmed a significant response from all three emergency services, with police units and ambulances also in attendance.
The cause of the fire is not yet known, and no further details have been released.
Eyewitness accounts
One eyewitness said: "I was driving down the A650 and I could just see all this smoke.
  "I pulled over to have a look and I couldn't believe the size of the fire.
  
  "It's unbelievable."
  The blaze at Dalton Mills (Image: T&A)
A Keighley resident said: "Very saddened and shocked.
"This site has given a lot to the film industry and consequently the country."
Another eyewitness from Keighley said: "It seemed to start on the top floor. The roof had already gone, then we think the floor collapsed about 8:45pm to 9pm."
MP reaction
In a statement on social media Robbie Moore, MP for Keighley & Ilkley, said: "Extremely concerning scenes at Dalton Mills in Keighley this evening."
He added: "Huge thanks to our emergency services for all their efforts and bravery as they continue to tackle the blaze and put out this major fire, and ensure all are safe."
  The blaze at Dalton Mills (Image: T&A)
Statement in full
On social media, a spokesperson for West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue said: "At approximately 8:00pm, we were called to a large fire involving Dalton Mills, Keighley.
"We currently have 12 fire engines at the incident as firefighters continue to tackle the large incident.
"Please avoid the area while emergency crews work at the scene. Residents nearby are advised to keep their windows and doors closed until further notice.
"Thank you for your cooperation. Further incident updates to follow, link will be added to the comments."
The T&A has approached West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service, West Yorkshire Police and Yorkshire Ambulance Service for comment.
summary: A major fire broke out at the historic Dalton Mills complex in Keighley, prompting a large response from emergency services including 12 fire engines, police units, and ambulances. Reports of the blaze emerged around 8:00 pm on Saturday, with eyewitnesses noting extensive damage to the roof and upper floors. The cause of the fire remains unknown, and local residents have been advised to keep their windows and doors closed.
key_points: A major fire was reported at Dalton Mills in Keighley at around 8:00 pm on Saturday.
West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue confirmed 12 fire engines were deployed to tackle the blaze.
Police units and ambulances also responded to the scene in a significant emergency effort.
The cause of the fire is currently unknown and no further details have been released.
Nearby residents were advised to keep windows and doors closed while crews worked.

title: Second crypto billionaire donates record $49m to far-right Reform UK
author: Daniel Khalili-Tari
content:
![Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage (C), flanked by Deputy Leader Richard Tice (L) and shadow Home Secretary Zia Yusuf, at the end of his address on the third day of the party's annual conference](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa5ae12056c-1789242898.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A second British billionaire has made a record donation of almost $49m to the far-right Reform UK party, matching the amount pledged by another businessman the day before.
Writing in the Daily Telegraph British newspaper on Saturday, donor Christopher Harborne said the $48.7m (£36m) donation was a “philanthropic gift” to the country, adding that he felt “inspired” to match the contribution made by fellow billionaire Ben Delo 24 hours earlier.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why is Farage’s Reform accused of violating the UK’s foreign funding rules?
- list 2 of 3Nigel Farage heckled as he denies Reform UK took illegal funding
- list 3 of 3Reform UK says Britain is broken. Birmingham tells another story
Sixty-three-year-old Harborne is a Thailand-based cryptocurrency investor and Delo, 42, is the co-founder of the BitMEX cryptocurrency exchange.
Both donations bring the total sum of money pledged to Reform since Friday to $97m.
They coincide with a flurry of questions surrounding the party’s finances, with London’s Metropolitan Police confirming earlier this week the launch of a criminal investigation into whether Reform accepted illegal foreign donations.
Reform’s leader Nigel Farage celebrated the contributions in a post on X.
“You know what Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne want? Nothing,” Farage said.
“Just a government that will fix Britain. And that’s what Reform UK will deliver,” he added.
The leader of the right-wing Conservative Party, Kemi Badenoch, criticised Reform, accusing Farage and his colleagues of lacking integrity.
“You can buy staff and advertising, but you can’t buy judgement or integrity,” Badenoch posted on X.
“Sometimes a bigger cheque just means you make more of the same mistakes. The Conservatives are up for the fight.”
Reform has emerged as a major political force in the UK. However, the latest polling data suggests that the party has lost some voters since left-leaning Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister and Labour Party leader.
Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said both of Reform’s latest donors believe they are making British politics fairer.
“One of the reasons that Ben Delo gave for this huge record-breaking donation was to level the political playing field,” Nedelec said.
“That’s certainly a sentiment echoed by fellow billionaire Christopher Harborne, who compared Reform UK to a startup in need of a boost, because unlike the mainstream political parties, it doesn’t benefit from this inbuilt infrastructure of financial support and recurring donations.
“They certainly see this as a way of making British politics fairer. If we zoom out, Reform historically has had very few donations compared to the mainstream political parties,” she added.
Reform is the successor to Farage’s Brexit Party, which changed its name to Reform in 2021. Farage, who played a significant role in the Brexit movement, has long portrayed himself as an anti-establishment figure and has experienced a surge in popularity as voters grow increasingly disillusioned with the Conservatives and Labour. The two parties have historically dominated British politics, but a dramatic decline in living standards in recent years has fuelled demand for alternatives.
summary: British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne has donated a record $48.7m (£36m) to the far-right Reform UK party, matching a $49m pledge made by fellow crypto businessman Ben Delo a day earlier. The massive contributions bring Reform's total recent funding to $97m as the party faces a criminal investigation by the London Metropolitan Police regarding potential illegal foreign donations. Reform leader Nigel Farage celebrated the gifts, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch criticized the party, arguing that money cannot buy integrity.
key_points: Christopher Harborne donated $48.7m (£36m) to Reform UK, describing it as a philanthropic gift.
The donation matched a $49m pledge made 24 hours earlier by fellow cryptocurrency billionaire Ben Delo.
The donations coincide with a Metropolitan Police criminal investigation into whether Reform accepted illegal foreign donations.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch criticized Reform over the funds, stating that money cannot buy integrity.
Donors Harborne and Delo view the contributions as a way to level the political playing field for the anti-establishment party.

title: Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests
author: Sammy Gecsoyler; Raphael Boyd
content:
Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration.
Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.
They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.
One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.
A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.
![Protesters with Stand Up to Racism and other placards gather for a counter demonstration in Portsmouth on Saturday.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/dc69fea4e767a8d051863bf6eaf380637d27858a/697_0_5328_4264/master/5328.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Donna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.
Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.
“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.
“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”
![People at an anti-immigration march in Portsmouth waving union and St George flags and with placards.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bb5edaf040cc5c79e21d0c1a545b7a503bc5a7ce/0_0_4944_3296/master/4944.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.
Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.
A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.
In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.
Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.
![Union and saltire flags flying at the Pink Ladies anti-immigration event in Glasgow.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1ecba93683caf8b691f1c9dd237e8d084a1123a4/0_0_2975_2380/master/2975.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.
The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.
Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.
MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.
![A line of police officers face down a handful of protesters beside the People’s Palace. A crowd waving union jacks and saltires is visible behind the police line](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/43e7b1962839d09a0ae30e5ea93f78e6d060f701/229_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.
Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.
Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”
The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.
![Lifejackets abandoned by people seeking asylum who made the crossing from France on Sunday 6 September.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f129db7fa624fd248e437ebd648ef1099dedfb0a/442_0_4909_3928/master/4909.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.
Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.
Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.
The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.
![Police officers in riot gear at night at Eastney beach, Portsmouth.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c2a3840a8d6743190813d001f4d4362351ca26b4/251_0_4001_3201/master/4001.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.
Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.
The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.
Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.
“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”
summary: Portsmouth experienced a second weekend of anti-immigration protests and counter-protests, prompted by the recent arrival of a small boat carrying asylum seekers. Police made three arrests during Saturday's demonstrations, including one for concealing identity under new face-covering regulations. Meanwhile, similar rallies and counter-protests took place in Glasgow, as authorities maintained a heavy police presence to prevent violence.
key_points: Two men and a teenage boy were arrested in Portsmouth during the far-right anti-immigration protests and counter-demonstrations.
Police enforced powers under the Crime and Policing Act to arrest a 76-year-old man for concealing his identity with a face covering.
Saturday's protests followed a previous weekend of unrest in Portsmouth where asylum seekers were targeted and police officers were assaulted.
A separate anti-immigration rally and counter-protest also took place at Glasgow Green with a heavy police presence separating the groups.

title: Farage: £72m war chest will make Reform ready to rule
author: Gordon Rayner
content:
![Farage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000501085239_17892105534500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Farage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000501085239_17892105534500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Nigel Farage has declared that Reform UK will soon be “ready to form a government” after his party received £72m in donations from billionaire backers.
Just 24 hours after announcing it had been given a record £36m by Ben Delo, a cryptocurrency mogul, Reform went public with an identical donation from Christopher Harborne, its biggest donor.
The donations amount to a huge show of force by Reform’s wealthy supporters, and will turbocharge its attempts to build a party machine to rival the Conservatives and Labour as it prepares for the next general election.
Reform has now raised more than £86m in donations this year, dwarfing the £10.2m raised by the Conservatives and £7.7m by Labour and giving Mr Farage a personal boost after a testing summer during which his family urged him to quit politics.
Mr Farage still faces a parliamentary inquiry into a £5m personal gift from Mr Harborne and a police inquiry into donations from elsewhere, but the new influx of cash is intended to provide the momentum to carry him through to the next general election.
The Reform leader told The Telegraph: “The money will be used for one purpose only: to make certain we are ready to form a government at the next election.
“Reform UK will fund the best research and policy department British politics has ever seen. They will ensure our policies are properly costed and workable. And they will allow us to hire the best minds in every area in which expertise is required.”
Although Reform’s donations this year are more than eight times what any other party has raised, Mr Harborne and Mr Delo have pointed out that over the past five years the Tories and Labour had still raised more than Reform, which was why Mr Delo told The Telegraph on Friday that he was simply trying to level the playing field for the next election.
Writing for The Telegraph, Mr Harborne said that as a start-up party, Reform needed “more money than can be provided by membership fees alone” so that it could create the sort of infrastructure older parties had built over more than a century.
![Christopher Harborne pictured with Nigel Farage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000481554910_17892103303250_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqN4ePBoE4ef7kaLHd_OTbYyncIrmX9xxDOUHdD4MISRo.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Opponents of Reform have suggested Mr Farage has been given millions by his super-rich backers in exchange for championing their favourite causes.
In response, Mr Harborne writes: “What do I expect in return for my donations: nothing personally. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government. I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am now committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole.”
He describes his donation as “a philanthropic gift to our country”.
![Poster](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000500620740_17892113656770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqXfGug2YH0toTID9kulmfYSOwwQH1iiegFd5INOxSjBk.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Harborne says his three main concerns are the “existential threats” facing humanity of nuclear war, AI and climate change, and he believes Reform is the only party that has the policies to tackle them, by restoring the economy and creating the wealth needed to pay for defence, AI policies and clean nuclear energy.
Since January 2021, Reform has raised £110m, including the two latest gifts, while the Tories have raised £150m and Labour £128m.
As well as membership fees and donations, the Conservatives receive £5.5m in so-called Short money, which is allocated by Parliament to opposition parties based on how many MPs they have.
With eight MPs, Reform receives just over £400,000 in Short money, meaning it is almost entirely dependent on donations, while Labour receives between £5m and £10m each year from the trade unions.
Earlier this year, Labour imposed a cap of £100,000 on donations to political parties from expatriate donors in what was widely seen as an attempt to choke Reform’s funding.
The Government is proposing further restrictions on donations in its Representation of the People Bill, and some Labour MPs want Andy Burnham to go further by imposing caps on UK-based individual donors to match the cap on foreign donors.
Mr Delo has accused the Government of wanting to “rig” the next election and the donations from him and Mr Harborne have come before Labour has a chance to make major changes to donation rules.
Mr Harborne admitted that when he heard Mr Delo was giving £36m – which equates to £1m a month between now and the latest date Mr Burnham can call the next election – “my competitive spirit inspired me to match it”.
He writes: “I want us to be able to afford to fund healthcare, education and other public services like social care which are incredibly important to me and the whole of our country.
“But these vital services can only be delivered if our country is strong. And a strong country is one that is funded by a vigorous economy which is creating jobs.”
He believes Reform is the party with the best chance of delivering that.
The money comes as a shot in the arm for Mr Farage after a summer in which he has become the subject of not only a parliamentary investigation but also a police investigation into party funding, partly as a result of a Channel 4 undercover sting.
Reform’s polling has been faltering since Mr Burnham became Prime Minister, and the Tories have been enjoying increased public support under the leadership of Kemi Badenoch.
The extra £72m will enable Reform to recruit more staff at its headquarters, particularly in its policy team, and employ campaign managers in target constituencies to prepare for battles on the ground.
Mr Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne have shown such confidence in Reform.
“Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election. Thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field.”
Mr Harborne has been based in Thailand for decades but is registered as a UK resident for voting and donating purposes.
A Labour Party spokesman said: “Farage and Reform are showing exactly whose side they’re on. Crypto-billionaire ultra donors are lining up to help Farage buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he’s drowning in.
“It won’t work and shows the public exactly who he is and who pays for him. The Labour Government is taking action to safeguard our democracy, action that will ensure we clean up politics for good.”
Writing on X, Mrs Badenoch said: “You can buy staff and advertising, but you can’t buy judgment or integrity. Sometimes a bigger cheque just means you make more of the same mistakes.
“The Conservatives are up for the fight. We are raising millions, attracting new donors and winning back old ones.
“Britain does not need another protest party. It needs common sense, a serious plan and a party capable of bringing the country together. That is who we are. And it is what Reform will never be.”
summary: Nigel Farage announced that Reform UK is preparing to form a government after receiving a combined £72m in donations from cryptocurrency mogul Ben Delo and investor Christopher Harborne. The substantial funds will be used to build a robust party infrastructure, fund research and policy departments, and hire expert staff for the next general election. While donors frame the gifts as a philanthropic effort to level the political playing field, political opponents from Labour and the Conservatives have criticized the funding.
key_points: Reform UK received two record-breaking £36m donations from billionaire backers Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, totaling £72m.
Nigel Farage stated the funds will be used to ensure the party is ready to form a government and build a top-tier policy department for the next election.
Reform has raised over £86m this year, significantly outpacing donations received by the Conservative and Labour parties.
The large influx of cash arrives while Nigel Farage faces parliamentary and police inquiries regarding past party funding and personal gifts.
Both Labour and Conservative figures have criticized the massive donations, arguing that money cannot buy integrity or proper political judgment.

title: I feel overwhelming relief for my daughter after the defeat of assisted dying
author: Rosa Monckton
content:
![Domenica Lawson, photographed with her mother, Rosa Monckton, for The Telegraph last year](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000438701307_17892150734550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_0UVPLIn5jC2o33F3LxcIkpdK1dOhi8msHrRyS-GuMA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Domenica Lawson, photographed with her mother, Rosa Monckton, for The Telegraph last year](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/12/TELEMMGLPICT000438701307_17892150734550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_0UVPLIn5jC2o33F3LxcIkpdK1dOhi8msHrRyS-GuMA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The assisted dying bill, which was rejected in the House of Commons on Friday, was a deeply flawed and ill-thought-out piece of legislation. The more than 1,000 amendments that were tabled in the House of Lords, of which I am a member, (including over 70 by its sponsor in the upper house, Lord Falconer) reflected this.
I tabled two. The first to insist that people with a learning disability be allowed to have either a family member or a specialist nurse with them when the subject of “assisted dying” was raised. The second was to exclude hospices from the obligation to offer this “service”.
My 31-year-old daughter, Domenica, who has Down’s Syndrome, thankfully has had no idea of the battle being waged on her behalf. It has been a battle not just for her, but for everyone with Down’s Syndrome or other learning disabilities who could be easily coerced into making a life-or-death decision.
One of the traits of Down’s Syndrome seems to be a desire to please, and therefore people with this condition are more vulnerable to coercion. The thought of my daughter, with no-one by her side, being told by a doctor who will not have met her before to consider whether it would be best for her to have her life ended because she has a terminal condition is unimaginable. She is terrified of hospitals and anything medical.
We parents of a vulnerable adult spend an inordinate amount of time worrying about what will happen when we are dead. To add to that, the concern that there could be a moment when this option of having yourself killed, but never described as such, is discussed with our son or daughter, with no family present, is too much to bear.
There would be no choice: the implicit coercion, the malleability and vulnerability, the lack of understanding would be configured to lead in only one convenient direction.
So many parents wrote to me, parents exhausted from fighting for the rights of their children. One mother, as she digested the implications of the bill for her own child, wrote: “Sometimes, it’s easier to cry about the small things.”
Lord Falconer, in his ever-courteous way, in replying to my proposed amendment, said: “Whatever happens to the bill – and I very much hope it becomes law – what she said will, I am absolutely sure, have an influence on its terms, and we should respect that.” But my amendment was never put to a vote.
Earlier, the now-shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds MP, tabled an amendment in the House of Commons to protect people with Down’s Syndrome from assisted suicide.
However, Kim Leadbeater and several members of the assisted suicide committee voted down the amendment by 13 votes to eight. Why? On what possible grounds? Such a lack of understanding and compassion is incomprehensible to me.
Danny Kruger was among many who spoke passionately about this, and of how difficult it would be to ensure “informed consent”. He pointed out that the Down’s Syndrome Research Foundation had said that a discussion with someone with the condition “can often feel to them as if a suggestion is being made”.
When I heard the result on Friday I felt overwhelming relief. Also, huge gratitude to the indomitable Baroness Finlay and Nikki da Costa for their expertise and research. I have not been a member of the House of Lords for very long, but I was proud to play a small part in this.
It was the Lords at its best, doing its proper job of scrutinising and revising legislation. Ultimately the decision to kill the bill was down to the House of Commons. We did our bit, and they did theirs.
The fee for this article has been donated to Team Domenica.
summary: A member of the House of Lords expressed overwhelming relief following the rejection of the assisted dying bill in the House of Commons. The author had raised deep concerns that the legislation posed severe risks of coercion for vulnerable individuals, including her 31-year-old daughter who has Down's Syndrome. While amendments to protect people with Down's Syndrome were previously voted down in committee, the author praised the rigorous scrutiny of the bill by parliamentarians before its eventual defeat.
key_points: The assisted dying bill was rejected in the House of Commons on Friday.
The author raised amendments to protect people with learning disabilities from potential coercion.
Individuals with Down's Syndrome can be particularly vulnerable to coercion due to a desire to please.
An amendment tabled by Damian Hinds MP to protect people with Down's Syndrome was previously voted down by 13 votes to eight.
The author expressed immense relief and gratitude toward parliamentary colleagues who helped scrutinize and defeat the legislation.

title: Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo
author: Geraldine McKelvie
content:
The cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from fellow billionaire Ben Delo.
The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on funding from individual donors.
Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the payments, which come at a time when the party is facing intense scrutiny regarding its funding.
The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.
After Harborne’s donation was announced on Saturday afternoon, Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.
![Nigel Farage, wearing a sky blue suit, gestures](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/46ec951ae1aeba72d3431036ca7f9b5eec645c4f/244_0_6538_5233/master/6538.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Rachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping” on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.
The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.
Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.
“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.
Announcing the new donation on Saturday, Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field.”
Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.
“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.
“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”
Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to the UK from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.
The Guardian understands Delo and Harborne are registered to vote in the UK, although it is unclear exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.
after newsletter promotion
Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.
“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”
Many senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.
“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.
However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.
Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.
“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”
summary: Cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has matched a £36m donation from Ben Delo, injecting £72m into Reform UK within 24 hours to form the largest joint donations in UK political history. The massive funding has intensified calls from various politicians and transparency advocates for strict limits on individual donor contributions. Meanwhile, Reform UK and its leader Nigel Farage face ongoing scrutiny, including a Metropolitan police inquiry into party finances and a parliamentary standards investigation.
key_points: Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo each donated £36m to Reform UK, totaling £72m in 24 hours.
The pledges are jointly the largest donations ever made to a UK political party.
The donations have heightened calls and parliamentary amendments for caps on individual political donors.
Reform UK and Nigel Farage are currently facing a Metropolitan police inquiry and a parliamentary standards investigation regarding party finances.
Under proposed legislation, donations from Britons living abroad or those who recently returned would be capped at £100,000 annually.

title: UK police ban face coverings at planned anti-migrant protest
author: Greta Ruffino
content:
Small-boat crossings remain a highly contentious political issue in the UK, where tens of thousands of migrants arrive across the Channel each year.
Police in southern England have banned face coverings at an anti-immigration rally as well as in a counter-protest planned in Portsmouth on Saturday, amid concerns over potential unrest.
The demonstration, organised by protesters calling themselves “patriots”, is expected to begin at around noon.
Hampshire Police, which has responsibility for Portsmouth, said the mask ban was to "reduce opportunities for violence, intimidation and criminality".
It said the move followed "recent incidents of violence and intimidation by a minority of those who have been intent on disrupting peaceful protest".
A separate order will allow police to require people to remove masks or other items covering their identity.
Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo, quoted by the BBC, said: "It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially.
"Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest, but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer."
The demonstrations come less than a week after clashes between protesters and police in Portsmouth. Masked protesters attempted to prevent a group of asylum seekers who had crossed the English Channel in a small boat from leaving the area.
Police said official vehicles were damaged and several officers were injured during the unrest, which the government condemned as “thuggish”.
A day earlier, hundreds of masked protesters gathered in Dover and briefly blocked access to the Channel port during a demonstration against migrant crossings.
The unrest in Portsmouth and Dover was condemned by political leaders.
Police were given powers last year to ban face coverings used to conceal identities at protests.
summary: Police in southern England have banned face coverings at an upcoming anti-immigration rally and a counter-protest in Portsmouth following recent unrest. Hampshire Police stated that the measure aims to prevent violence, intimidation, and criminality rather than stop peaceful protests. The decision follows recent clashes in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked demonstrators protesting small-boat migrant crossings.
key_points: Police banned face coverings for an anti-migration rally and counter-protest in Portsmouth.
The restriction aims to reduce violence, intimidation, and crime during the demonstrations.
Officers have been granted the authority to order individuals to remove identity-concealing items.
The ban follows recent violent clashes involving masked protesters in Portsmouth and Dover.

title: Reform UK given record £36m donation by British crypto billionaire
author: Rowena Mason
content:
Reform UK has been given a record £36m donation by Ben Delo, a British cryptocurrency billionaire convicted in the US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls.
The businessman, who has moved back to the UK from Hong Kong, is now the biggest UK political donor by far, dwarfing the £15m contribution to Reform UK from Thailand-based Christopher Harborne.
The huge donation will be a boost for party leader Nigel Farage at a time when he is facing a police investigation into overseas funding for Reform, plus a standards inquiry into a £5m undeclared personal gift from Harborne.
It had been thought Delo could be caught by the overseas cap requiring donors to have been resident in the UK for 12 months before giving more than £100,000 but Reform insisted earlier this month that they were confident Delo would not have to take back any cash.
