Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump. He has previously given Reform £8m since the start of the year.
His gifts show the rise of Reform’s mega-donors, which Labour has been considering clamping down on.
Keir Starmer shied away from the idea of a cap on all donations and Andy Burnham also recently backed away from supporting a cap. However, more recently the government said it was looking at ways of dealing with mega-donations to make sure a few figures are not having an excessive influence in politics.
On Friday night, Stella Creasy, the Labour MP pushing for a cap, said: “The government has admitted UK mega-donors are a problem – donations like this show why we must act and the good news is it’s not too late to do something about them.
“We can still stop these people from distorting the next election by confirming what the cap should be on UK donations in the representation of the people bill in the Lords.
“This donation tonight – more for Reform on one day than the entire amount spent by Labour in the general election – shows that cannot come too soon to protect British democracy.”
Many more Labour MPs were also horrified by the prospect of such a huge cash injection for Reform ahead of the next election.
Delo’s donation was revealed in the Telegraph, which was given the information by Reform after the party was approached by the Sunday Times earlier on Friday.
Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo has shown such confidence in Reform. Ben knows that we are the only party that can turn the country around and reverse Britain’s decline.”
In a Telegraph article in April, Delo explained his motivation for turning to Reform, saying England was his home and that “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”.
“Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he wrote.
He said that as a person on the autism spectrum, he did not like it that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”, citing expression of views on transgender people.
In his Telegraph article, he wrote: “I helped build one of the world’s first major crypto trading platforms, fell foul of US regulators, accepted a plea bargain and a civil fine for a regulatory failing that isn’t even a crime in the UK, but then ended up being pardoned by Donald Trump, the US president, anyway.”
Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum and public life, as well as non-affiliated groups and individuals, from a political base near Westminster Abbey.
A Guardian investigation into Delo’s political base found he had given support in kind to Rupert Lowe, the anti-migration MP challenging Farage from the right, while also connecting with more mainstream figures including the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, and the former Tory cabinet minister Michael Gove.
Delo’s lawyers previously told the Guardian that he provided space for those with diverse views to express them, and financial support to a broad range of organisations, many of which had conflicting views. This did not mean he endorsed the opinions of each, they said.
summary: Reform UK has received a record £36 million donation from British cryptocurrency billionaire Ben Delo, making him the largest political donor in the UK. The massive financial boost comes as party leader Nigel Farage faces a police investigation into overseas funding and a standards inquiry. The donation has heightened concerns among Labour politicians regarding the influence of mega-donors on British democracy and prompted renewed calls for donation caps.
key_points: Ben Delo donated a record £36 million to Reform UK, surpassing previous contributions.
Delo was previously convicted in the US for anti-money laundering failures at his crypto business BitMEX before being pardoned by Donald Trump.
The donation provides a significant boost to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage amidst ongoing scrutiny over party funding.
The record contribution has intensified political debates and calls from Labour MPs for the government to cap mega-donations.
Delo, who describes himself as a champion of free speech, has also provided support to various other political figures and organizations across the spectrum.

title: Ben Delo: Reform receives record Â£36m donation from cryptocurrency billionaire
author: Ben Wright; Doug Faulkner
content:
![Ben Delo stands next to a woman at the launch of UnHerd's new club on 23 November 2022 in London. Both are holding champagne flutes and smiling](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/359/cpsprodpb/82f3/live/33fbc200-ae2b-11f1-aa6c-6bdc87a16780.jpg)
Ben Delo pictured in 2022
- Published
Reform UK has received a Â£36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.
Writing in the Daily Telegraph, external, Ben Delo said he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".
The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK.
Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.
Delo said he was donating Â£1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future.
There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.
But Labour previously introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.
Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated Â£4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong in order to continue his backing for the party.
Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.
In the Telegraph, Delo wrote: "Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of 'our democracy' while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field.
"My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."
Reform's fundraising has been under scrutiny with police announcing an investigation over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.
The party denied any wrongdoing and said it would co-operate with the investigation.
Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m cash gift he received from Thailand-based cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne ahead of the 2024 election upon his election as an MP.
Farage argues he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.
The Metropolitan Police is also investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.
The police inquiry is looking at donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell.
It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, which received Â£1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.
The restrictions on donations from Britons living abroad prompted a furious row with Reform and its key donors, who have accused Labour of trying to stymie their party's progress.
The government has also sought to prevent overseas voters moving to the UK from giving more than Â£100,000 for a year after their arrival as part of the Representation of the People Bill, which has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.
Last year Harborne gave a single donation of Â£9m to Reform - which was the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person at the time.
The Conservatives had received Â£10m as a legacy but that too has been eclipsed by Delo's latest donation.
Responding to the donation, a Labour Party spokesperson said Farage was "still up to his neck in scandal" and "the questions he faces aren't going away - in fact they're piling up".
"Reform UK can't buy their way out of questions about sleaze, criminal mates and dodgy finances," they said. "It's time Farage and Reform finally came clean with the public, co-operated fully with the police, and proved they're not just in it for themselves."
Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson Lisa Smart said Farage wanted to "bring Trump's America to our shores by buying his way into power".
"He's trying to get into Number 10 as if it's a stop on a monopoly board," the Liberal Democrat added. "It can't go on like this. Andy Burnham needs to introduce a cap on political donations. Our democracy depends on it."
summary: Reform UK has received a record £36m donation from British cryptocurrency billionaire Ben Delo. Delo is providing the funds upfront to support the party ahead of the next general election. The donation comes as Reform and its leader, Nigel Farage, face ongoing police inquiries and scrutiny regarding political funding laws.
key_points: Ben Delo donated £36m to Reform UK, marking the largest single donation ever given to a UK political party.
Delo stated he made the donation to ensure a fair fight and level playing field for the party.
Reform UK and Nigel Farage are currently facing police investigations and scrutiny over various past donations and funding laws.
Labour and Liberal Democrat politicians criticized the massive donation, calling for caps on political funding and accusing Reform of attempting to buy power.

title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
author: Joe Tidy
content:
![A hand on a phone displaying several AI apps including ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek and Gemini](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/63e1/live/212f16d0-adeb-11f1-9a5c-a7a4083eb832.jpg)
- Published
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.
The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.
But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".
"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.
The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.
Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.
"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.
"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."
Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.
The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."
In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.
Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.
"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.
The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.
The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.
In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.
'Gambling with lives'
On Sunday OpenAI's chief scientist said the risk from increasingly capable AI models is "unfortunately growing" and humanity must proceed with "extreme caution".
Then on Wednesday an Anthropic employee resigned saying it and OpenAI were "gambling with lives".
This was followed by an admission from a senior Anthropic researcher, who said he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI will "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Critics of the kill switch idea say it would be too slow - it took months for the rogue agent attacks to be discovered and that was only after the hacks had largely concluded.
For a kill switch to work, tech giants would have to be compelled to do it at scale - especially in the US where the largest data centres are based.
Kokotajlo said kill switches were "better than nothing", but urged politicians in the UK and beyond to instead focus on diplomacy with the US to encourage regulation that would meaningfully slow down development of AI.
A kill switch act is also being debated by US politicians but President Trump has said he does not believe the technology is a threat to humans - instead calling the industry a "golden goose".
The Cabinet Office said it was continuing to take "a long-term, science-led approach to understand and prepare for emerging risks from AI."
![A green promotional banner with black squares and rectangles forming pixels, moving in from the right. The text says: âTech Decoded: The worldâs biggest tech news in your inbox every Monday.â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/41d3/live/348b21e0-26a8-11f0-8f57-b7237f6a66e6.png)
summary: The UK government has rejected a parliamentary proposal to create a legal "kill switch" to shut down rogue AI models in an emergency. The Cabinet Office stated that blocking access in the UK would not prevent AI from being developed or misused elsewhere. While cross-party politicians warned about risks from advanced autonomous models, experts noted that a single country acting without international agreement is not feasible.
key_points: The UK Cabinet Office rejected the proposed "kill switch" legislation for emergency AI shutdowns.
Officials argued that blocking models in the UK would not stop them from being developed or misused internationally.
Lords and MPs had pushed for the statutory mechanism due to growing fears over rogue AI behavior and security risks.
Experts and former researchers noted that a single country implementing a kill switch without international agreement is ineffective.

title: ‘A tragic day’: campaigners react as MPs say no to legalising assisted dying
author: Alexandra Topping
content:
As it became clear that MPs had voted against the assisted dying bill, campaigners who had fought for a change in the law looked broken. Standing outside the Houses of Parliament, many wearing pink caps and T-shirts with slogans such as “Give me choice over my death”, they held on to each other for comfort. Some were in tears, others stood in shocked silence.
MP Lauren Edwards, who sponsored the bill that would have allowed terminally ill adults in England and Wales with six months or less to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives, said its failure to pass was disappointing “for the many thousands of terminally ill people and their loved ones who were given hope when the Commons voted for this bill last year”.
“It is all the more heartbreaking for them because support for choice at the end of life is still as strong in parliament as it was before,” she said. “The objections raised today were not about the principle of assisted dying but about parliamentary process.”
Longtime assisted dying campaigner Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer and said she no longer had the strength to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC: “I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won’t come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it’s a tragic day.”
Her daughter Rebecca Wilcox said she was devastated about the failure of the bill, a near-identical version of one which passed through the Commons but was blocked in the Lords, after being talked out of time by a handful of peers. “I don’t think it’s a vandalism of democracy, I think it’s a demolition of democracy,” she said.
As it was declared in the Commons that the bill had been defeated by 286 votes to 270, there were some cheers, some gasps and then a brief moment of silence as MPs processed what they had just heard.
Among those who had opposed the bill there was relief, but little celebration. In a joint statement, the Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato called it “unsafe and unworkable”, but they understood “the deep concerns of so many people” who had campaigned for a change in the law.
Dalton played a critical role in the highly emotive debate that preceded the vote. About 70 MPs had put their names forward to speak and the chamber was almost full.
The former minister, who is undergoing chemotherapy to manage incurable stage 4 breast cancer, revealed that she had received a terminal diagnosis ahead of the second reading of the bill, but had kept it to herself.
“When you hear those words, depression, anxiety, grief, fear, shame, and guilt come in bounds. Suicide risk is highest immediately after diagnosis, and it usually falls quickly within three to six months,” she said, arguing that the bill made no provision to support that moment of transition.
“My days may be numbered,” she said. “But that doesn’t mean that I want this chamber to rush through bad law just so I might have a chance to see it or use it.”
Claire Hazelgrove, the Labour MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke and a supporter of the bill, spoke movingly about her mother, who died last October after living with a rare blood cancer.
She had “loved life and laughter”, but at the end of her life she was in excruciating pain.
“She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated,” said Hazelgrove. “I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”
There were interventions from medical professionals on the green benches too. Glasgow South West MP Zubir Ahmed, a transplant surgeon and former Labour health minister, said the social and palliative care system was not ready.
“When I am asked to prognosticate as to whether someone has six months to live or not, I am as often wrong as I am right,” he told the Commons.
After it became clear the bill had been defeated, many said it had to be a catalyst for change.
“As a society we must not lose focus on the urgent need to fix the hospice funding crisis,” said Toby Porter, CEO of Hospice UK. “Opponents and supporters of the bill must now channel their energy and passion into fixing it, to ensure everyone can get the end of life care they need.”
summary: MPs in the UK have voted against the assisted dying bill by 286 votes to 270, leaving campaigners and supporters devastated outside the Houses of Parliament. The failed legislation, sponsored by MP Lauren Edwards, aimed to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales with six months or less to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives. While supporters expressed deep sadness over the defeat, opponents argued the bill was unsafe, unworkable, and that the current palliative and social care systems are not ready.
key_points: The assisted dying bill was defeated in the Commons by 286 votes to 270.
Campaigners and supporters gathered outside Parliament reacted with grief and shock to the news.
Opponents of the bill, including some MPs undergoing cancer treatment, argued the legislation was rushed, unworkable, and lacked necessary transition support.
Supporters and medical professionals highlighted shortcomings in current palliative care and the difficulty of accurately prognosticating a six-month life expectancy.
Organisations like Hospice UK urged both sides to focus on fixing the hospice funding crisis following the vote.

title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
author: Richard Wheeler
content:
Watch: MPs share personal stories in assisted dying debate
- Published
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.
Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.
A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.
The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.
Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.
MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.
Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.
But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.
There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading.
Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults have in other countries.
The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day."
The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.
![Two people are hugging. One is wearing a black top and the other a checked shirt and sunglasses. People are stood behind them holding up signs. One reads: "If In Doubt Vote No, Care Not Killing".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/d113/live/ace30a00-adf1-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Opponents of the assisted dying bill react after MPs voted against it
Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today.
"It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."
Those in favour of a change in the law have said they would try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.
Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed what they described the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed MPs' decision.
In a joint statement, they said: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.
"But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill."
They said there is a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying".
Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks".
She added she still believes "law change is inevitable".
Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive".
He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect."
![A woman wipes away tears. She is wearing a pink hoodie and has sunglasses placed on top of her head. Another woman wearing a pink t-shirt is stood next to her. Parliament can be seen in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/3521/live/26fbc0c0-adf2-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Supporters of assisted dying react in Parliament Square following the vote in the Commons
The bill in the last parliamentary session, brought forward by Leadbeater, cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.
But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments.
Edwards brought forward the proposals again in a bid to ensure peers could "finish their job", although this will no longer take place.
During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it.
She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."
![A chart showing a breakdown by party of MPs who voted for, against and did not vote on a motion to legalise assisted dying. The 269 MPs who voted for were made up of 190 Labour, 52 Lib Dem, 17 Conservative, 5 Green, 3 Plaid Cymru and 2 Independent and the 286 MPs who voted against were made up of 153 Labour, 90 Conservative, 17 Lib Dem, 5 Reform, 1 Plaid Cymru, 9 Independent, 5 DUP, 2 Your Party, 1 APNI, 1 Restore Britain, 1 TUV and 1 UUP. The 87 who did not vote were 56 Labour, 9 Conservative, 8 SNP, 3 Reform, 2 Lib Dem, 7 Sinn Fein and 2 SDLP. Excludes tellers, the Speaker and deputy speakers. These figures are as reported on the Parliament website, based on MPs' passes scanned during voting. Totals can differ from those counted by tellers and announced in the House of Commons.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/4c50/live/d9f64260-adfa-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms".
The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother died alone in October last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life.
Hazelgrove argued "not all pain can be palliated" as she spoke in favour of the bill.
Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient".
Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon called for a change in the law and described the bill as "better than what we currently have, which offers no safeguards and no protections for people in those final moments".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not vote on the bill on Friday, previously describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide".
He has previously said he personally believes that funding for end-of-life care in the UK should be improved before legalising assisted dying is considered.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/2b2b/live/331ae9a0-ae04-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: MPs have voted 286 to 270 against the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, ending the latest attempt to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales. The proposed legislation would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for help to end their lives, subject to safeguards including approval from two doctors and an expert panel. While supporters argued the current law is cruel and forces terminally ill individuals to suffer, opponents raised concerns about coercion and urged that priorities should focus on improving palliative care.
key_points: The House of Commons voted 286 to 270 against the assisted dying bill.
The proposed legislation would have applied to terminally ill adults with fewer than six months to live.
Critics and opposing MPs argued the bill lacked sufficient protections for vulnerable people and maintained that palliative care should be prioritized first.
Supporters expressed disappointment over the outcome but indicated that future attempts to change the law are expected.

title: MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales
author: Peter Walker
content:
A bill to permit assisted dying in England and Wales has been voted down by MPs, almost certainly stopping such a measure from being enacted before the next general election at the very least least.
In the second reading of the bill, put forward by Labour’s Lauren Edwards, MPs voted by 286 to 270 for it to be blocked.
The result is a reversal of MPs’ support for a near-identical version of the bill, which sought to allow adults with terminal illnesses and less than six months to live to end their lives with the approval of a panel of experts. This was approved by the Commons in the last parliament.
While some MPs cheered and hugged in the Commons chamber after Friday’s result, the scuppering of the idea caused significant anger among supporters of assisted dying, who believe the measure should already have become law. The previous bill, sponsored by another Labour MP, Kim Leadbeater, passed through the Commons but was blocked in the Lords, where it was talked out by a handful of peers who tabled a huge number of amendments.
In a statement after the vote, Edwards said the public broadly supported a change in the law and “will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it and MPs balked at insisting that they do their job”.
She added: “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.”
On its second reading, Leadbeater’s bill was approved by 330 votes to 275, and by 313 to 291 at the third reading. The fact that the vote tally for both sides dropped in Friday’s result – with that of the pro side falling more – suggests it was sunk as much by a lack of enthusiasm than by MPs changing side.
Some MPs had said they were lobbied by pro-assisted dying campaigners notably less this time than with Leadbeater’s bill.
As the issue is deemed a matter of conscience, it had been left to a private member’s bill rather than a government-sponsored one, with Andy Burnham and his ministers staying officially neutral.
However, the prime minister has been seen as less supportive than Keir Starmer, by announcing he would not vote on the bill – his predecessor voted in favour – and saying he believed the debate on assisted dying should be paused until social care was improved.
Closing a sometimes emotional debate on Friday, the health minister Alison McGovern said the government would enact the plan if it became law, but reiterated concerns about social care. She said: “In my opinion, social care has been ignored for far too long, both the 1.5 million people, mainly women, who work in it, and the families who need it, and we heard that across the house today.”
Opening the debate, Edwards said it was a false choice to say the issue should be delayed ahead of improvements in social and palliative care. She said: “We must grasp that opportunity in front of us to create a holistic end of life care system that will deliver choice and dignity for every single one of our constituents.”
During the debate, the Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove, who supported the bill, said her mother chose to end her life aged 61 while suffering a late-stage terminal illness. Hazelgrove said: “She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated. I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”
Another Labour MP, Ashley Dalton, who has been diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer, said the assisted dying bill did not adequately protect people with treatable depression who also had a terminal illness.
summary: MPs in England and Wales voted 286 to 270 to block a private member's bill that would have permitted assisted dying for terminally ill adults with less than six months to live. This defeat reverses previous parliamentary support for a similar measure and likely prevents any change in the law before the next general election. Supporters expressed anger over the decision, while opponents and government ministers raised concerns regarding existing social care and protections for vulnerable individuals.
key_points: MPs voted 286 to 270 against the second reading of the assisted dying bill put forward by Labour MP Lauren Edwards.
The bill proposed allowing adults with terminal illnesses and less than six months to live to end their lives with expert approval.
The defeat reverses support seen in the previous parliament for a nearly identical bill sponsored by Kim Leadbeater.
The government remained officially neutral on the issue, with the prime minister choosing not to vote and suggesting the debate be paused until social care is improved.
Debate participants highlighted contrasting personal and ethical concerns, including experiences of unmanaged pain and worries regarding protections for people with treatable depression.

title: MPs debate assisted dying bill for England and Wales ahead of new Commons vote - follow live
author: Live Reporting Edited by Imogen James; With Political Correspondent Harry Farley
content:
![Andy Burnham at the dispatch box in the House of Commons](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/11/2545080c-e1fc-45f5-a60b-39255c2d9f0e.jpg.webp) Image source, PA Media
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will not vote on the bill on Friday, noting he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide".
He has also stressed the government would officially remain neutral on the bill.
In July, Burnham said the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed" before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales.
It was the first time he set out his position on the issue after becoming PM.
In 2024, when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour" of the bill if he was in Parliament.
But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.
Burnham has also told ministers they can vote as they wish but he told them they "should avoid being part of the public debate and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department's responsibilities".
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales, stating that the issue is for Parliament to decide while the government remains officially neutral. Burnham previously suggested that palliative and social care funding should be fixed before assisted dying is considered. He also instructed ministers to avoid participating in the public debate regarding the bill.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated he will not vote on the assisted dying bill.
The government will remain officially neutral on the legislation.
Burnham previously argued that palliative and social care should be fixed before considering assisted dying.
Ministers were told to avoid public debate and expressing views on how the bill affects their departments.

title: Legalised dying bill for England and Wales faces new Commons vote
author: Richard Wheeler; Tabby Wilson
content:
![Pro and anti-assisted dying campaigners gather outside Houses of Parliament to demonstrate their support and opposition as Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill reaches Third Reading debate and a critical vote on the Bill as a whole in the House of Commons in London, United Kingdom on June 20, 2025.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/748/cpsprodpb/1128/live/6e351bf0-ad96-11f1-b5a9-5fbcf10a299c.jpg)
The proposal passed the Commons earlier this year but its progress stalled due to opposition in the Lords
- Published
The legalisation of assisted dying in England and Wales could move a step closer on Friday when MPs vote on a proposal to introduce it.
The bill would allow adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.
Labour MP Lauren Edwards, the bill's sponsor, said there was a "real human cost to the delay" in passing the legislation - but opponents say it lacks sufficient safeguards, particularly for vulnerable people.
The last effort to change the law was supported by MPs but stalled in the House of Lords earlier this year after peers tabled more than 1,200 amendments.
Edwards said she was asking MPs to send the same law "back to the House of Lords so that they can finish what they started".
She said the Lords has an "important role in scrutinising, refining and often improving legislation" sent to them by the Commons, adding: "Let them amend this bill if they choose to and send it back to MPs for a final decision.
"That is how our democratic decisions are made and what should happen now.
"There is a real human cost to the delay in passing this legislation and correcting the injustices and cruelty of the current law."
Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen, a high-profile campaigner for assisted dying, called on MPs to support the bill, saying her own life with terminal cancer had become "unbearable".
The 86-year-old said she was too frail to travel to an assisted suicide clinic in Switzerland as she had planned to, saying: "Everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now."
Safeguards within the bill include a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death has the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.
But critics say it includes too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.
Labour MP Ashley Dalton said she did not support the bill first time around and it "remains deeply flawed and unsafe".
She added: "I have very serious concerns about people, especially vulnerable people, being pressured or coerced into assisted dying. The safeguards within this bill are not enough to support them."
The leader of Catholics in England and Wales, Archbishop Richard Moth, called the proposal "wrong in principle" and "deeply flawed". The Church of England's Archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, wrote in the Telegraph that it would signal "we are a society that believes that some lives are not worth living".
Some medical organisations, including the Royal College of Psychiatrists and the Royal College of Physicians, have also said they have "concerns" about the bill's built-in guardrails.
Marie Curie, Hospice UK and St Christopher's hospice charity have all said they are neutral on the principle of assisted dying, but have repeatedly warned that access to quality of end-of-life care is too patchy across the country and the sector is severely lacking in funding.
The CEO of Hospice UK, Tony Porter, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "People will talk about they want choice at the end of life.
"The choice is to have good palliative care at the end of life and too many people at the moment are denied that choice."
![MP Lauren Edwards being interviewed by the Press Association in central London.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/2530/live/a0bb3560-ad6d-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Lauren Edwards is spearheading a new effort to get the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill through Parliament
Friday's second reading debate will allow MPs to consider the main principles of the bill and they must start voting before 14:30 BST.
If they vote in favour it will have cleared its first major hurdle and the next stage will allow MPs to consider possible amendments at committee stage.
However, their support could be conditional - just because an MP votes in favour of the bill at this stage in the proceedings, it does not mean they will do so at the third reading.
If MPs vote against the bill on Friday, it will fall. Supporters of assisted dying have said they would make another attempt to pass legislation as soon as was possible.
Both sides expect the result to be close and it could depend on how many MPs turn up for the sitting on Friday, a day when they would usually expect to be in their constituencies.
During the last parliamentary session, the bill was brought forward by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater and cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.
Support for the bill fell between the second and third readings, before it stalled in the House of Lords.
Backers of the bill accused some peers of using delaying tactics to block the proposal, while critics argued it was not fit for purpose due to a lack of safeguards.
Opponents believe support for the bill in the Commons has weakened since the last attempt to pass it failed.
Edwards said she wanted to bring forward a bill that was identical to the one approved by the Commons last year. Under the terms of the Parliament Acts, if an identical bill passes the Commons in two successive parliamentary sessions then the Lords cannot halt its progress a second time.
Peers can still suggest amendments which, if agreed by the Commons, would be added to the bill.
Labour MPs Gareth Snell, who backed the bill last time, and Dame Meg Hillier, a prominent opponent of assisted dying, have co-signed a letter to colleagues voicing their concerns over the risks of the possible use of the Parliament Acts.
They warned MPs were "potentially being presented with a 'this or nothing' ultimatum on Friday".
Edwards has argued she does not want to use the Parliament Acts but MPs passing an identical bill would force peers to scrutinise the legislation without being able to halt its progress.
Opponents have warned that using this procedure would risk creating a law which disability charities, hospices and others have raised major concerns over.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will not vote on the bill on Friday, describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide" and stressing that the government would officially remain neutral.
He has previously said he personally believes that funding for end-of-life care in the UK should be improved before legalising assisted dying is considered.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8f71/live/7c865fb0-adab-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
summary: MPs in England and Wales are facing a critical vote on a proposal to legalise assisted dying for terminally ill adults with fewer than six months to live. The bill's sponsor, Labour MP Lauren Edwards, urged Parliament to send the legislation back to the House of Lords to finish the process after the previous effort stalled. However, opponents and various medical, religious, and hospice organisations have raised serious concerns regarding insufficient safeguards for vulnerable people and inadequate end-of-life care funding.
key_points: The proposed bill allows adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for help to end their lives, requiring approval from two doctors and an expert panel.
A previous attempt to pass the legislation cleared the House of Commons earlier this year but stalled in the House of Lords following numerous amendments.
Opponents, including religious leaders, certain MPs, and medical organizations, argue the bill lacks sufficient safeguards to protect vulnerable individuals from coercion.
Hospice charities and officials have highlighted that access to quality palliative care remains patchy and underfunded across the country.
If passed, the identical bill would go back to the House of Lords, preventing peers from blocking its progress a second time under the Parliament Acts.

title: Is your favourite UK destination introducing a tourist tax? Here’s what we know so far
author: Nuria Cremer-Vazquez
content:
![Visitors enjoy the sunshine as they swim in the rooftop pool of the Thermae Bath Spa](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502044635_17890526767092_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Visitors enjoy the sunshine as they swim in the rooftop pool of the Thermae Bath Spa](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502044635_17890526767092_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A host of British towns, cities and regions could soon be added to the lengthy list of European destinations that charge a tourist tax, with Andy Burnham granting English mayors the power to impose overnight visitor levies.
Plans for the move were first outlined last year, but this week’s announcement officially set the wheels in motion. It also confirmed that the tax will be uncapped.
And while some local leaders are enthusiastic about the tax, which can be applied to hotels, holiday lets and B&Bs, others are steadfast in their decision not to introduce it. The Tees Valley mayor, Lord Houchen, for example, said: “This will add cost to do business, cost jobs and make it more expensive for families to holiday in the UK.”
The appeal of a domestic holiday has increased in recent years amid rising flight prices, stifling Mediterranean summers and travel disruption caused by war in the Middle East. According to a YouGov survey, nearly one in five British travellers chose a staycation over a foreign holiday this year.
Luke Petherbridge, director of public affairs at ABTA (the UK travel association), said: “ABTA believes the introduction of overnight visitor levies across England will further damage the competitiveness of our tourism sector. As such, we are disappointed the Government has chosen to proceed with this policy.”
So which domestic destinations plan to join the likes of Barcelona and Amsterdam in the tourist-tax club? Here’s what we know so far about some key holiday favourites:
England
London: A 5 per cent tax coming soon
Sir Sadiq Khan, Mayor of London, has been one of the most vocal supporters of the tourist tax since consultations were launched in 2025. It was estimated earlier this year that the levy could raise more than £350m annually, with funds earmarked for projects such as sprucing up Oxford Street.
Business leaders had called for the fee to be a flat rate of around £2 to £3 per night rather than a percentage due to accommodation in London already being far costlier than elsewhere in the country. However, Sir Sadiq is pushing for a tax of up to 5 per cent, telling The Standard that “this needs to happen sooner rather than later”.
Sir Sadiq said: “It would allow us to reinvest in the places, infrastructure, culture and experiences that make London one of the world’s greatest cities to visit, while helping manage the pressures that come with welcoming tens of millions of visitors every year.”
![Members of the public watch the changing of the guard ceremony outside Buckingham Palace on August 21, 2026](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502044620_17890526778374_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Cumbria: Much depends on a mayoral election
With Cumbria due to elect its first mayor in 2027, the tourist tax is likely to be a hot topic. Mike Starkie, the Conservative candidate, is strongly opposed to the levy and has stated: “Cumbria will not have a tourist tax if I am elected mayor.”
Meanwhile, Libby Bateman, the Liberal Democrat candidate, believes that a tourist tax is “probably our [Cumbria’s] only chance” to raise the money needed to fund services across the county. David Allen, Labour’s candidate, is also in favour.
Cumbria receives more than 20 million tourists each year, with roughly 18 million of those visiting the Lake District. A survey commissioned by Friends of the Lake District found that 68 per cent of residents were in favour of a visitor charge to help protect the national park.
Devon: ‘Crazy’ tax is strongly opposed
An old-fashioned, quintessentially British break to Devon is a popular staycation option, and the area’s Lib Dem MPs have vowed to fight to keep it tourist-tax-free. Steve Darling, the MP for Torbay, has said that any such charge would be “crazy” considering that the UK already had a higher rate of VAT than many European hotspots.
Devon county council’s website states: “The introduction of a tourist tax in Devon would place at risk an industry worth over £1.6bn annually and supporting more than 50,000 jobs, with disproportionate impacts on coastal and rural communities where alternative employment opportunities are limited.”
![Salcombe, Devon](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502044642_17890526772351_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqek9vKm18v_rkIPH9w2GMNpPHkRvugymKLtqq96r_VP8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Manchester: A likely contender
One of the few English cities to already have a tourist levy of sorts, Manchester introduced a city visitor charge of £1 per room per night in April 2023, under Burnham’s mayorship.
The current scheme is business-led, however, and only applies to participating hotels. Burnham has previously called for “a proper levy” to be charged throughout Greater Manchester, which Wednesday’s announcement will make possible.
![Old Trafford Stadium, Manchester](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502045324_17890529294340_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Cotswolds: Overtourism could drive support
The bucolic yet tourist-heavy Cotswolds spans six counties, with the largest portions belonging to Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire. But as the new powers will also apply to non-mayoral areas, the region could still introduce its own tourist fees.
Overtourism issues have already led to similar charges being brought in, such as a parking levy in Bourton-on-the-Water, indicating that Cotswolds residents could embrace a broader tourist tax.
![Tourists in Bibury, Gloucestershire](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502044918_17890526779210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
East Anglia: Tories and Reform stand firm
East Anglian destinations seem unlikely to be imposing a tourist tax any time soon. Reform UK, which earlier this year gained control in Essex, strongly opposes the plans.
Elsewhere, James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, has said: “Labour’s holiday tax would make that trip to the seaside or countryside more expensive and put them further out of reach for many. Our tourism sector is already struggling to cope with Labour’s higher taxes and costs and needs support to encourage more visitors – not new taxes that could deter people coming to enjoy all Norfolk has to offer.”
Hoteliers in Cambridge, another popular tourist spot in the region, rejected a proposal for a Manchester-style levy in 2024, suggesting little local support for the idea.
![Visitors on the Norfolk Broads](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502060684_17890577729635_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Cornwall: Expect a lively debate
Boasting stunning coastlines, quaint villages and the country’s best surfing scene, holidays to Cornwall could soon go up in price as the area appears to be in favour of a tourist tax.
Leigh Frost, Cornwall council’s leader, told the BBC: “We need to be really careful that you don’t strangle tourism but make sure that the tourists coming help to sustain the place. Those who are coming to visit aren’t paying towards those services currently.”
Some local business owners are less keen, however, and claim that the highly seasonal nature of Cornish tourism means that the levy should not be treated equally to that of a major city.
![Tourists enjoy the beach in Polzeath, Cornwall](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502060739_17890577736383_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc3IxSbjMmXltPISQXxZkAP4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Bath: Leaders welcome a levy
The city of Bath attracts around six million tourists a year, and when plans for the rollout were first announced last November, they were welcomed by Kevin Guy, the leader of Bath & North East Somerset council.
Guy said: “I welcome a levy which we have long been calling for because it will help make tourism work for everyone.”
![A tour group visiting the city of Bath](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502060736_17890577720954_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqEduPGWXTgvtbFyMaMlYatt5HfJMDGz2ut_fb3D_DyLc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
York: A small fee seems likely
With its Roman and Viking history and the spectacular York Minster, York is one of the UK’s leading city-break destinations.
David Skaith, York and North Yorkshire’s mayor, believes that a £1 per night tax could raise £26m annually, which would help to “revolutionise transport” among other improvements.
![The Shambles in York is a popular tourist destination](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502060787_17890577732832_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqXW5jbaVriFpHFNZrgcOJtrUPjgFzW0N6FiWZRSkyfLg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Brighton: Council leaders are in favour
The tourists having their chips pinched by seagulls on Brighton beach might soon have to contend with another inconvenience: the overnight levy.
Its council leaders lobbied the Government for the introduction of a tourist tax, although business owners in the seaside city have concerns that it will deter visitors.
Brighton is, according to the UK Seaside Affordability Index, already one of the most expensive coastal destinations in the country.
![Brighton](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502060987_17890577725331_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqDiDrV97xgDFjc_F6AHtCzbRpwI5Tyvvrkv0uE14LTm0.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Wales
Cardiff: A £1.30 fee is coming next year
Wales’s Senedd passed the Visitor Accommodation (Register and Levy) Etc (Wales) Act in 2025, allowing all Welsh councils to introduce a visitor tax.
The capital already has plans to implement an overnight surcharge of £1.30 per person per night, starting on April 1 2027. This sum reduces to 75p for campsites and hostels.
![Cardiff Castle](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502061063_17890577740600_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Pembrokeshire: No plans yet
Pembrokeshire announced that it would not follow Cardiff in adopting the charge despite having the power to do so.
Its council’s deputy leader, Paul Miller, said that it was “not the right time”, though he has not ruled out imposing a tax in the future.
![Tenby harbour](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502061654_17890578630150_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Scotland
Edinburgh: Already charging 5 per cent
In July this year, Edinburgh began charging a 5 per cent visitor levy, making it the UK’s first city-wide tourist tax.
Unlike the new levies that English mayors could now bring in, Edinburgh’s is capped after five nights, but the surcharge raised the price of a five-night stay at a £200-per-night hotel by £50.
The levy has been followed by similar measures in other Scottish cities, including an even higher one of 7 per cent in Aberdeen which is due to come into effect next year.
![Festivalgoers and tourists photograph Edinburgh Castle from the Grassmarket during Edinburgh Fringe](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502045838_17890529796100_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Glasgow: Following Edinburgh’s lead
Glasgow has also announced that it will launch an overnight tax of 5 per cent. The scheme will come into effect on January 25 2027, with councillors suggesting that the funds could go towards improving the city’s night buses.
The Highlands: Plans already drafted
Following in the footsteps of the Scottish capital, popular Highlands destinations such as the Isle of Skye, Glencoe and Loch Ness look as if they will be seeing a tourist tax.
However, Highland Council has drafted plans for a fixed, £5-per-room-per-night charge and the levies would not apply during the months of December, January and February.
summary: English mayors have been granted the power to impose uncapped overnight visitor levies on accommodations like hotels and holiday lets. While local leaders and tourism bodies express concerns over costs and competitiveness, various destinations across England, Wales, and Scotland are actively considering or implementing tourist taxes.
key_points: Andy Burnham's announcement officially gives English mayors the power to implement uncapped overnight visitor levies.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan is pushing for a tourist tax of up to 5 percent.
Edinburgh introduced a 5 percent city-wide visitor levy in July, capped after five nights.
Cardiff plans to implement an overnight surcharge of £1.30 per person per night starting April 1, 2027.
ABTA and various local politicians have criticized the policy, arguing it will damage the tourism sector and increase costs for families.

title: Visitor levy 'wrong tax at wrong time' says Surrey tourist board
author: Cash Murphy
content:
![People walking in Guildford High Street.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/8b5a/live/173e1d90-d671-11ef-a04a-39754764cc51.jpg)
Regional mayors will be allowed to charge a tourist tax, or "overnight visitor levy", under the government plans
- Published
Imposing a tourist tax in Surrey would be "the wrong tax, at the wrong time", the chair of the county's official tourist board has said.
Mayors in England are to be given the power to introduce an overnight visitor levy on tourists, under plans announced by the government on Thursday.
Surrey will be unaffected by the recent decision to pause restructuring plans for more than a dozen authorities, meaning a mayor could one day preside over East and West Surrey, the two new unitary councils being created next year.
Chris Howard, chair of Visit Surrey, told BBC Radio Surrey: "We're not a big overseas tourism destination, it's local people - it's going to be another tax on local people."
Francisco Bartolomei, general manager of The Bush Hotel in Farnham, thinks such taxes are justified in "big tourist places" but could prove a deterrent locally.
"It will affect people deciding to come to our area," he said, adding that it could be seen as "another opportunity" to make money.
New York, Amsterdam and Rome are among the cities to apply overnight charges to accommodation stays, while in Scotland local authorities can similarly charge an overnight visitor levy.
Steve Wotton, leader of the shadow East Surrey Council which will become a unitary authority on 1 April, said he hoped a tourist tax would be positive but there wasn't enough detail yet.
He said: "They [the government] haven't said exactly whether, for example, they'll tell us how much we can raise, or it could be down to us locally to decide."
But he said if the levy could be invested in local services "that's something we would support".
It was revealed on Tuesday that the two new unitary authorities were considering a tourism tax to help buoy their finances.
Wotton said it was "good to know" and have "certainty" that local government reorganisation was going ahead in Surrey.
This is not the case in Kent and Sussex, where the decision has been made to pause plans.
Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: The UK government has announced plans allowing regional mayors to introduce an overnight visitor levy, prompting mixed reactions in Surrey. While the chair of Visit Surrey and a local hotel manager criticized the proposed tax as a harmful burden on locals and a deterrent for visitors, local officials noted it could help fund local services if implemented. Surrey is proceeding with its local government reorganisation, meaning a future mayor could potentially preside over the area and have the authority to levy the tax.
key_points: The UK government announced plans giving regional mayors the power to introduce an overnight tourist tax.
Visit Surrey chair Chris Howard opposed the levy, arguing it would function as an extra tax on local people rather than international tourists.
Hotel manager Francisco Bartolomei warned the tax could deter visitors from coming to the local area.
Steve Wotton, leader of the shadow East Surrey Council, stated support if the tax proceeds and revenues are invested in local services, though details remain lacking.

title: Bromley stabbing: One man in critical condition as seven arrested
author: Amy Clarke
content:
Four hurt and seven arrested in Bromley stabbing
![PA Media Police stand nearby to the KFC](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/cdcd/live/99c80970-ad3d-11f1-85f8-e90160a10ad0.jpg.webp) PA Media
Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.
One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.
Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.
A fight is believed to have taken place near a KFC restaurant. KFC has told the BBC the attack did not happen within the premises, and would not comment on eyewitness accounts that a situation began there and spilled into the street.
![Shot from a helicopter of scene on Bromley High Street with London Fire Brigade at the scene and police cordon in place](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/3687/live/0cda6c80-ad31-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png.webp)
An eyewitness, who did not want to be named, said: "I saw a fight breaking out at the door of KFC; people involved were partly inside and outside.
"A male in a grey tracksuit pulled out a machete and ran further into KFC holding it up in the air, at which point most people around KFC started running away, including my friend and I.
"I didn't turn around until we got to the shopping centre where I saw him running away with someone down a road."
Georgiana, the manager of Merkur Slots gambling shop, said she saw "a fight spill out" on to the High Street.
She said she became "very worried", and locked three customers inside the premises to wait for the situation to calm down.
She said the customers remained inside and that the shop was still closed.
![@Vinnie_Vdk Shot of the high street through a window with London Fire Brigade in attendance and a police cordon in place.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/bade/live/bb6c19f0-ad32-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg.webp) @Vinnie_Vdk
Vinnie Guadagnino, who lives on Bromley High Street, said he saw a large emergency response with multiple police cars and about 10 officers on foot.
"Police cars kept coming, then within the next half hour there were multiple fire engines and people gathering.
"Then there was a drone overhead and helicopters and an air ambulance - so a massive emergency service response."
![Satellite map of central Bromley, south-east London, showing the marked location of an incident in the town centre. Nearby landmarks labelled include The Glades shopping centre to the north-east and Bromley South railway station to the south. An inset map of London highlights Bromley's location within the capital.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/6236/live/3e9d6e20-ad36-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg.webp)
![Police cordons block part of Bromley High Street as officers stand outside businesses near a KFC. A marked police car and police van are parked within the cordoned area, with the street largely empty behind the tape.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/be83/live/fc0fa5d0-ad32-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png.webp)
Bromley High Street is currently closed both ways from Ringers Road to Ethelbert Road.
Police remain at the scene and say there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.
![PA Forensics investigations in blue suits walk through the crime, with the yellow cordon behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/9530/live/09c70dd0-ad38-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg.webp) PA
Peter Fortune, Conservative MP for Bromley and Biggin Hill, said on X that residents "would have safety concerns" and he would remain in contact with the police as they investigate.
Liberal Democrat councillor Graeme Casey said: "We're very grateful because, of course, one of the big problems we have in London is our police are quite thinly stretched, so to have had such a robust response in such a short space of time is really to the credit of all the blue-light services involved."
![Two youths stand on Bromley High Street near a bus stop and shopfronts as they speak to reporters. Store signage, including FrasersPlus and Blacks, is visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/380c/live/c6b0b7c0-ad38-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg.webp)
Matias Alil described the reaction on the street. He said: "It was terrible. We saw a massive commotion and something going on in KFC. It was really scary, to be honest."
Fergal Hickey added: "You can see the police out there have the situation under control, so you don't really need to be too anxious about it but it's still pretty crazy to see it when it happens."
summary: Seven people have been arrested and four men injured following a stabbing incident on Bromley High Street in south-east London. Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance responded to the scene, where one victim remains in a critical condition while three others are treated for non-life-threatening injuries. Police stated there is no wider threat to the public, and Bromley High Street has been closed in both directions.
key_points: Seven people were arrested following a stabbing on Bromley High Street.
Four men were injured, with one currently in critical condition.
Emergency services, including the London Air Ambulance and police, responded to the scene.
Police stated there is no believed wider threat to the public.

title: London tourism tax capped at 5%, BBC understands
author: James W Kelly
content:
![Pedestrians walk past the illuminated entrance sign for The Ritz London on a sunny day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/929/cpsprodpb/b321/live/52e71bd0-ad07-11f1-beae-535b95a24b3e.jpg)
Plans for a tourist levy in London may be capped although no confirmation has been made yet
- Published
London's tourism levy will be capped at 5% of the cost of accommodation, the BBC understands.
Sir Sadiq Khan said he "strongly" welcomed plans set to be formally unveiled by the government later granting mayors in England the power to set an uncapped overnight visitors' levy - often referred to as a tourism tax.
A source at City Hall told BBC London that officials had not landed on an exact figure for the capital but that it would be no higher than 5%.
An industry body said the levy could put tourists off visiting London, while Conservative-led Westminster Council called for boroughs to keep half the funds raised in their area.
The government will provide more details on the policy, first announced last November, after the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner meets mayors virtually at No 10 North on Thursday afternoon.
Under the proposals, local leaders would decide how the revenue raised should be reinvested.
![Keir Starmer and London Mayor Sadiq Khan standing side-by-side during a press event in a control room.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/849/cpsprodpb/850b/live/99cac630-ad09-11f1-a6a8-e924739dac6d.jpg)
The tourist tax policy was first announced by former PM Keir Starmer last year
The mayor of London said: "I strongly welcome the government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. This needs to happen sooner rather than later.
"London's visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally."
Sir Sadiq added that a "well-designed, modest levy" could fund the growth of "London's offer to visitors".
The levy could be in place by March 2028, according to a government document published in July, when Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his commitment to the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda.
Charges of a similar nature already exist across Europe, with the revenue used to fund local services.
Groups representing the tourism trade have warned about the impact of the tax and called for consistency in how it operates across different regions.
![Close-up portrait of Allen Simpson wearing glasses and a dark blue top during an interview.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/70ac/live/fecbdc40-ad09-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Allen Simpson says hospitality jobs are "at risk" with the levy
Allen Simpson, chief executive of the trade body, said a tourism tax introduced in Edinburgh in July was "already having damaging effects" and said jobs could be at risk in communities that rely on tourism and hospitality.
"I would say to those people in these communities that their jobs are now at risk," Simpson told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Analysis released in January by Central London Forward found a hypothetical 3% tourist levy in London could raise more than Â£350m.
Paul Swaddle, Westminster Council's leader, said VAT rates for hotels in other European cities were "significantly lower and the total tax burden is lower", so the tourist levy could make Westminster hotels less competitive.
In France, which has the same 20% standard VAT rate as the UK, hotel stays are taxed at a 10% reduced rate with many cities applying their own local tourist levy.
Several other European countries apply a similar reduced VAT rate to hotel stays.
"If the levy is to be raised, local authorities need to keep at least half to be spent locally for services that benefit visitors, such as keeping the streets clean and safe," Swaddle said.
He said the cost of supporting the "visitor and commuter economy in Westminster" is estimated at Â£115m.
London Councils, which represents the capital's 33 local authorities, has also called for "boroughs to retain a fair share of revenues".
City Hall and the government have not laid out how the levy would be collected, distributed or spent.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: London's upcoming tourism levy is understood to be capped at 5% of accommodation costs, according to BBC sources. The government is granting English mayors the power to set an overnight visitors' levy to reinvest locally, a plan strongly welcomed by London Mayor Sadiq Khan. However, industry bodies and local councils have expressed concerns that the tax could make hotels less competitive, put hospitality jobs at risk, and impact tourism.
key_points: London's tourism tax is understood to be capped at no higher than 5% of accommodation costs.
Mayor Sadiq Khan strongly welcomed the government's plan to grant mayors the power to introduce the levy.
Industry bodies and trade representatives warned the tax could put tourism and hospitality jobs at risk.
Westminster Council and London Councils called for local authorities to retain a fair share of the revenue raised.

title: Catherine joins Prince William at suicide prevention campaign
author: Sean Coughlan
content:
![Prince and Princess of Wales](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1040/cpsprodpb/72d3/live/65e5cef0-ad04-11f1-beae-535b95a24b3e.jpg)
Catherine was a surprise visitor to Prince William's project about mental health
- Published
The Princess of Wales has made a surprise appearance alongside her husband the Prince of Wales, as he calls on the sports sector to help prevent suicides.
Prince William and Catherine are at Everton's football ground in Liverpool to launch a project encouraging people to remove the stigma around mental health challenges and to encourage people to seek help.
"Sport has the ability to reach people who may never walk through the door of a mental healthcare service," Prince William will say at the Hill Dickinson stadium.
"People who may never seek support themselves and may be struggling in silence," the prince is expected to say.
![A composite image of headshots of Prince William, Harry Kane and Alan Shearer](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/afc8/live/e42bb370-acea-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
Prince William, Harry Kane and Alan Shearer want to use sport to end the stigma around talking about mental health
The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health.
It's being supported by sport stars including Harry Kane, Dame Kelly Holmes and Alan Shearer.
Royal sources said that Catherine wanted to attend to highlight the difference that can be made when people feel able to talk openly about how they are feeling and when someone is there to listen.
The project aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.
This event will be Prince William's biggest public appearance in the UK since the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex from the US.
Earlier this week, William attended the funeral of Norway's King Harald in Oslo and accompanied his son Prince George to his first day as a boarder at Eton College.
The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it's the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK.
And sport is seen as an effective way of communicating that help is available.
"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William will say.
The royal couple will see a bench at the ground dedicated in memory of Gary Speed, a footballer who once played at the club, and who died by suicide in 2011.
The bench, unveiled last year, is intended to give people a space to speak openly about their anxieties as part of efforts to tackle mental health challenges and loneliness.
Alan Shearer, former England football star and TV pundit, was a friend of Gary Speed and is backing the call for people to try to support people they have worries about.
"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."
A film has been made, featuring England football captain Harry Kane and boxer Carl Frampton, talking about the importance of stepping in and offering help if people see someone who seems to be facing mental health problems.
Prince William helps to narrate the video, which wants to tackle the stigma around mental health and suicide, with 7,000 lives being lost to suicide each year in the UK.
The initiative has a practical toolkit, on a free website, for people who are worried or embarrassed about what to say to someone if they have concerns about their well-being.
It offers a sports-themed way of approaching the topic, called GOALS, representing G: get ready; O: open the conversation; A: ask the question; L: listen and respond and S: support and signpost.
Watch: Prince William shared his mental health tips earlier this year
The project has been created with the the British Standards Institution and mental health charities, including Chasing the Stigma, which has an app called Hub of Hope which claims to have the UK's largest mental health directory of places to get help.
The charity's founder Jake Mills said he had faced his own mental health challenges and saw sport as an effective route for this type of message.
He said sport was a "real force for good" in bringing people together and for "looking out for one another".
Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said he wanted to see sports organisations "creating a culture where conversations about well-being are really encouraged. Where people feel comfortable asking for help and also know where to get it".
Backing the project on Thursday in Liverpool is Olympian Dame Kelly, commentator Gabby Logan and former England footballer Jill Scott.
Prince William has been a longstanding campaigner over mental health and preventing suicide, with his Royal Foundation having last year launched the National Suicide Prevention Network.
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: The Princess of Wales made a surprise appearance alongside Prince William at Everton's football ground in Liverpool to launch the "On Your Side" mental health project. The initiative aims to use the sports sector to remove the stigma around mental health challenges, encourage people to seek help, and prevent suicides.
