Supported by major sports organizations and star athletes, the project provides a practical toolkit and a free website to help people initiate difficult conversations about well-being.
key_points: Prince William and Catherine launched the On Your Side project at Everton's football ground to encourage people to seek help for mental health challenges.
The initiative leverages the reach of sport to reach individuals who might never walk through the door of traditional mental healthcare services.
The project is supported by sports stars such as Harry Kane, Alan Shearer, and Dame Kelly Holmes.
A sports-themed approach called GOALS was introduced to give people confidence in starting difficult conversations about mental well-being.
Suicide is the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK, making sport an effective communication channel for crisis support.

title: Tourist tax plans for England set to be outlined
author: Jack Fenwick; Chris Graham
content:
![Tourists walking across Westminster Bridge in London with the London Eye in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/7581/live/b9bf1460-acbd-11f1-b473-659b8af1c846.jpg)
Cities like London are expected to use the new powers to introduce a levy on overnight stays
- Published
Plans to give mayors in England the power to introduce a levy on tourists are expected to be outlined on Thursday.
Under the proposals, a fee would be charged to people staying overnight and local leaders would decide how the revenue raised should be reinvested.
The idea - dubbed the tourist tax - was first raised by Sir Keir Starmer's government in November and is similar to a scheme running in Scotland.
The levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of accommodation, rather than as a flat fee - a move the government argues will protect budget holidays.
In theory, there will be no upper limit - though ministers are said to believe mayors are unlikely to make it too expensive.
The government will announce more details after the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner meets mayors on Thursday.
A government source said "it will be up to local leaders and local voters" in England "to decide what is right for their area".
The Overnight Visitor Levy, which was outlined in the King's Speech in May, means a holiday in England could become more expensive if local leaders decide to implement the tax.
Sir Keir had planned to bring forward legislation to introduce the levy before he was replaced as prime minister by Andy Burnham but the bill has not been brought forward yet.
The prime minister has framed the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda, and No 10 previously said local leaders would be "able to set out plans for how revenues will be invested by March 2028".
Burnham was mayor of Manchester when the city introduced the City Visitor Charge in April 2023 - a Â£1 per room, per night fee - to pay for measures aimed at attracting more visitors.
Regional mayors say the levy is needed to raise more income to invest in local priorities and support economic growth.
However, trade body UK Hospitality warned earlier this year that such a tax would raise the cost of holidays as households continue to face costâofâliving challenges.
It said additional charges risked undermining international competitiveness and discouraging domestic breaks, particularly for families and young people.
These taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, with New York, Amsterdam and Rome applying overnight charges to accommodation stays to fund local services.
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan supports a tourist tax on overnight visitors, which could raise more than Â£350m a year for the capital, according to analysis in January.
The figure from Central London Forward (CLF), which represents 12 central London local authorities, was based on a 3% levy on the cost of a room, whether a hotel or short-term let.
In Scotland local authorities can introduce a visitor levy on overnight accommodation set as a percentage rate.
Edinburgh became the first city there to introduce the tax in July, with those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering accommodation charged an additional 5% on top of their original booking cost. However, the charge is capped at five nights.
Elsewhere in Scotland, a 5% levy in Glasgow is due to come into force from January 2027.
In Wales, a capped levy of Â£1.30 per person per night is set to be introduced in April next year.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/4201/live/b5ec3770-acde-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
summary: Plans to grant mayors in England the power to introduce a tourist tax on overnight stays are expected to be outlined following a meeting between the Housing Secretary and regional leaders. The levy would be charged as a percentage of accommodation costs rather than a flat fee, allowing local leaders to decide how the revenue is reinvested. While supporters argue the funds will support local priorities and economic growth, hospitality trade bodies warn it could increase holiday costs and discourage visitors.
key_points: Mayors in England are expected to receive powers to implement a tourist tax on overnight stays.
The fee will be charged as a percentage of accommodation costs to protect budget holidays.
Local leaders will decide whether to implement the tax and how the resulting revenue is reinvested.
UK Hospitality warned the levy could raise holiday costs and harm international competitiveness.
Similar overnight visitor levies are already operating or planned in Scotland, Wales, and various international cities.

title: Harry blames King’s letter for Uganda’s withdrawal from Invictus Games
author: Victoria Ward; Ben Farmer
content:
![They sit together in a sports stadium stand](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000293088617_17889572176580_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqplGOf-dgG3z4gg9owgQTXF5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![They sit together in a sports stadium stand](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000293088617_17889572176580_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqplGOf-dgG3z4gg9owgQTXF5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duke of Sussex has blamed Uganda’s decision to pull out of the Invictus Games on the King’s letter that described them as “private citizens”.
Uganda withdrew from Prince Harry’s international event for sick and injured military personnel on Wednesday, claiming it did not have the King’s “approval”.
The extraordinary move was announced by Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the country’s military chief and son of the Ugandan president, who blamed the “Harry and Meghan nonsense”.
It came just two days after Buckingham Palace circulated a letter on the direction of the King confirming that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were “private citizens” and that their work was not on behalf of the monarchy.
A source close to the Sussexes told The Telegraph on Wednesday evening that they believed the letter was to blame.
“Intended or unintended, this is clearly a consequence of the Lord Chamberlain’s guidance regarding the Duke and Duchess of Sussex that was rushed out without consultation on Monday,” the source said.
“Sadly, the only people who will suffer are the Invictus Games competitors.”
Gen Kainerugaba had earlier written on X: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the invictus games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”
![He wears a walrus moustache and military uniform](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501833424_17889574115040_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He told The Times: “I have factions in the ministry of defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”
The Invictus Games Foundation was unaware of the development before Gen Kainerugaba’s post was published on social media, The Telegraph understands. The organisation is now in discussions with its partners in Uganda to clarify the position.
In response, a Buckingham Palace source insisted that the King encouraged all organisations and endeavours in support of wounded service personnel.
Fears were immediately raised that Uganda’s decision was prompted by the letter circulated by the Lord Chamberlain, head of the royal household, on the direction of the King.
‘Duke and Duchess do not represent the sovereign’
The letter was sent to a small number of “key stakeholders” in Government and the military, specifying that the Duke and Duchess did not represent the sovereign, and were not working members of the Royal family.
It said the couple’s use of their HRH titles would remain in abeyance and that any charity work was “a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity”.
The letter added: “In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
This marked the first sign of tension between the two camps since the pair returned to the UK with their two children last month.
The Sussexes admitted they were “surprised” not to have been given more than an hour’s advance notice of its circulation.
It was made public on the eve of a crunch meeting that is expected to decide whether or not the Sussexes are entitled to taxpayer-funded police protection now they are back in the UK.
The all-important Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec) meeting is scheduled to take place this week, marking the climax of a deeply personal battle that Prince Harry has fought for more than six years.
Gen Kainerugaba, who is widely expected to follow in the footsteps of his 81-year-old father, Yoweri Museveni, is sometimes known as the “tweeting general” for his fiery and provocative posts.
In 2022, Mr Museveni was forced to step in and apologise after his son posted a series of messages threatening to invade neighbouring Kenya.
![Speaking into a microphone, he wears a broad-brimmed hat and gesticulates](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000500478219_17889574917780_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Gen Kainerugaba was also condemned for posts that were subsequently deleted, in which he threatened to have Bobi Wine, a defeated opposition candidate, castrated.
The general has stepped down from the social media platform at least twice, but has returned each time.
Uganda only joined the Invictus Games in July, becoming the 26th nation to take part and the first country from East Africa.
Its involvement was announced at an event at Chatham House in London, as Prince Harry began the one-year countdown to the Invictus Games 2027.
He was joined at the reception by Kiryowa Kiwanuka, Uganda’s defence minister, who praised the Duke.
Mr Kiwanuka said: “This milestone reflects our shared commitment to wounded, injured and sick servicemen and women who have sacrificed greatly in service to our nation.”
The minister said the decision to take part affirmed Uganda’s belief that “those who have borne the burdens of service deserve every opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity, purpose, and hope”. “They are our living heroes,” he added.
The Duke posed for a picture with Ugandan delegates, raising a laugh as he held up a cardboard plaque the size of a tea tray and pretended to throw it like a Frisbee across the room.
The about-turn announced by Gen Kainerugaba will come as a blow to Prince Harry, who has recently moved back to Britain and plans to make the build-up to next year’s Games, which will take place in Birmingham, a central plank of his work.
Crucially, as palace sources indicated, the King’s lack of involvement in the Invictus Games, which is very much the Duke’s project, should not be interpreted as a lack of approval.
When the event was launched in 2014, the King, then Prince Charles, joined his younger son at the opening ceremony, with the now Queen and Prince William.
Beyond that show of support, palace sources have previously insisted that senior members of the Royal family never involve themselves in each other’s work.
The Invictus Games and the Duke’s office have been approached for comment.
summary: Prince Harry and sources close to the Sussexes have blamed Uganda's withdrawal from the Invictus Games on a recent letter from Buckingham Palace. The letter, issued on the direction of the King, clarified that the Duke and Duchess are private citizens whose work is not on behalf of the monarchy. Ugandan military chief Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba cited a lack of the King's approval as the reason for pulling the country out of the event.
key_points: Uganda withdrew from the Invictus Games, claiming the event lacked King Charles III's approval.
A source close to the Sussexes blamed the withdrawal on a palace letter stating the couple are private citizens.
The controversial letter was issued by the Lord Chamberlain on the direction of the King.
Uganda had only joined the Invictus Games as the 26th participating nation in July.

title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
author: Caroline Davies
content:
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.
Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”
The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.
When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”
The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.
At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.
The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”
The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.
The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.
Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.
summary: Uganda has announced its withdrawal from the Invictus Games, citing a desire to show respect for King Charles III and avoid participating in events without his approval. Military chief General Muhoozi Kainerugaba made the announcement on X, stating he wanted to quash internal ministry factions supporting Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. The decision follows a royal household letter clarifying that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are no longer working royals.
key_points: Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced the country's withdrawal from the Invictus Games on X.
The decision was made out of respect for King Charles III and to counter internal support for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle.
The move comes shortly after an official letter from the royal household clarified that the Sussexes are not working royals.
Uganda had only recently been announced as the 26th participating country in the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

title: 'It's been a nightmare': Passengers face airport chaos after UK air traffic issue
author: Alex Boyd; BBC Your Voice reporters
content:
'Horrendous experience': Passengers react to travel chaos
- Published
Passengers left stranded by an hours-long air traffic control issue at UK airports have told the BBC of nightmare delays, chaotic scenes and waylaid holiday plans.
Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been hit with flight cancellations and delays throughout Tuesday and Wednesday after a technical problem caused the air traffic outage.
That included newlyweds Sasha and James, who told BBC Your Voice they spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons at Gatwick after their flight to their honeymoon was cancelled.
Some also described sleeping on airport floors and chaos at baggage reclaim as thousands looked to reorganise their plans, while others have been stranded abroad while trying to get back to the UK.
Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, has said flight operations are now stable but airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status before travelling to airports.
The boss of Nats Martin Rolfe apologised for the disruption and also met with Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday, who asked for a full investigation.
Most of the UK's main airports were hit by the problem including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Wednesday, newly married couple Sasha and James Graham said they were boarding their flight from Gatwick to Funchal on the island of Madeira when they were "turned right back around".
![James (left) and Sasha (right) smile at the camera while sat at a table in the airport Wetherspoons](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/542/cpsprodpb/2c68/live/f2cee0a0-ac63-11f1-be57-03729df1d736.png)
The newlyweds spent three hours at a Wetherspoons in Gatwick after a flight to their honeymoon was cancelled
Sasha said: "We spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons, making the best of it.
"It's certainly not the experience we planned, but I think starting your marriage with a national disruption is certainly very memorable!"
They weren't able to reclaim their luggage but have since booked onto a new flight.
"It feels like we will spend our honeymoon at Gatwick," Sasha added.
![Phil White smiles at the camera as he sits on an EasyJet plane](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/569d/live/c0857750-ac66-11f1-80f0-9795d1a5edbc.jpg)
Phil White said tempers frayed at Gatwick as people tried to reclaim their luggage on Tuesday
Phil White also spoke of incredibly busy scenes in the airport's baggage reclaim hall, describing it as "carnage" as an influx of disrupted passengers tried to find their luggage.
"All the bags from every cancelled flight were sent to one reclaim carousel. So there were a thousand or so people trying to get close enough to get their cases," he said.
"The baggage hall was the worst and they're very lucky that there wasn't any sort of incident as tempers frayed and the concourse was getting hotter."
Elsewhere, people spoke of spending the night on the floors of airports and hotels across the globe when flights back into the UK were cancelled.
Sukie Perera, from Cardiff, describing her experience of being stuck in Turkey said "it has been a nightmare" and communication at the airport was poor.
She won't be able to fly home until Thursday but joked that at least "the view is beautiful".
Paul Willows, currently in Rhodes, Greece, with his family said they had to sleep on the floor of a hotel's conference room on Tuesday night.
He said: "They stripped all the cushions off the sunbeds and laid them in the conference room. I dare say there were about 80 of us on the floor."
Despite it having "not been a comfortable night at all", Paul said there was a "good element of pulling together" from those impacted.
Alan Jones and Kelly Fewery also said their family was "absolutely exhausted" after sleeping on the floor of Dalaman Airport in Turkey without blankets or pillows.
More than 340 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.
Airlines are still obliged to get passengers to their destinations - even if that is via another carrier - when their flight is cancelled, or give a refund.
Those delayed may have the right to food, or a hotel stay, depending on the length of the wait. But no extra compensation payments should be expected as the air traffic control issue was not the fault of any airline.
summary: An hours-long technical problem with the UK air traffic control provider, Nats, caused widespread flight cancellations and delays across major UK airports on Tuesday and Wednesday. Hundreds of thousands of passengers faced severe disruption, including stranded holidaymakers sleeping on airport floors, chaotic baggage claims, and postponed honeymoons. Although Nats reported that flight operations are now stable, airlines have warned of continued knock-on effects, prompting the transport secretary to request a full investigation.
key_points: A technical issue at Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, caused widespread flight cancellations and delays across major UK airports on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Passengers reported chaotic scenes, including crowded baggage claims and sleeping on the floors of airports and hotels both in the UK and abroad.
More than 340 flights were cancelled on Wednesday alone, and airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met with Nats boss Martin Rolfe and requested a full investigation into the incident.

title: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security
author: Becky Morton; Harry Farley
content:
National security 'can't come at the expense of social security', says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Minister's Questions.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pressed Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for this.
The PM said the government's commitment to defence was "absolute" and he would set a target date to reach the 3% figure in the spring.
Burnham said he would fund defence and get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by changing education, supporting young people and providing more mental health support.
The Conservatives seized on the comments, with a party spokesperson saying: "Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country.
"The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful."
After PMQs, Burnham's team was at pains to stress his commitment that "national security is the most important duty of any government", and stressed the prime minister had been "consistent about getting the welfare bill down".
But they said that did not mean "crude cuts" that could "put people into crisis" by making them homeless and so creating higher costs elsewhere in the system to support them.
In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.
The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".
However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".
She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.
In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."
However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit.
"I don't think, myself, that taking Â£4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.
"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."
He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."
Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."
Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.
"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.
"That is the right way to fund defence."
Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".
"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.
As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.
Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.
Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.
There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training â known as "Neets".
The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: During Prime Minister's Questions, Andy Burnham stated that national security cannot come at the expense of social security when pressed by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch over defence funding and the welfare bill. Burnham reaffirmed the government's commitment to meeting NATO defence targets by 2035 and promised a target date for 3% GDP spending in the spring. However, he rejected Conservative proposals to fund defence by cutting housing benefit, arguing it would increase homelessness, and instead proposed reducing the welfare bill by supporting young people.
key_points: Andy Burnham stated that national security cannot come at the expense of social security during Prime Minister's Questions.
Kemi Badenoch challenged Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for it.
Burnham reaffirmed plans to meet NATO's 3.5% defence spending target by 2035, with a target date for 3% to be set in the spring spending review.
Burnham rejected Conservative plans to fund defence through housing benefit cuts, arguing it would cause widespread homelessness.
The prime minister stated he plans to reduce the welfare bill by focusing on education, young people, and mental health support.

title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
author: Kate Whannel
content:
![Dan Jukes and Nigel Farage](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9b95/live/beba2b00-ac57-11f1-be57-03729df1d736.jpg)
Dan Jukes (left) stood down from the party after the allegations around foreign donations emerged
- Published
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into allegations Reform UK broke the law in relation to foreign funding, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.
An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled Â£500,000.
The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.
A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation".
"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."
A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening.
In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."
"Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."
The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.
The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.
In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.
Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.
Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.
Elsewhere James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.
Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".
Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".
The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.
The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.
It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received Â£1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.
summary: The Metropolitan Police has launched a criminal investigation into Reform UK following allegations that the party broke electoral law regarding foreign funding. The inquiry follows a Channel 4 News broadcast featuring undercover recordings of two senior Reform aides, Dan Jukes and James Orr, suggesting methods to bypass rules on foreign donations. Both figures subsequently stepped down from the party, which denies any wrongdoing and is cooperating with the investigation.
key_points: The Metropolitan Police's Special Enquiry Team is investigating Reform UK over potential violations of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.
An undercover Channel 4 News report showed senior aides suggesting ways to circumvent laws preventing direct foreign donations.
Chief of staff Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr both stepped down following the allegations.
The new probe has been folded into an ongoing Met investigation into other party donations involving Fiona Cottrell and Richard Tice.
Reform UK has denied any wrongdoing and stated it will fully cooperate with authorities.

title: UK flight cancellations pass 1,900 as pressure grows on air traffic control boss on second day of travel chaos – business live
author: Julia Kollewe
content:
UK flight cancellations pass 1,900 as pressure grows on air traffic control boss on second day of travel chaos – business live
Technical issue at Nats resolved but flights to and from UK airports still disrupted; oil prices hit $100 a barrel for first time since July and gas prices also jump
Passengers at Heathrow Airport in west London, during disruption after a system issue hit Nats, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Further cancellations and delays are expected today. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA
Passengers at Heathrow Airport in west London, during disruption after a system issue hit Nats, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Further cancellations and delays are expected today. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA
More than 1,900 flights cancelled over two days, according to Cirium
In total, more 1,900 flights had been cancelled by 5am today, according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, since yesterday’s system issue at National Air Traffic Services.
Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. While the technical problem has been resolved, the flight chaos has continued into a second day. Other flights have been delayed, causing chaos for tens of thousands of passenggers travelling to and from the UK.
Cirium says:
8 September: More than 1,750 flights arriving into and departing from UK airports were cancelled — 902 departures and 860 arrivals, out of 5,800 scheduled. A normal day is under 1–2%.
9 September: So far, 153 flights are cancelled — 55 departures and 98 arrivals. Just over 3%.
European stock markets slide while energy stocks are higher
Energy companies BP, Shell and British Gas parent Centrica are among the main risers on the FTSE 100 index today, as the oil price surged through $100 a barrel, for the first time since 24 July.
Centrica shares are up 2.1%, BP has gained 1.5% and Shell is 0.9% ahead.
The wider FTSE 100 index is trading lower, down 0.6% or 66 points at 10,745. The German, French, Italian and Spanish indices have fallen even more, between 1.1% and 1.9%.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at the trading platform capital.com, said:
Markets remain on the defensive as the latest escalation in the Middle East pushes Brent to $100 a barrel. US forces have struck Iranian oil tankers following attempted attacks on US naval vessels, while Iran retaliated against a US-used base in Jordan and says it targeted vessels attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities have widened the threat further, raising concerns that disruption could spread beyond Iranian supply to the infrastructure and alternative routes that have helped keep Gulf crude flowing.
That has brought the inflationary consequences of the conflict firmly back into focus. Wall Street fell on Tuesday as higher crude revived concerns that the energy shock could stall disinflation and force central banks to remain restrictive. US rate expectations have shifted accordingly, while upcoming inflation data will be particularly important in determining whether $100 oil is beginning to feed more materially into the Fed[eral Reserve] outlook.
Europe faces an even more immediate policy test with the European Central Bank meeting on Thursday. Markets are widely positioned for a 25 basis point hike, after the ECB explicitly warned in July that the full inflationary impact of the energy shock had yet to emerge. The latest surge in oil, and European gas prices, makes that concern harder to dismiss. Focus will be on Christine Lagarde’s guidance on whether this is sufficient insurance against the energy shock or whether further tightening remains likely.
UK and European gas prices surge to multi-year highs
UK and European gas prices have risen to a multi-year highs, while the oil price jumped above $100 a barrel.
The escalating Middle East conflict, cooler weather and rising Asian gas prices has led to aggressive gas buying ahead of the winter.
The benchmark Dutch gas contract leapt nearly 4% to €78.73 per megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023.
The British contract rose 7.77 pence 196.57p per therm, the highest since late December 2022.
In oil markets, Brent crude surged through $100 a barrel for the first time since July, rising 2.7% to $100.68 a barrel.
European gas stores are only 67% full, compared to 79.5% a year ago, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
Analysts at HSBC are forecasting that European stock levels will reach 73% by 1 November, the lowest since data collection began in 2009, and do not expect Qatari liquefied natural gas exports, excluding damaged facilities, to return to normal until early next year at the earliest.
More than 1,900 flights cancelled over two days, according to Cirium
In total, more 1,900 flights had been cancelled by 5am today, according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, since yesterday’s system issue at National Air Traffic Services.
Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. While the technical problem has been resolved, the flight chaos has continued into a second day. Other flights have been delayed, causing chaos for tens of thousands of passenggers travelling to and from the UK.
Cirium says:
8 September: More than 1,750 flights arriving into and departing from UK airports were cancelled — 902 departures and 860 arrivals, out of 5,800 scheduled. A normal day is under 1–2%.
9 September: So far, 153 flights are cancelled — 55 departures and 98 arrivals. Just over 3%.
UK boss of Wizz Air urges Nats CEO to consider resigning
The UK boss of Wizz Air has urged Martin Rolfe to consider resigning over the repeated technical failures at National Air Traffic Services.
Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, said Wizz Air had 24 cancellations on Tuesday and more than 21 flights had long delays, so over 10,000 passengers coming in and out of London were disrupted at the Hungarian budget carrier alone.
“It’s completely unacceptable that the travelling public has to pay for this,” told BBC radio 4’s Today programme.
This is now the third time that we have had an ATC [air traffic control] failure, and during the peak period as well. So major questions need to be asked. At the moment, of course, the immediate priority is getting passengers to their destinations. But the longer term question really is understanding what exactly has happened and how has this happened on three different occasions? There are serious questions about the resilience of the system.
Asked whether the Nats boss should resign, she said:
In any industry when you’ve had three failures you need to consider three strikes and you’re out. It’s certainly something that he needs to look at.
A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability. There are serious questions about the resilience of the system.
I think Nats and the leadership need to look deep inside themselves.
What we need to see from the leadership is accountability and reassurance that we won’t face these repeated failures.
Oil price hits $100 a barrel for first time since July
Brent crude has just hit $100 a barrel for the first time since 24 July, as military strikes in the Middle East escalate.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, jumped to $100.19 a barrel, up more than $2, and a 2.2% increase. The oil price has risen by a quarter since early last month as hopes vanish for a deal between the US and Iran to end the six-month war that began with air strikes by the US and Israel on Tehran on 28 February.
This week, attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels from Yemen have set Saudi oil facilities ablaze, in an escalation of the conflict. The attacks could threaten oil shipments via the Red Sea, an alernative route to the strait of Hormuz which has been effectively closed for months.
The boss of National Air Traffic Services, which is half-owned by the government, has insisted that the organisation has invested enough in its systems.
Martin Rolfe told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme:
Nats was actually a partial privatisation, 25 years ago, and since that point has had access to funding, we’ve invested way more than a billion [pounds], in technology over that time. Our service has consistently improved. Our safety has consistently improved from a very good base. But all of those things don’t detract from the fact that when these things happen, it is disappointing and upsetting, for which I apologise.
We are in a critical national infrastructure business where safety is our priority and it runs 24/7. It runs, you know, every single day of the year, every minute of the day, every minute of the night. It is never quiet in UK skies. Inevitably, things do go wrong in complex systems. We never want them to. We always hope they won’t, but we absolutely plan for them to and make sure we handle them properly.
When asked if they “go as wrong in other countries”, Rolfe replied:
Absolutely. In fact, I would say the UK has one of the best reputations in the world for its air traffic control service, both from a safety perspective and from a resilience perspective.
We do have one of the best systems and one of the best services in the world. and that’s consistently recognised globally.
The UK cannot have a repeat of the travel disruption seen at airports, the foreign secretary has said.
Asked about the flight chaos, Ed Miliband told BBC Breakfast:
First of all, I want to apologise to all of the passengers who have faced disruption.
This is frankly unacceptable. It was a problem at the National Air Traffic Service, but we can’t have this happen again.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, is calling in the head of the National Air Traffic Service this morning to get answers to this. Miliband added:
Frankly, we’ve got to have our airports running smoothly and properly, without those problems, and that is what the transport secretary will be asking for from the head of the National Air Traffic Service.
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband speaks at the House of Commons in London, Britain, 8 September. Photograph: House Of Commons/Reuters
Nats boss rules out cyber attack as he apologises to passengers
The boss of National Air Traffic Services, Martin Rolfe, has ruled out a cyber attack as a cause of the flight chaos, and apologised to passengers caught up in the flight chaos caused by a system issue on Tuesday, and said he understands their frustration –- but stressed that safety comes first.
Speaking to BBC radio 4’s Today programme, he said:
I’d like to start, as you might expect, by apologising to everyone who’s been impacted by the issue that we had yesterday.
In terms of the recovery, I absolutely understand the frustration. There is nothing we hate more than delaying people, and not allowing them to get to their destination. It disrupts airports and disrupts airlines. And we absolutely take accountability and responsibility for that. That is our job. But our job is also to make sure that people stay safe. We never do this lightly.
He ruled out a cyber attack.
We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation. We have at this point ruled out cyber. We don’t believe it was a cyber attack.
Obviously my focus and that of the team has been on both getting our system operating back up normally, which it is now. But there’s obviously a huge tail to the disruption. And we’ll be working on that through the course of today.
And then obviously our attention will turn to exactly what’s happened, this particular incident. What I will say is I don’t believe we’ve ever seen an incident happen more than once. So this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation.
Rolfe insisted that Nats dealt with the issue as quickly as it could:
We had everybody on site. Everybody was in the right place. We had all the engineers in place. We had our various partners from software industries and so on, all on hand. So this was resolved as quickly as it could be, but within the limits of making sure that it all stayed safe.
In the markets, oil prices are rising towards the $100 a barrel level for the first time since July.
Brent crude has jumped 1.5% to $99.36 a barrel, as escalating attacks across the Middle East are fuelling fears over supply disruptions.
Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen launched strikes on several Saudi cities while US forces hit several Iranian oil tankers and Iran targeted a US base in Jordan and attacked ships.
There is some confusion over the situation at Heathrow airport.
Heathrow said on X this morning:
Following yesterday’s NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.
We apologise to those affected and have extra colleagues across our terminals to support passengers while we work with NATS and airline partners to restore normal operations as quickly as possible.
However, the flight tracking website Flightradar24 says 177 flights have been cancelled so far on Wednesday, nearly all at London-Heathrow.
Air traffic control boss to meet UK transport secretary as second day of flight chaos takes cancellations past 1,300
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
The boss of the air traffic control provider Nats has been summoned by the UK transport secretary, as flight chaos carried on into a second day after a system issue, with after more than 1,300 flights cancelled to and from UK airports.
National Air Traffic Services provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Its chief executive Martin Rolfe is due to speak to Heidi Alexander, before she addresses MPs in the Commons for the second reading of the Civil Aviation Bill.
Tens of thousands of passengers have been caught up in the chaos, with more cancellations and delays expected as airlines deal with the knock-on effects at airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.
According to FlightRadar, 246 flights had been cancelled at Heathrow Airport by 6am on Wednesday, while Gatwick passengers faced 33 cancellations.
Rolfe said he “always accept(s) full responsibility” when asked if he was considering his position after the incident.
He told Sky News:
I am the CEO of a piece of critical infrastructure, so it is my job to take responsibility for that.
What I absolutely take responsibility for is keeping people safe and delivering the best service we possibly can on a day like today.
You will understand my focus is entirely about how we actually resolve this issue, get things back to normal, help our airlines, our airport customers and the travelling public.
The “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused Britain’s third major stoppage in just over three years. Nats said on Tuesday evening:
This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.
The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. By the time Nats said it had fixed its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart were yet to take off. The disruption spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.
summary: More than 1,900 flights have been cancelled over two days following a technical system issue at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), causing widespread travel disruption across the UK. While the technical problem has been resolved, pressure is mounting on Nats boss Martin Rolfe, with the UK boss of Wizz Air suggesting he consider resigning and government officials demanding answers. Simultaneously, global oil prices surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time since July due to escalating Middle East conflicts, contributing to surging UK and European gas prices and sliding European stock markets.
key_points: Over 1,900 flights have been cancelled over two days due to an air traffic control system issue at Nats.
The UK boss of Wizz Air urged Nats CEO Martin Rolfe to consider resigning following repeated technical failures.
Brent crude oil prices surged past $100 a barrel for the first time since July amid escalating Middle East tensions.
UK and European gas prices reached multi-year highs as aggressive buying occurred ahead of winter.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander summoned the head of Nats for answers regarding the unacceptable travel disruption.

title: UK airport disruption: what are your rights if you have been affected?
author: Zoe Wood; Rupert Jones
content:
Airports across the UK including Manchester, Birmingham and all those in London were hit by problems at air traffic control on Tuesday.
The technical issue was announced shortly before 2pm and was resolved about three hours later. By that time, hundreds of flights had been cancelled, with knock-on disruption across Britain and at destination airports abroad likely to continue into the evening and possibly Wednesday.
Here we explain what you can expect if you have been affected.
Is your flight delayed or cancelled?
The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) website explains how long the delay has to be before you are entitled to care and assistance from your airline while you wait. The timeframe differs by flight distance. This assistance should cover food and drink and the ability to make phone calls or send emails, plus accommodation and the necessary transfers if the flight is delayed until the next day.
Many airlines will provide vouchers for you to buy food and drink, and overnight accommodation will typically take the form of a nearby hotel (unless you live nearby, in which case your airline may reimburse your costs for getting to and from home).
Sometimes airline staff are unable to arrange care and assistance for all passengers, in which case you can sort yourself out and claim the cost back later.
But don’t splash the cash – and keep receipts. The CAA says airlines may have guidelines on this, adding: “Airlines are unlikely to consider alcoholic drinks, luxury hotels or luxury meals to be reasonable.”
If your flight has been cancelled and is covered by UK law – that means one departing from an airport in the UK on any airline, or arriving at an airport in the UK on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline – your airline must offer you the choice of another flight or a refund.
If you select an alternative flight, it is up to you whether you fly as soon as possible or at a later date.
If the delay is more than five hours you can choose not to travel and receive a refund.
I am due to fly imminently – should I still go to the airport?
If you are due to travel on Tuesday evening or Wednesday, check the latest advice from your airport or tour operator, or airline apps and airport social media feeds, for the most up-to-date information.
The air traffic control service provider Nats had advised that it would “take some time” to rectify the problem but at about 5pm it posted on social media that it had “implemented a fix and our flight system is starting to recover”. The knock on impact on flight schedules could take some time to be resolved.
Will I be entitled to compensation from the airline?
If your flight was cancelled or delayed as a result of Tuesday’s issue, you are unlikely to be owed compensation by the airline. This is because the technical issue affecting flights will be considered an extraordinary circumstance and out of the airline’s control.
Causes of disruption classed as outside an airline’s control also include severe weather and security alerts.
Anna-Marie Duthie, a travel insurance expert at the financial ratings company Defaqto, says: “Travel insurance may cover you if you cannot claim costs back from the airline, operator, or credit card but that will all depend on whether your policy includes cover for delay, travel disruption, missed connection or abandonment.”
summary: A technical issue at UK air traffic control on Tuesday caused widespread cancellations and delays across major airports like Manchester, Birmingham, and London. Although the system issue was resolved within three hours, knock-on disruptions are expected to continue. Passengers facing significant delays are entitled to care and assistance from airlines, while cancelled flights qualify for a refund or alternative travel.
key_points: A technical issue at UK air traffic control on Tuesday led to hundreds of flight cancellations and ongoing disruptions.
Airlines must provide care and assistance, such as food, drink, and accommodation, for qualifying delays, though passengers can arrange their own and claim reasonable costs back with receipts.
Passengers with cancelled flights under UK law are entitled to a refund or an alternative flight of their choice.
Passengers are unlikely to receive compensation from airlines because air traffic control technical issues are considered extraordinary circumstances outside the airline's control.

title: Balaclava-clad anti-migrant protesters descend on Glasgow
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Police disperse the protesters](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501733607_17889023048850_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpFcVB2ds_3OVwUA_xFA0AMZ053JTmIECyPoDv5jg3S4.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Police disperse the protesters](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501733607_17889023048850_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpFcVB2ds_3OVwUA_xFA0AMZ053JTmIECyPoDv5jg3S4.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Balaclava-clad protesters chanting “stop the boats” descended on Glasgow on Tuesday.
A group of approximately two dozen demonstrators dressed in black walked through the city centre before being “contained” by police.
The group, which was dispersed and caused no disruption, was dressed similarly to the Patriot Platform group that demonstrated in Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend.
However, there appears to be no connection between the groups and Daniel Thomas, the activist behind Patriot Platform, who has not commented on the protest.
According to posts on social media the protest was organised by the Scottish Citizens Army.
In a social media post they said: “We apologise to drivers delayed later today. This afternoon’s protest will hold up journeys home from work. We know that will anger people.”
Naming the protest Operation Standstill, the post continued: “We regret the disruption. Until the Government listens, it will continue.”
Police Scotland said the group gathered in Buchanan Street, in Glasgow’s city centre, shortly after 4pm before making their way to Charing Cross, a mile to the east.
Witnesses heard the group shouting “stop the boats”, according to the Glasgow Times.
The protesters were then “contained” by officers to “maintain public safety”.
A spokesman for Police Scotland said: “The group made their way through the city centre towards Charing Cross where officers contained them to engage, maintain public safety and minimise disruption.
“They are in the process of being dispersed from the area and there was no wider risk to the public or disruption to travel networks.”
The protest came two days after as many as 200 anti-migrant activists and residents gathered in Portsmouth to protest the arrival of 120 migrants from a mega-dinghy in the Channel on Sunday.
The mega-dinghy had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy at 1am on Sunday. The beach lies more than 250 miles west of Calais, and is the westernmost point from which a migrant dinghy has crossed the Channel.
The subsequent demonstration in Eastney, Portsmouth, was led by Mr Thomas.
On Saturday an anti-migrant protest took place in Dover, when some 200 protesters, also dressed in balaclavas and black clothes, brought traffic to a standstill around the port.
An estimated 300 to 500 people, dressed in black and wearing masks, caused long tailbacks on roads surrounding the UK’s busiest ferry port.
The protest was organised by Patriot Platform, which initially threatened to blockade Dover for three days.
Mr Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, is understood to be a close associate of Tommy Robinson, the hard-right activist.
In recent weeks, Mr Thomas has been travelling around the country attempting to drum up support for his organisation, and has called for more protests.
summary: Balaclava-clad anti-migrant protesters chanted "stop the boats" as they marched through Glasgow city centre on Tuesday. Police contained the group of approximately two dozen demonstrators near Charing Cross before dispersing them without causing wider disruption or risk to the public. Social media posts indicated the event, dubbed Operation Standstill, was organized by the Scottish Citizens Army.
key_points: A group of about two dozen balaclava-clad protesters marched through Glasgow city centre on Tuesday chanting "stop the boats."
Police Scotland contained the demonstrators near Charing Cross and successfully dispersed them to maintain public safety.
Social media posts attributed the organization of the Glasgow protest, named Operation Standstill, to the Scottish Citizens Army.
The demonstration followed similar anti-migrant protests held over the weekend in Dover and Portsmouth led by the Patriot Platform group.

title: Two ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats
author: Nikki Mitchell; Stuart Rust
content:
![A general view looking across the Solent towards Portsmouth Harbour including the Spinnaker Tower and Eastside Plaza Tower residential apartment building in Gunwharf Quays.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/32d0/live/67c12eb0-ab90-11f1-aa04-efbf6a882854.jpg)
The King's Harbour Master Portsmouth declined a request to allow the migrants into the harbour, the BBC understands
- Published
Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.
When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road.
Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".
The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters.
The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.
The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.
They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.
RNLI lifeboats with migrants on board changed direction after being refused permission to land in Portsmouth and Southampton
An RNLI spokesperson said: "We are working with the relevant parties to understand the decision to deny access, and we are disappointed with the nature of the communication with our crews, who voluntarily give their time to save the lives of others at sea."
The narrow peninsula at Eastney has only one road leading in and out, which demonstrators used to block coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the area.
It led to a stand-off that lasted into the early hours of Monday.
Portsmouth City Council said it was a "completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore" and brought "needless disruption" to the area.
![Protesters face off against riot police in Portsmouth. The officers, to the right of the image, are wearing hi-viz and carrying shields.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1ed3/live/496bc9f0-aa5c-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Hundreds of people protested in Portsmouth after migrants were brought ashore on Sunday
Langstone Harbour Master Billy Johnson said the coastguard was coordinating "a search and rescue operation" and there was "no reason not to accept" the landing of the vessels at Eastney.
"The problem was managing the public order aspect that was also taking place and the geography of the area made that very challenging for the police," he said.
"This is a new thing in the Solent and the degree to which it attracted public interest and the speed at which the public reaction was mobilised was unusual and surprising.
"The way the emergency services mobilised was really effective, with the police, Border Force, coastguard, the RNLI, ambulance and fire service working completely together - all of whom were hindered by the activities of protesters."
ABP said it received an enquiry about landing recovered migrants.
It said in a statement: "We had to decline the enquiry as the Port did not have suitable reception facilities available.
"If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role.
"Neither was the case in this situation."
'Fear and tension'
The leader of Portsmouth City Council, Steve Pitt, said: "The Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement."
In the House of Commons yesterday, Dame Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Gosport, referred to the boat containing 120 migrants in the Solent as an "extraordinary mega dinghy".
She said: "MPs across the Solent region were scrambling for reliable information with complete radio silence from the Home Office. As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension."
Responding for the government, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said the department would "learn any lessons that we need to" following the weekend's protests.
Asked why Eastney had been chosen as the landing site, she said: "We are of course making sure we understand what exactly happened in that circumstance."
summary: Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port both refused requests to land RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight. The migrants were ultimately landed at Eastney in Langstone Harbour on Sunday, where anti-migrant protesters blocked the only access road, leading to a stand-off with police. Local authorities and port operators criticized the lack of planning and communication from the Home Office regarding the operation.
key_points: Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port declined coastguard requests to land RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants.
Associated British Ports stated Southampton did not have suitable reception facilities and was not the closest port.
Migrants were landed at Eastney in Langstone Harbour instead, where protesters blocked the road and caused a stand-off.
Port officials and city council leaders criticized the Home Office for poor planning, lack of communication, and choosing an unsuitable location.

title: All flights into Heathrow and Gatwick airport halted - live updates
author: Ruby Cline; Tom Jeffreys; Gareth Corfield; Neil Johnston
content:
![A miserable passenger at Heathrow](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501682435_17888877016240_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqlnoKbsnqupgsmdP1L78oDclaDlfF5Xha6GNIFIMmbLw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A miserable passenger at Heathrow](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501682435_17888877016240_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqlnoKbsnqupgsmdP1L78oDclaDlfF5Xha6GNIFIMmbLw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Flights have been grounded throughout Britain after an air traffic control technical failure.
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled across the country, with all arrivals into London Heathrow and Gatwick halted.
Airports including London City, Manchester, Stansted, East Midlands, Birmingham and Belfast City are also experiencing disruption.
The Telegraph understands that equipment at the headquarters of Nats, the air traffic control company, at Swanwick, near Southampton, has failed. Controllers based at the HQ are responsible for safely guiding flights across all UK airspace.
The “data processing” failure happened just after 1pm, multiple sources said.
Nats acknowledged a “technical issue” had occurred but gave no details of what had broken or why it had happened.
Later on Tuesday, Nats said its flight system was “starting to recover” after a fix was implemented.
Air traffic control: Outage recovery taking ‘longer than hoped’
National Air Traffic Services (Nats) have said recovery from today’s outage has taken “longer than hoped”.
In a post on X, the service said: “Recovery from today’s system issue has taken longer than we had hoped.
“Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights.”
It added: “We are truly sorry for the ongoing flight disruption. We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly. Passengers should continue to check with their airline.”
Wheelchair-bound passenger offered no assistance
A woman assisting her wheelchair bound uncle home to Belfast said they’d been offered no assistance by Gatwick Airport.
Charlene Farrell, 39, was scheduled for the 19.00 EasyJet flight to Belfast but has been given no update beyond an updated time of 01.05 tomorrow.
She told The Telegraph: “He’s only just out of hospital so it’s awkward, not great.
“It’s inconvenient, he’s in a wheelchair and would usually be in bed at this time. We have not had very much information because our flight is not cancelled, it just says keep checking.
“I don’t think there’s much they can do. We need airport assistance but they just said stay here before security just in case you have to come back. There’s been nothing [for him], but surely they have to do something? And we’ve heard nothing about compensation.
“You have to stay positive but it’s not great. He’s stiff and sore, he’s tired.”
Gatwick pubs packed with delayed passengers
Gatwick’s South terminal Wetherspoons pub is packed with travellers consoling themselves over a pint. The neighbouring Giraffe Restaurant has a queue outside.
Catrina Sutton, 68, has had two flights returning home to Dublin cancelled at 18.20 and 21.25.
She said a fellow punter had been in a plane for Greece, and was on the tarmac for four hours before finally being sent back through customs without the offer of food or a hotel.
Ms Sutton told The Telegraph: “No one’s telling me anything. Ryanair just goes straight to voicemail, it’s scandalous.
“I’m consoling myself by having a pint, what can you do? The really bad thing about this, the really big annoyance – they will compensate you but you have to organise a hotel, organise a taxi, and keep receipts, but when you go to put them in you only get half back, no apology, no nothing, just shut up and put up with it.”
She added: “There’s two Ryanair girls at bag drop but they haven’t a clue, I rang my husband and he told me everything, rebooked my flight – there was no help from anybody here.
“Where am I going to get a hotel? Here’s going to be packed. This is the s--- people have to put up with, it’s scandalous.”
Night flight restrictions lifted to clear backlog
Flights from the major London airports will be allowed to take off and land all night long to help clear the backlog, The Telegraph understands.
A government source confirmed that usual restrictions on night-time flights at Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted has been lifted after the Nats meltdown.
Normally, flights at Heathrow and Stansted all but cease after 11.30pm, while Gatwick has a tight quota for the noisiest aeroplanes during the hours of darkness.
Lifting the curfew is a sign of how seriously the government is taking the prospect of tens of thousands of people being stranded at British airports.
Transport Secretary: ‘Lessons will be learned’ from air traffic chaos
The Transport Secretary has thanked workers involved in solving the air traffic control outage – but has said “lessons will be learned” from the chaos.
In a post on X, the MP for Swindon South said: “Pleased Nats have fixed the issue, and huge thanks to those working to get people moving.
“It will take time to fully resume flights, so continue to check with airlines. I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”
London airports will not accept arrivals until 11pm
Major London airports will not start accepting new arrivals until at least 11pm.
Eurocontrol, which runs European air traffic control services, issued an update to controllers saying that Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Stansted will not be available for arriving flights until late tonight.
This raises the prospect of tens of thousands of passengers being stranded overnight at airports.
All other UK airports will be operating at a reduced rate until 1am because of the Nats outage, the air traffic control organisation added.
summary: An air traffic control technical failure at Nats caused widespread flight cancellations and disruptions across British airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick. Although the system issue has been resolved and is recovering, the outage left thousands of passengers stranded and prompted the government to temporarily lift night-flight restrictions to help clear the backlog. Transport officials have acknowledged the severe disruption and stated that lessons will be learned from the incident.
key_points: A data processing equipment failure at the Nats headquarters in Swanwick caused widespread flight groundings and disruptions across the UK.
Arrivals into London Heathrow and Gatwick were halted, with multiple other airports experiencing delays.
Nats confirmed the system issue has been resolved, though recovery has taken longer than hoped.
The government lifted night-time flight restrictions at Heathrow, Gatwick, and Stansted to help clear the massive backlog of flights.
Passengers faced long delays, communication difficulties with airlines, and a lack of airport assistance.

title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
author: Daniela Relph; Sean Coughlan
content:
![Meghan holding onto Harry's arm, while Harry waves his hand](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/977/cpsprodpb/49f9/live/385da4e0-ab5f-11f1-9647-01c7ddc5a2b1.jpg)
- Published
A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.
The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".
But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.
It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.
The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - decides security for royals and public figures and Prince Harry has previously complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK.
The Home Office does not comment on such decision making - and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.
"The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.
In terms of Prince Harry and Meghan being "surprised" by the King's message on Monday - it's understood that reflects the lack of time given to them to respond.
They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.
What was in the King's letter about Harry and Meghan?
The letter, sent on behalf of the King, spelt out the non-working royal status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.
They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.
The letter was sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.
Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.
This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.
It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.
This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.
The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.
This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals.
"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.
It adds: "The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity".
![Graphic showing immediate order of succession of UK royal family, with King Charles on the left, Princes WIlliam and Harry in the centre, and the Princes' children on the right](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/d06c/live/87b4f2f0-ab8c-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
It is expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.
There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.
On security, the letter sent on behalf of the King says: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."
Additional reporting by Harriet Whitehead
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan expressed surprise over a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that they remain non-working royals. A spokesperson for the couple stated they were not given advance notice, though royal sources claim they were shown the letter shortly before public release. The message reaffirms the 2020 Sandringham Agreement, confirming the couple cannot use HRH titles, represent the Royal Family, or treat their engagements as official duties. Meanwhile, a security committee is meeting to review taxpayer-funded protection for the family following their recent relocation back to the UK.
key_points: A letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifies that Prince Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals and private citizens.
The Sussexes' spokesperson stated the couple were surprised by the letter, having received sight of it only about an hour before publication.
The message reiterates the 2020 Sandringham Agreement, ruling out any official representation of the Royal Family or 'half-in and half-out' status.
A security committee, including Home Office representatives, is reviewing taxpayer-funded security arrangements for the family in the UK.
The couple recently moved back to the UK from California and are expected to make public appearances supporting charities this autumn.

title: Israel and US warn UK as it plans sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
author: Live Reporting Edited by Rorey Bosotti; Jamie Whitehead; With Yolande Knell Reporting
content:
As we've been reporting, the West Bank is an area west of the River Jordan which has been occupied by Israel since the 1967 war. Settlements there are illegal under international law.
Israel has built around 160 settlements housing 700,000 people in that time. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
Israel recently opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 new homes in a strategically important part of the West Bank, known as E1.
For decades, Israel had held off on plans to build in this location amid international pressure. The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two.
Settlement expansion has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power in late 2022 - and after the start of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
Settler violence has risen as well, our Middle East correspondent reports. Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026.
![Israeli settlements on outposts pictured on a map from December 2022 to July 2026, which shows more dots on the 2026 graph and thus more settlements](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/8/07685271-e170-4240-bf02-2e51947c766e.png.webp)
summary: Israel and the US have warned the UK over its plans to sanction Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Settlement expansion and violence have increased sharply since late 2022 and the start of the Gaza war, with Israel recently opening tenders for about 1,200 new homes in the strategic E1 area. Settlements are considered illegal under international law, and the proposed E1 development would effectively divide the West Bank in two.
key_points: Israel and the US warned the UK regarding proposed sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Israel has built around 160 settlements housing 700,000 people in the West Bank since the 1967 war, alongside 3.3 million Palestinians.
Israel recently opened tenders for roughly 1,200 new homes in the strategic E1 area, which would divide the West Bank in two.
Settlement expansion and settler violence have increased significantly since late 2022 and the onset of the Gaza war.

title: UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements
author: Paul Adams; Nicholas Watt; Henry Moore
content:
