![Israeli bulldozers near a new settlement in the West Bank](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/270b/live/676c01e0-ab24-11f1-993d-a17289144c06.jpg)
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to announce the measures on Tuesday
- Published
The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.
Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.
The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.
Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.
One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different.
"It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."
BBC News has not seen the full details of the measures.
But Labour MPs who have been briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement, according to a number of MPs present.
The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.
Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.
An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US - which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals - has not commented.
Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty - who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister - told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.
He said: "At the moment, we can sanction where there is evidence of it being linked to settler violence, but not, for example, in relation to a contractor working on the settlements. We need to expand our sanctions powers."
While ministers are said to recognise that banning a relatively small quantity of mostly agricultural products is a largely symbolic gesture, the government is expected to frame this announcement as a major reset in Britain's wider policy on Israel.
The expected announcement by the UK government comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.
Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.
![Map showing Israeli settlements and built-up Palestinian areas in the West Bank around Jerusalem â highlighting the E1 settlement in red. Other Israeli settlements are marked in blue and Palestinian areas in light purple. The municipal boundary of Jerusalem is outlined in red. An inset map shows the regionâs location within Israel and Jordan.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/b624/live/b0d42550-a625-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
Speaking in his first address to Parliament as foreign secretary last week, Miliband said those plans were "illegal under international law", and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's announcement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.
Tuesday's expected intervention will come almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.
The government believes the prospect of a two-state solution is being jeopardised by the rapid expansion of settlements.
The proposal for an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital, to exist alongside Israel has received international backing over several decades.
It proposes an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital. It would exist alongside Israel.
Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.
The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.
Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
- ![Three Israeli settlers stand outside houses after the reopening of a settlement at Ganim in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 13 August. One is a man armed with a rifle. The image has a blue border with the BBC Verify logo in the the top left corner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/c529/live/3bc5a6a0-9d8b-11f1-adf5-2dc21c9cc109.jpg)
  - Published29 July
 ![Screengrabs from a video showing a teenage Israeli settler using a stick to hit a metal gate and fence during an attack on a Palestinian home in the village of al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank (11 July 2026)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1a9c/live/a9fea910-8aa2-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- ![Palestinian kids walk to school. They are wearing blue school uniforms.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1ded/live/26dbafb0-aaff-11f1-a2a8-b5ca0233056a.jpg)
summary: The UK government is expected to announce new trade restrictions targeting goods and services from Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will outline the measures in the Commons as part of a comprehensive reset of British policy on Israel. The move follows Israel's controversial plans to build settlement homes in the E1 area, which officials warn threatens the viability of a two-state solution.
key_points: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to announce new trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The measures are part of a broader reset of the UK's Israel-Palestine policy following recent settlement expansions.
Israeli plans to build homes in the E1 area have drawn widespread international condemnation and warnings from UK leaders.
The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate against any new measures introduced by the UK.

title: Police used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrest
author: Rajeev Syal; Steven Morris; Ben Quinn
content:
Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.
After police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers in Hampshire were pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”.
Activists wearing balaclavas clashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday evening after a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage.
Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest.
Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours.
![Daniel Thomas speaks, looking animated and with one hand raised, as Zia Yusuf looks on.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ead47d9ce15f9093219bbf3b078304aaa0d08a1b/0_0_2506_1582/master/2506.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.”
Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said.
About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours.
The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline.
![A pile of orange lifejackets by the road at Eastney Ferry Landing. Two police officers stand by.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/46538317a8764aca3c9da7bf099862bc50dd137c/0_0_5152_3440/master/5152.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
An estimated 200 protesters gathered and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order.
Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.”
Speaking to MPs and peers at a closed-door meeting on Monday, the prime minister Andy Burnham said Labour’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”.
Burnham is understood to have told the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) that Britain would never accept any form of racism in its communities and stood for a sense of fairness and justice.
“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the prime minister said.
“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.
“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”
Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth.
Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs.
The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?”
![Sarah Jones making a statement to MPs in the House of Commons. She has long blond hair with a fringe and wears thick-framed black glasses.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/41e74201fc31829e9f278f4afd72dd18f0ba8df7/0_0_3750_2120/master/3750.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Jones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder.
In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, that the Patriot Platform group he led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas.
Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.”
Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said.
Police could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said.
Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment.
Ministers have been criticised for failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.
“We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”
The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants.
Kent police defended the force’s action after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”.
Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows.
summary: Police in Portsmouth used batons and synthetic pepper spray to repel masked demonstrators during unrest linked to the arrival of asylum seekers by boat. Officers were injured and pelted with bricks after approximately 200 protesters gathered to block migrants from leaving the port. The protests followed similar weekend disruptions in Dover, prompting questions from MPs regarding police intelligence and preparedness.
key_points: Police used batons and Pava spray against hundreds of masked protesters in Portsmouth on Sunday.
The demonstrations were organised following the arrival of a dinghy carrying asylum seekers to Hampshire.
Far-right agitator Daniel Thomas claimed responsibility for arranging the protests, which also followed disruption in Dover.
Lawmakers questioned why police appeared to be caught off guard by the coordinated weekend unrest.
Authorities are investigating potential assaults and criminal damage, and officials are considering a potential balaclava ban for future demonstrations.

title: Breaking: Ministers to review LGR decisions
author: Kirsty Weakley
content:
The government will review local government reorganisation decisions after getting updated legal advice.
Communities secretary Angela Rayner is due to make an announcement today in Parliament following “updated and privileged” legal advice.
Decisions on Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn and the other 14 areas are being paused and reviewed.
Decisions for 20 two-tier areas were made in two waves earlier this year. The government has not made decisions in Cambridgeshire & Peterborough and West Sussex.
Ms Rayner is expected to say: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new secretary of state I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay.
“The prime minister told the House last week, he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his Communities Secretary to ‘do that’.
“[..] In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law. And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations.
“[..] I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas, and I am very grateful for it.”
Several councils had launched legal challenges. Essex CC revealed in June that the letter from the Government Legal Department showed ministers and gone against officials’ advice.
Reorganisation in Surrey will not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities – East and West Surrey – will go live in April 2027.
summary: Communities secretary Angela Rayner is set to announce a review of local government reorganisation decisions following updated legal advice. Decisions regarding Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk, and Suffolk have been withdrawn, while 14 other areas are paused and reviewed. Surrey's reorganisation into two unitary authorities remains unaffected and is scheduled for April 2027.
key_points: Communities secretary Angela Rayner will announce a review of local government reorganisation decisions in Parliament.
Decisions for Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk, and Suffolk have been withdrawn.
Fourteen other areas are being paused and reviewed.
Surrey's reorganisation is unaffected and will proceed to go live in April 2027.

title: Police seek to identify protesters behind Portsmouth anti-migrant disorder
author: Henry Moore
content:
![Police officers stand in line in riot gear at scene of Portsmouth protest](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/dbc9/live/51c266c0-aaea-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear at the protest
- Published
Police are seeking to identify protesters after several officers were injured and vehicles damaged in Portsmouth at a demonstration sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy.
Policing Minister Sarah Jones told the House of Commons the disorder on Sunday night was "intimidating and thuggish" and warned "those who cross into illegality" would "face the full force of the law".
The protests followed a large group of masked men holding a demonstration over small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing major disruption.
Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had "serious questions to answer" over the decision to bring the migrants, who had crossed the English Channel from France, to shore in the area.
Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".
Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.
Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.
In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.
It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.
"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."
Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."
Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.
The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".
Watch: Anti-migrant protesters block roads in Portsmouth
Footage shared online appeared to show protesters following the convoy of coaches along a motorway after it had left.
Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent.
In a statement to the House of Commons on Monday, the policing minister said: "Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy and it must be defended But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference â and there can be no excuse for threatening behavior or serious disruption."
Sarah Jones added: "Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated and those who cross the line from peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law."
Responding, shadow home secretary Chris Philp condemned the violence in Portsmouth but added: "This should also be a wake-up call for the government because it's not just those protesters in Dover and Portsmouth who feel so angry about large-scale illegal immigration.
"It is millions and millions of people up and down this country who feel angry as well."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country is on the edge of "serious civil disturbance" and called on protests to remain peaceful.
In a video posted to social media, he said: "Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution."
Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, who represents Gosport near Portsmouth, accused the Home Office of failing to provide local officials with details of Sunday's protest.
"As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension," she said.
The Labour MP for Portsmouth North, Amanda Martin, said the "emergence" of the route across the Channel taken in Sunday's crossing was "deeply worrying for my city".
Some 625 migrants on eight boats were brought to shore at Dover and Portsmouth on Sunday, according to Home Office figures.
A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September - which is 43% lower than the same period the previous year.
UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012.
This weekend's disruption comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.
But while the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".
In August, a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.
It is thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.
  - Published4 days ago
 ![A group of migrants on a dingy off the coast of Gravelines, in a grab from the BBC video.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/2bb1/live/cf1e6580-a764-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
summary: Police are seeking to identify protesters after a demonstration in Portsmouth involving around 200 people turned violent following the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy. Several officers sustained minor injuries, and police vehicles were damaged during the confrontation near the ferry port. Authorities and government ministers condemned the violence, warning that those engaging in illegal behavior will face the full force of the law.
key_points: Around 200 protesters confronted riot police in Portsmouth after 120 migrants arrived on a single dinghy.
A handful of police officers were treated for minor injuries, and police vehicles were damaged during the disorder.
No arrests were made initially, but police have launched an investigation to identify the offenders.
Portsmouth City Council criticized the Home Office for causing needless disruption by bringing the migrants to the area without local details.
Coaches carrying the migrants eventually left for processing outside of Hampshire.

title: Healey fails to rule out tax rises as Budget headroom ‘shrinks by £19bn’
author: Chris Price; Emma Taggart; Dominic Penna
content:
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501518550_17887854771090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqL9Aj_pOhAZuj7YG39CNoPFtTxElrmZDHbulh00hNrkY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501518550_17887854771090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqL9Aj_pOhAZuj7YG39CNoPFtTxElrmZDHbulh00hNrkY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
John Healey has failed to rule out Budget tax rises as economists warned his breathing space to balance Britain’s books has shrunk by £19bn.
In his first major speech as Chancellor on Monday, Mr Healey said he would be “honest” with the country about the need to control public spending.
However, he refused to answer questions on whether he would raise taxes next month, warning it would “fuel more speculation”.
It came as new analysis from the Resolution Foundation found that unfunded spending commitments and the fallout from the Iran war had significantly reduced his financial buffer to meet the Government’s fiscal rules.
The Labour-linked think tank said Mr Healey’s headroom to balance the books would fall from £24bn to just £5bn because of a combination of factors.
Those include the impact of higher borrowing costs, filling a £1.7bn black hole in the Government’s defence plans, handing teachers an above-inflation pay rise and funding Andy Burnham’s commitment to end rough sleeping by Christmas.
The yield on 10-year UK gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose to its highest level since 2007 last week.
Although it has fallen back since, the 10-year yield rose from 5.13pc to as high as 5.17pc on Monday, as traders responded to renewed strikes between the US and Iran.
Mr Healey insisted that “fiscal discipline” remained his “first priority”, adding: “It underwrites every promise this Government makes.”
He also suggested he would use the Budget on Oct 28 to repair the public finances: “The Prime Minister and I are in lockstep in our commitment to meeting the fiscal rules at the upcoming Budget, to balancing the books with a buffer to protect against uncertainty.”
However, Mr Healey repeatedly declined to comment on the prospect of tax rises. He said: “You were trying to take me on to questions of tax, questions that are part of anticipating the Budget I will deliver on October 28.
“And I say to you, ‘Look, if I respond to speculation now, that will only fuel more speculation.’”
The Chancellor said in his speech in Coventry that he wanted to tell an “optimistic story” about Britain and its growth prospects.
However, this pledge was immediately overshadowed by Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) 4,000 job cuts, which were confirmed by the carmaker while Mr Healey was speaking.
Sophie Hale, at the Resolution Foundation, said “positive vibes can’t hide the painful policy trade-offs facing the Chancellor”.
She said: “While the outlook remains uncertain, the economic fallout from war in the Middle East, higher borrowing costs and unfunded policy commitments could mean that most of the £24bn in headroom against the fiscal rules from March has been wiped out.
“This means measures are likely to be needed at the Budget to repair vital fiscal buffers and will bring to a head tough trade-offs on how much the Chancellor can afford to tax and spend.”
Mr Healey referred to former prime ministers Lord Cameron of Chipping Norton, Boris Johnson and Liz Truss as he sought to blame the Conservatives for the challenges facing the economy.
He claimed Britain had been paying a “[Liz] Truss penalty” to borrow since the former Tory leader’s mini-Budget in 2022.
This caused a sharp increase in borrowing costs at the time as bond market vigilantes baulked at Ms Truss’s unfunded tax cuts.
Mr Healey is now facing a similar uptick in borrowing costs.
He pledged to address the “scar of youth unemployment” and to double the number of unicorn companies in the UK – tech start-ups with a valuation of more than £1bn.
However, Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Mr Healey “sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves”.
He said: “Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.
“Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises, failed to set out a serious plan to reform welfare and failed to commit to funding defence properly – the very issue he resigned over as defence secretary.”
Reform UK also accused the Chancellor of setting out a “dire and dreary” plan for the British economy in the wake of JLR’s job cuts, which it blamed on competition from low-cost Chinese rivals and the shift to electric vehicles.
summary: Chancellor John Healey has declined to rule out tax rises in the upcoming October Budget after economists warned that his financial breathing space has shrunk by £19bn. Analysis from the Resolution Foundation indicates that his fiscal headroom has fallen from £24bn to £5bn due to higher borrowing costs, unfunded spending commitments, and fallout from the conflict involving Iran. During his first major speech, Mr Healey emphasized fiscal discipline while Jaguar Land Rover simultaneously announced 4,000 job cuts.
key_points: John Healey refused to answer questions regarding potential tax rises in the October 28 Budget, stating that responding would fuel more speculation.
The Resolution Foundation reported that the Chancellor's budget headroom has shrunk from £24bn to £5bn.
Shrinking fiscal space is attributed to higher borrowing costs, unfunded policy commitments, and the economic impact of the Iran war.
Jaguar Land Rover confirmed 4,000 job cuts while Mr Healey was delivering his speech in Coventry.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith criticized Mr Healey for failing to rule out tax rises and address welfare and defence funding.

title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
author: Mitchell Labiak; Henry Jones
content:
![A photo taken in Halewood in 2025 shows rows of Range Rovers on the tarmac at a JLR factory outside on a sunny day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/c067/live/5d770b70-aaa3-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
- Published
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.
The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.
JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.
Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.
"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.
JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.
The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save Â£1.7bn over the next two years.
The carmaker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.
In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.
Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.
"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.
He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party in terms of producing their first electric car which is just about to go into production".
Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".
Chief Treasury Secretary Emma Reynolds told the BBC's Today programme: "My thoughts are with the workforce.
"The business secretary is working closely both with the leadership of the company but also with the relevant trade unions," she added.
At the weekend, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would be meeting JLR bosses this week to "mitigate any job losses", but he ruled out a bailout for the company.
'Death by a thousand cuts'
Some have blamed the issues facing JLR and the wider UK car industry on the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which was introduced by the previous Conservative government and kept under Labour.
It requires that all new car and van sales in the UK must be zero emission vehicles by 2035, but it does not apply to cars sold overseas, which is where JLR makes most of its revenue.
Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the ZEV mandate and higher energy costs were "crippling the British automotive industry", pledging to scrap the mandate.
At the weekend, the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, said the ZEV mandate was "unsustainable" and that the UK car industry had suffered from "years of underinvestment" under both Labour and the Conservatives.
"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said over the weekend.
The UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association has defended the ZEV mandate, previously calling it "crucial for attracting finance into this infrastructure as it sets out a clear, predictable pathway for the growth of the electric vehicle market".
summary: Jaguar Land Rover plans to cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years, primarily affecting its UK head office, in an effort to save £1.7bn. The carmaker is struggling with US tariffs, intense Chinese competition, the transition to electric vehicles, and the lingering impacts of a cyber-attack last year. While JLR hopes to achieve these reductions through voluntary redundancy, compulsory redundancies remain possible if necessary.
key_points: JLR is cutting 4,000 jobs over the next two years, mostly affecting its UK head office.
The cuts aim to save £1.7bn in response to Chinese competition, US tariffs, and EV transition costs.
A cyber-attack last year caused production to shut down for over a month, worsening long-term issues.
The company is primarily targeting voluntary redundancies with a window open until 4 October.
Government officials and union leaders have responded, with the Business Secretary ruling out a bailout.

title: Chancellor John Healey to say UK economy 'turning a corner' despite debt concerns
author: Faisal Islam; Ella Kipling
content:
![An image of John Healey from the waist up. He is walking and wearing a dark suit with a white shirt and red patterned tie. He is carrying a red folder. The background is blurred by you can see that he is outside from the outline of bushes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/a295/live/6f3c1770-aa2f-11f1-bdbb-8bb5df16290b.jpg)
- Published
The chancellor is set to give an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of next month's Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.
In a speech on Monday, John Healey will talk of a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner, but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".
He will also unveil a Â£150m fund for companies in the north of England.
Healey is facing pressures ahead of his first Budget, including concerns about government borrowing costs and inflationary impacts of the Iran war.
The Conservatives said Healey's plans would "do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses".
The Â£150m fund is part of a wider plan to generate more economic growth around the UK.
Healey will detail plans to use public investment to "unlock private investment, to support our innovation economy, and to create the new jobs their areas need".
The fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide investments of between Â£5m and Â£15m to the "most innovative and fast-growing firms".
It is expected to back university spin-outs and other "ambitious businesses" across the north.
Describing a country "turning the corner", the chancellor is expected to say: "The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places.
"The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places."
Recent ructions in government debt markets have made constrained public finances worse, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs, and the need to fund higher defence spending.
As he prepares to deliver his Budget on 28 October, the chancellor says he is as committed to balancing the books as his predecessor.
But the tone matters, and to get high saving consumers spending, and cautious businesses investing, Downing Street wants to point to sunnier times ahead for now, more than the prospect of tough Budgetary medicine.
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Economic growth in every postcode sounds great and is something we would all love. I think it'll actually be much harder to achieve in practice."
She said it would be easier to see how the government could make stronger second and third cities than to see "how it would drive growth in literally every postcode".
During his first Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham faced scrutiny over rising UK borrowing costs.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged him to say how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high.
Burnham blamed the previous Tory administration, and said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility".
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Healey's plan would do "little to comfort hard-working families and businesses across the country who are worried about more tax rises or the fact that government borrowing rates are near a 28-year high".
He added: "We are facing serious threats from Russia and Iran on our doorstep, as well as threats to the Falkland Islands.
"Yet the chancellor, the man who resigned over defence spending, seemingly does not want to mention our armed forces or how we will reach 3% of GDP on defence."
Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "Re-announcing Â£150m across the entire north of England will barely shift the dial on growth."
Robert Jenrick, Reform UK's economic spokesman, said: "Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy."
summary: Ahead of his upcoming Budget, Chancellor John Healey will deliver an upbeat speech arguing that the UK economy is turning a corner and demonstrating resilience. He plans to unveil a £150m fund directed at innovative and fast-growing firms in the north of England to stimulate regional growth. However, the chancellor faces significant pressure regarding rising government borrowing costs, constrained public finances, and criticism from political opponents.
key_points: Chancellor John Healey is set to state that the UK economy is resilient, optimistic, and turning a corner.
A new £150m fund from the British Business Bank will provide investments between £5m and £15m for innovative firms in the north of England.
The Treasury is currently managing pressures from rising government borrowing costs, public finance constraints, and higher defense spending needs ahead of the October 28 Budget.
Conservative critics and other political opponents argue that Healey's plans and funding announcements do enough to address increasing debt and economic worries.

title: Hundreds of far-right protesters descend on Portsmouth after small boat arrival
author: Diane Taylor; Charlie Moloney
content:
Hundreds of far-right activists have descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted heading towards the Portsmouth coast. It sparked a major response with a helicopter, an aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. It is thought to be the first time such a large boat containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a large group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.
The boat’s occupants have been brought to shore in the maritime city and the Home Office’s plan is to take them to Manston, outside Ramsgate in Kent, where small boat arrivals are processed.
Videos circulating on social media show large groups of protesters close to where coaches of newly arrived asylum seekers are parked. The protesters in Portsmouth were blocking the coaches carrying asylum seekers from leaving.
Hampshire police urged people to avoid the area, and said a dispersal order was in place.
The government has condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”
![Boats carrying migrants, one of them at the port with passengers disembarking](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a89277134f48ff84d91d8843437283df13891b43/0_0_7113_4878/master/7113.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo – a former bodyguard of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest.
Thomas has recently established Patriot Platform which blocked part of port of Dover on Saturday. He previously launched Operation Overlord which planned to send far-right activists to France to “stop the boats”. He and his supporters filmed themselves slashing abandoned dinghies on a French beach. The french authorities subsequently banned him from France.
Small boat crossings so far this year have reduced by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats such as the one that arrived on Sunday evening from different parts of the coast, much further from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.
Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI boats on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore in Dover.
A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: “In response to a report on 6 September of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams.
“Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire police and south central ambulance service were also sent.”
Stand Up To Racism posted on X: “another attempt by fascist Danny Tommo to whip up pogroms against refugees.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.
“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.
“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”
summary: Hundreds of far-right protesters gathered in Portsmouth to block coaches carrying 140 asylum seekers who arrived on a small boat. The government condemned the demonstrators' intimidating behaviour, while Hampshire police issued a dispersal order and urged people to avoid the area. The asylum seekers were brought ashore to be processed and transferred to Manston in Kent.
key_points: A small boat carrying 140 asylum seekers was intercepted heading toward Portsmouth.
Far-right protesters attempted to block coaches carrying the newly arrived asylum seekers from leaving.
Hampshire police put a dispersal order in place and urged the public to avoid the area.
The government strongly condemned the protesters' intimidating and thuggish behaviour.
The asylum seekers were scheduled to be taken to Manston in Kent for processing.

title: Protesters clash with police after mega-dinghy arrives in Portsmouth
author: Charles Hymas; Keith Perry
content:
![Around 500 protesters are believed to have joined the demonstration in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501455854_17887280834360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqf1s-wQoVbeXjDqs54TYD_tkM9MM8VM3G1BxlGUO4L8Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Around 500 protesters are believed to have joined the demonstration in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501455854_17887280834360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqf1s-wQoVbeXjDqs54TYD_tkM9MM8VM3G1BxlGUO4L8Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Hundreds of protesters have clashed with police in Portsmouth after a mega-dinghy carrying 140 migrants reached the UK from Normandy.
Around 500 demonstrators are believed to have joined a protest in the area on Sunday night, with some dressed in all black – similar to those who joined an anti-illegal migrant protest which blocked the Port of Dover on Saturday.
The large boat of migrants – believed to be the longest-ever Channel crossing by people-smugglers – was intercepted in the Solent between the Isle of Wight and Portsmouth earlier on Sunday.
![Hundreds stage protest in Portsmouth after migrant boat arrives](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501449769_17887264405260_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRXuknvhZsb7bf88i7wdmgjZw8X5mnmN5SzvuuWR43vQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![Police officers with riot shields form a line at the protest in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501456427_17887288364450_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWZZ9520Qrn8RyVs0byqFf0R8YSybYNWDTYrGStsI8ko.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Demonstrators blocked the only access road to the marina in Eastney, where it is thought the migrants are being held.
Police used riot shields and pepper spray to force the crowds back, but the line broke through the weight of numbers. Protesters then made their way inside the marina compound.
Earlier, George Madgwick, the leader of Reform UK in Hampshire, wrote in a post on X that “over 100 migrant men” had arrived on the Portsmouth shore.
The French coastguard said it had detected the mega-dinghy, which was shadowed by a number of rescue boats in case it got into difficulties. Authorities estimated that up to 140 people were on board the vessel, 90 short of the record 230 who crossed on a similar boat last month.
At least 30 people were thrown off the boat into the sea because it was so overcrowded, according to French officials.
![Migrants are brought ashore from a lifeboat in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501452442_17887271916470_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
It is understood that the boat’s occupants will be transferred to a facility in Manston, Kent, for processing, as is routine for small-boat arrivals in the area.
They were taken to shore in Portsmouth in two RNLI lifeboats after being rescued from a single dinghy south of the Isle of Wight in the English Channel.
Crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth on the Isle of Wight responded to reports of a small boat heading towards Hampshire.
One woman at the protest on Sunday, who did not want to give her name, said: “We want to stop them all coming in.
“We don’t need any more people in Hampshire.”
Another man, who gave his name as Matt, said: “People aren’t taking too kindly to it.”
![Hundreds of protesters descended on Portsmouth after a boat thought to be carrying asylum seekers sparked a major emergency response](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501452355_17887272085671_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo – an associate of Right-wing activist Tommy Robinson – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest.
Thomas could be seen standing in the sea at the Eastney shingle beach, alongside a small group of other protesters, with police officers looking on.
“Roads are all blocked, they are never going to be able to leave here,” Thomas said.
He added: “It was only yesterday (at the protests in Dover) when we warned them that we will not accept this any more, and that this is no longer an option to tell us that the boat numbers are down.
“This isn’t about the numbers being down… this is about understanding that this has to come to an end now.”
The mega-dinghy – launched from a beach east of Cherbourg in the Baie de la Seine – reflects a change in tactics used by people-smugglers, who have started loading more migrants on to fewer and larger vessels, partly because of the success of law enforcement in disrupting boat and equipment supply chains.
As well as turning to larger boats, smuggling gangs have started launching taxi boats further west to avoid increased numbers of police on the beaches and to evade interception on the water by a new seaborne police unit.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said: “This week Andy Burnham struck an agreement for 45 more officers on French beaches.
“Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. This is a joke. Only Reform will send the boats back.”
Joe Robertson, the Conservative MP for Isle of Wight East, posted: “Extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west.
“We don’t know if this migrant boat was headed for the Isle of Wight but I’ll be contacting the Home Office first thing. We need to know exactly what happened and if new routes are being used for mega-dinghies by people smugglers.”
A Hampshire Police spokesman said: “This evening, we have been working alongside and assisting our partners from Border Force, Maritime & Coastguard Agency and Portsmouth city council at Eastney Marina following the arrival of a boat crossing the Channel.
“We have officers in the area to ensure the prevention of any disorder. We ask that people please avoid the area. A dispersal order is in place until tomorrow evening (Monday, Sept 7). Anyone who refuses to comply with the direction to leave the area is liable for arrest.
“We can also confirm that Border Force has advised us that individuals will be transported outside of Hampshire for processing in the normal way after they have been safely disembarked.”
A Home Office spokesman said: “This Government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.
“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.
“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”
summary: Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in Portsmouth after a mega-dinghy carrying around 140 migrants arrived from Normandy, having been intercepted in the Solent. Demonstrators blocked access roads to the marina where the migrants were held, with crowds eventually breaking through police lines using weight of numbers. The incident highlights a shifting tactic by people-smugglers toward larger vessels launched further west.
key_points: Around 500 protesters demonstrated in Portsmouth on Sunday night following the arrival of a mega-dinghy carrying approximately 140 migrants.
Police used riot shields and pepper spray to hold back the crowds, but protesters broke through the line and entered the marina compound.
French officials reported that about 30 people were thrown off the overcrowded boat into the sea during the journey from Normandy.
Smugglers are shifting tactics toward larger vessels and launching from locations further west to evade law enforcement and police units.
The migrants are scheduled to be transferred to a facility in Manston, Kent, for routine processing.

title: Baby girl dies on camping trip in Staffordshire
author: Will Bolton
content:
![Staffordshire Police cordoned off a fishing lake close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933971_17887077765620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BquOv8qdqAtg5F-Rc30df4df4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Staffordshire Police cordoned off a fishing lake close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933971_17887077765620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BquOv8qdqAtg5F-Rc30df4df4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A three-month-old girl has died during a family camping trip in Staffordshire.
Police said their investigation into the “unexplained” death was in its early stages, describing it as an “isolated incident”.
Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane, near the village of Cheslyn Hay, at 8.45am on Saturday after a report of a child in cardiac arrest.
An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.
Officers cordoned off a fishing lake at the nature reserve, close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal. Drone images from the scene showed at least four tents and camping chairs next to each other, close to fishing platforms.
Det Insp Katie Gregory said: “While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident. The death is being treated as unexplained at this time.”
![Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, on Saturday morning](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933924_17887078021510_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqZTGkdds8SWJRzcZ4ZecXrf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The area is not an official camping site, but locals said teenagers often fished in two lakes there and camped overnight. A nearby nature trail is also popular with dog walkers and runners.
Robert Duncan, the South Staffordshire council district councillor for Cheslyn Hay, said: “I know how deeply upsetting news like this is for our community.
“It’s important that we allow the emergency services the space they need to complete their work with dignity and care.
“As soon as the full and confirmed details are formally shared with me, I will provide a further update to residents. Until then, please avoid speculation and allow the family and responders the privacy and respect they deserve.”
People living in Cheslyn Hay, which is three miles south of Cannock and has a population of about 7,000, left a floral tribute to the girl near to the scene.
Rev Samantha Hagerman, the superintendent of Cannock Chase Methodist Circuit, said: “Our thoughts and prayers are with family, friends and emergency services affected by the incident near Cheslyn Hay.”
summary: A three-month-old girl has died during a family camping trip at a nature reserve in Staffordshire. Emergency services responded to a report of a child in cardiac arrest, but she was pronounced dead at the scene. Staffordshire Police are currently treating the death as unexplained and described it as an isolated incident.
key_points: A three-month-old girl died during a family camping trip in Staffordshire.
Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane on Saturday morning.
Police and paramedics responded to a report of a child in cardiac arrest, but she was pronounced dead shortly after.
Authorities are treating the death as unexplained while the investigation remains in its early stages.

title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
author: Simon Jones; AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul
content:
![Migrants on an inflatable dinghy leaving the coast of northern France at Gravelines, near Calais](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5295/live/fa800b90-aa05-11f1-afb5-a367f96884d3.jpg)
Migrants on an inflatable dinghy near Calais in a separate attempt on Sunday
- Published
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.
The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.
It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.
In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.
The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.
It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.
French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.
Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy.
A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.
"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."
They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."
In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.
While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".
It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.
Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.
Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.
  - Published3 days ago
 ![A group of migrants on a dingy off the coast of Gravelines, in a grab from the BBC video.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/2bb1/live/cf1e6580-a764-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- ![Large numbers of bright orange lifejackets are seen in plastic bags inside a warehouse](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/3113/live/6ce86220-9815-11f1-a7ea-19f04b81e9a0.png)
  - Published4 days ago
 ![A young person wearing a baseball cap and a backpack and carrying a suitcase stands in the middle of the image. To the left of the image a passport with a boarding card is held up. To the right of the image is a migrant family of a man, woman and child on a beach, walking. In the top right corner is a partial view of a UK visa document](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a530/live/da608860-cb5a-11f0-a892-01d657345866.png)
summary: Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy that launched from the Normandy coast were rescued in UK waters by RNLI boats. The unusual 170-mile journey comes amid increasing reports of smugglers using larger vessels to avoid detection following stricter policing near Calais. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron recently met to discuss scaling up efforts against small boat crossings.
key_points: About 140 migrants aboard a single inflatable dinghy were rescued by two RNLI boats after requesting help in UK waters.
The vessel launched from the Normandy coast, an unusual departure point that made the crossing significantly longer at 170 miles.
Smugglers are increasingly loading more people onto larger vessels, or 'mega dinghies', to avoid detection following robust policing in the Calais area.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron recently met to discuss scaling up joint efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

title: Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform broke law
author: Pippa Crerar
content:
Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.
The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked if he could categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can. Never happened.”
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.
“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”
The questions overshadowed the start of Reform’s party conference in Birmingham, where numerous hecklers were removed from the hall during Farage’s keynote speech.
Footage has emerged online of one of the women being dragged by her hair, with a man also appearing to hit female protesters with his crutch.
When questioned about the incident by Jon Sopel on Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme, Robert Jenrick said: “Oh, boohoo. We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame.
“I mean, come on, get a life,” Reform’s treasury spokesperson added.
West Midlands police said they were aware of the footage, adding: “We would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September.”
After an official complaint that Farage and his aides had broken political funding laws, the Metropolitan police said it was assessing the evidence, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected. They all deny wrongdoing.
Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.
Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as about his £5m gift from a crypto billionaire shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.
![Robert Jenrick speaks on stage during the party’s annual conference on Saturday](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/87fc83af710fca376c8fef43a7ccdc7e1a128925/0_0_5900_3933/master/5900.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.
after newsletter promotion
Jenrick said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.
“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.
“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.
“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”
Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much, they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”
He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has admitted that a row over alleged overseas donations looks bad for his party, though he denies breaking electoral law. The controversy stems from an undercover investigation that captured two senior aides apparently plotting to circumvent funding rules, prompting their suspension and a police assessment of the evidence. Meanwhile, the party's conference in Birmingham was disrupted by protesters, leading to police involvement regarding footage of physical altercations in the hall.
key_points: Nigel Farage denied Reform UK ever accepted foreign money in breach of electoral law, despite admitting the donation row looks bad.
Farage suspended two close aides, Dan Jukes and James Orr, after they were filmed apparently plotting to bypass laws on foreign donations.
The Metropolitan police are assessing evidence after an official complaint was made regarding political funding laws.
Reform conference speeches faced disruptions from protesters, with police reviewing online footage of physical altercations in the hall.

title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
author: Craig Buchan
content:
Masked men chanting "stop the boats" at Port of Dover
- Published
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.
Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.
Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.
Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".
Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".
"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.
"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."
The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".
"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.
Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".
Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".
Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.
![Dozens of men dressed in black and wearing face coverings, being escorted down a dual carriageway in Dover by uniformed police officers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8b90/live/51566c00-a91d-11f1-a3dc-e78e2c02425d.jpg)
Hundreds of masked men blocked roads and prevented access to the Port of Dover
Reynolds, speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, condemned the protest.
"Peaceful protest is an essential part of British life but that is not what we saw there with that kind of intimidatory behaviour," the business secretary said.
"I feel sorry for the people around Dover and the people disrupted by that."
Police have not yet commented on who was behind the demonstration, which lasted from 07:00 BST to about 11:30.
Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network arranged it, saying the group began meeting in July and had brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.
Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached on Saturday.
Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.
Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."
He praised protesters for showing "discipline" and said they had "stuck to the plan".
Reynolds said that Robinson and others like him were "not interested in solving genuine problems this country has".
"They want to exploit their online following and take money from the people willing to follow them online, and that's what that agenda is," he said.
"This government is about solving the problems that really make a difference to people's lives."
Great Yarmouth MP and leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, said his party "proudly stands with those peacefully protesting against illegal immigration in Dover".
In a video on X, he said wearing balaclavas was "undesirable" but "perfectly fair for people living in this Orwellian age".
Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads and ground the Port of Dover to a halt for several hours on Saturday. Dover District Council leader Kevin Mills criticized Kent Police for being slow to respond to the well-organised demonstration, though cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds argued officers dealt with it swiftly. Kent Police initially described the event as a spontaneous protest and made no arrests. Meanwhile, anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate attributed the arrangement to the Patriot Platform network.
key_points: Hundreds of masked protesters blocked roads and access to the Port of Dover on Saturday.
Council leader Kevin Mills stated that police were slow to respond and keep networks open.
Cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds condemned the protest's intimidatory behaviour.
Kent Police described the event as a spontaneous protest and made no arrests.
Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network organised the demonstration.

title: Nigel Farage denies wrongdoing over foreign donor talks on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg
author: Live Reporting Edited by Alex Smith
content:
![Laura Kuenssberg interviews Nigel Farage](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/6/cf05bf4c-0a97-494a-b841-82643f9f60f8.jpg.webp)
This week's show has just finished - here's a recap of what we heard:
Nigel Farage
In a pre-recorded interview, the Reform UK leader told Laura Kuenssberg he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK - more on that in our previous post.
He is also asked about a proposed Reform policy that, if the party was in government, would see the threshold before people pay income tax increased to Â£15,000.
Asked how the party would pay for it, Farage says: "We are taking benefits away from foreign nationals and social housing away from foreign nationals and from some Brits we donât think should qualify and we canât afford.â
Jonathan Reynolds
On the Reform foreign donor story, the business secretary says: âWe have rules in this country, about how our democracy works, and everyone has to stick to them.â
Reynolds also condemned a protest by masked 'stop the boats' demonstrators in Dover on Saturday, which blocked traffic from entering and leaving the port for hours.
Andrew Griffith
The newly-appointed shadow chancellor talks about the state of the public finances, saying the government is "signing up to more and more debt to our children".
He says any future government would have to "take difficult decisions" to get the country growing.
We're ending our live coverage. You can watch back the episode in full in the watch & listen tab at the top of the page - and read Laura Kuenssberg's write-up of her Farage interview here.
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage denied wrongdoing in an interview with Laura Kuenssberg regarding discussions about funneled foreign money, stating he was not listening during the conversation. Farage also explained that a proposed income tax threshold increase to £15,000 would be funded by removing benefits and social housing from foreign nationals and certain British citizens. Meanwhile, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds emphasized the importance of following democracy rules and condemned a Dover protest, while Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith discussed public finances and national debt.
key_points: Nigel Farage denied wrongdoing over talks involving potential foreign funding for Reform UK.
Farage proposed raising the income tax threshold to £15,000 by cutting benefits and social housing for foreign nationals and ineligible Brits.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds stated that everyone must adhere to UK democracy rules.
Reynolds condemned a masked 'stop the boats' protest in Dover that blocked port traffic.
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith warned about increasing national debt and the need for difficult economic decisions.

title: Chancellor warns of tough Budget as Iran war puts strain on economy
author: Maryam Zakir-Hussain
content:
The upcoming autumn Budget is expected to be tough, the chancellor has warned, as the US-Iran war continues to damage the economy.
John Healey issued the warning following a leap in government borrowing earlier this week, reflecting concerns among lenders about the inflationary impact of Donald Trump’s war with Iran.
However, Mr Healey also told the Financial Times he would ensure the UK emerges from his first Budget, on 28 October, with a solid “buffer against uncertainty”.
The chancellor told the FT: “What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs.”
He added: “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].”
![Chancellor John Healey warns the autumn Budget will be tough](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/07/aeb88c87603ecee43892dd7897d3d44fY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MjA3NzA2-2.85365880.jpg)
Economists have predicted that the fiscal buffer Rachel Reeves built up in her last Budget, through a combination of tax rises and departmental spending cuts, will be squeezed by the inflationary pressures of ongoing global turmoil.
This could limit Andy Burnham’s ambitions to tackle the cost of living crisis, and spending plans across his wider agenda for government.
Mr Healey declined to tell the newspaper how much fiscal headroom he planned to maintain above his spending plans after the Budget.
A key fiscal rule requires the Treasury to bring the Budget into surplus by the end of the parliament, excluding investment.
He told the newspaper that both he and the prime minister were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules” and added that it would be achieved “with a buffer against the sort of uncertainty that we have talked about”.
![Donald Trump’s war with Iran is putting strain on the UK economy](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/04/20/2026-09-04T193216Z_1523549726_RC2JCNAF4UTJ_RTRMADP_3_USA-TRUMP.JPG)
Mr Healey has come under fire from the Conservatives for not recommitting to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.
When he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer’s defence secretary, he suggested hitting this target was vital to keep the country safe.
He did however tell the FT that the UK would hit its goal of raising defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035, a Nato commitment, but said this would be set out at next year’s spending review.
The chancellor has also announced changes to Treasury rules aimed at helping to speed up regional regeneration across the country.
A major change to the Treasury’s green book, its guide to evaluating the costs and benefits of government projects and programmes, will be to lower something called the “discount rate”.
Reducing this from 3.5 per cent to 3 per cent will make it easier to demonstrate the long-term value of spending public money on building new schools and roads, among other projects.
The announcement comes ahead of a major speech on the economy Mr Healey is due to make on Monday.
